I've watched a lot of couples over the years and there's one thing almost nobody notices they're doing.
You're talking to your spouse through the dog.
You know exactly what I mean. Front door opens. And instead of saying "hey, you're home," you crouch down and you say, in that voice, the one you'd never use on another adult:
"Well look who finally decided to come home. Yes he did. Yes he did."
And he hears it. Course he hears it. It was for him. The dog was just the delivery vehicle.
I've got two doodles, Jasper and Sati, so believe me when I tell you I know the voice.
Here's what I've watched happen in that room, over and over, with people who've been married twenty, thirty years.
It starts out funny. It's a bit. You're being cute. "Somebody's in a MOOD today, isn't he." Everybody laughs, including the person it was aimed at, and nobody has to admit anything happened.
Then it stops being a bit.
"We ate without him again, didn't we." Said to a dog. Not one word of it for the dog.
"Don't worry, buddy, at least YOU'RE happy to see me."
"Ask your mother. Your mother knows everything."
And the wild part is, you'd never say any of those things straight to their face. You've got too much respect, or too much fear, or you're just too tired for what would happen next. But route it through a golden retriever who doesn't understand a syllable of it and suddenly you can say anything.
The dog's not a pet at that point. The dog's a hostage negotiator.
I sat with a woman once who realized, out loud, mid-sentence, that the last time she'd said "I missed you" in that house, she'd said it to a cat. Her husband was six feet away on the couch. She'd said it to the cat, in the cat voice, while looking at the cat.
She stopped talking for a while after that one.
So why do we do it? It's not because we're passive aggressive, or at least that's not the whole thing.
It's because saying it directly costs too much now.
If I say "I feel like you don't want to be here," you can defend yourself, or roll your eyes, or go quiet for two days, and then I've spent all that courage for nothing and I'm worse off than before I opened my mouth.
But if I say it to the dog? Nobody can hold me to it. I was just playing. I can always say I was just playing.
That's the whole system. It's a way to send the message with the return address torn off.
And look, I'm not here to make you feel bad about it. Honestly, some of it's sweet. Some of it's just how a house sounds.
But if you're doing the sad version, if the dog's carrying stuff that's got real weight to it, you should know something.
Every one of those sentences is a reach.
That's all they are. That's all they ever were. Somebody in that house wanting to be seen, and finding the only door left that doesn't cost anything to walk through.
"At least YOU'RE happy to see me" means I don't feel wanted here anymore.
"We ate without him again" means where the hell are you, I'm lonely at my own table.
"Yes he did, yes he finally came home" means you used to come home to me.
You didn't stop reaching. You just started using the dog as a translator, because the direct line got too dangerous somewhere along the way and neither one of you noticed when.
So here's what I'd try tonight, and it's small, it's not some big dramatic thing.
Next time you feel one of those coming, one of the loaded ones, stop. Don't say it to the dog.
Turn to the actual person. And say the flat, unarmored, slightly embarrassing version instead.
"I missed you today."
"I felt kinda forgotten at dinner."
"I don't like how far away we've gotten."
It'll feel awful. Your face will get hot. You'll want to laugh it off or wrap it in a joke, and every part of you is gonna want to grab that dog and use him as cover one more time.
Do it anyway.
Because a marriage doesn't die from fighting. It dies quietly, in a warm house, where two people who love each other say everything true to an animal and nothing true to each other.
The dog's been carrying it long enough.
Say it to them. See less

When you're ready to understand, I mean really understand, relational dynamics and vulnerability, you will hear a different take on boundaries. Boundaries are no different from anything a romantic couple discusses when they hurt each other.
Set a boundary. The other feels abandoned. No opinions about this make them feel better.
A boundary, without gentleness, is probably set in the first place because of feeling relationally disconnected.
So do you want:
1) To take care of yourself and set a boundary?
or
2) Connect
You often cannot have both. See less

A Complicated Father's Love
Growing up with a father who struggled with rage was like living in a house where the weather could change without warning. At 60 pounds to his 300, I was a small child in the shadow of a man whose anger filled every room. 
His yelling and screaming became the soundtrack of my childhood, leaving me with a tremor that would follow me into adulthood, a nervous shake that still surfaces around angry men, a reminder of feeling so small and powerless.
It took me 12 years of counseling to be able to pee next to another man in a public restroom. The feeling inside me was that I could be killed by the person next to me at any time.
It took 16 years to not shake during a movie with anger from men.
It's taken me most of my life to untangle the knots that rage tied into my nervous system. To learn that not every raised voice means danger. 
To understand that I deserved gentleness, even when the world felt anything but gentle.
But there's one memory that refuses to fit neatly into the story I've told myself about my father.
We were sitting in the car when it happened, I can still feel the vinyl seats, the 1977 orange Cadillac, still remember the way the afternoon light cut through the windshield. Three grown men stood in front of our car, and their language was... colorful. 
Profanity flowed from their mouths like water, casual and constant.
Then my dad did something that terrified me in a completely different way. He got out of the car.
All 300 pounds of him marched right up to these three adult strangers and began yelling, not at me this time, but *for* me. He screamed at them about their inappropriate language, about how they were talking in front of a child, about respect and decency. 
His voice, usually a source of fear, became a shield.
I sat frozen in that car, watching my father, this man whose anger had been the monster under my bed, use that same anger to defend something precious: my innocence. He was trying to protect me from a world that could be harsh and crude, even if he didn't always know how to protect me from himself.
I never thanked him.
The contradiction of it still takes my breath away. The same rage that traumatized me was the force that made him stand up to three strangers. 
The same voice that made me shake with fear was raised in my defense.
He would have gladly fought all 3 of them to the death. They might have lost.
Healing from a complicated childhood means holding multiple truths at once. It means acknowledging that the person who hurt you might have also loved you in the only way they knew how. 
It means recognizing that people can be both the storm and the shelter, sometimes in the same moment.
I'm older now, and that shake around angry men has mostly faded. I've learned to separate the past from the present, learned that I'm no longer that 60 pound child. 
But I carry this memory with me, not as an excuse for what was, but as proof that love sometimes wears the strangest costumes.
Maybe that's what I needed to understand: that my father's love was real, even when it was delivered imperfectly. Even when it came wrapped in rage. 
Even when it left marks I'm still learning to heal.
I never thanked him, but maybe understanding is its own kind of gratitude.
Some stories don't have neat endings. Some fathers don't fit into simple categories. Some love is complicated, messy, and painful, and still love, nonetheless.
He's turning to dust now, but he's wrapped in his official Los Angeles Dodgers uniform, his most favorite team and activity of his baseball-filled life. See less

UNTIL I FOUND YOU
My life has hurt so much.
Until I found you.
I'd like to think and feel that my past relationships got me here, and they were just stepping stones, that they were the exact messes I needed to make in my life.
Until I found you.
Some days I feel so optimistic, like it was a brilliant Universe that made me mess up in all the perfect ways, but sometimes, I feel pessimistic, that it was such a struggle to feel so alone in relationship. I felt that way most of my life.
Until I found you.
We're keeping our love so private right now. It makes me so happy. It's just ours. Nobody else gets to have it. I've never had this experience. I always needed to tell everybody about my relationship, because my relationship was not fulfilling enough on its own. I needed the outside world's stamp of approval.
Until I found you.
I was disappointed with my partner choices, even while in them.
Until I found you.
The love bombing, the ease of perfect romance, the in love infatuation. Was perfection. And then the peace and calm and comfort of far deeper love, is a love that I have not experienced before.
Until I found you.
A thought in my day, a difficult moment in my day, a struggle in my day, takes less effort to lift, and was never this easy.
Until I found you.
One day we may encounter a difficult moment, between us, and the tens of thousands of love notes, of voice memos, of positive wishes to conquer the day, will transcend anything that tries to get between us.
Because I found you. See less

You're going to be the last woman I ever kiss.
If that is the end of my story I will be greatly fulfilled.
Because we lasted.
I haven't had it last.
I've never wanted it to last.
That's the truth.
I've changed.
I know what's important.
To me.
And I know what's important to you.
We both want the same thing.
Brilliantly orchestrated failures finally taught us how.
We don't control.
We remain curious.
I already know ahead of schedule that your intention is to understand me.
And because of this I don't have to struggle to be understood.
I hope I can offer you the same.
I trust the look on your face.
I trust you when I can't see your face.
And the one thing I've never had until you.
I trust me entirely to make choices related to us.
Not just me. See less

You've been Googling "signs of a narcissist" again.
Or maybe it's "emotionally unavailable partner" this time.
Or "avoidant attachment."
You're building a case. Collecting evidence. Screenshots of articles that prove how damaged they are.
Here's the trap you can't see:
The moment you need to diagnose your partner is the exact moment you've lost access to the only thing that could save your relationship.
Compassion.
You can't simultaneously build a case against someone AND feel compassion for them.
Your brain won't let you.
So you're stuck in the most brutal paradox of relationships:
The time when you most need to figure out "what's wrong with them" is precisely when you've lost the ability to see their pain underneath the behavior that's killing you.
Meanwhile, they're doing the same thing to you.
Two people, both convinced the other is the problem.
Both searching for the right label to explain why this hurts so much.
Both completely unable to access the tenderness that could actually change everything.
You're not fighting your partner.
You're fighting the same terror that lives in both of you.
The terror of being unseen. Unloved. Left behind.
Every criticism becomes proof you don't matter.
Every withdrawal becomes evidence you're too much.
Every sigh becomes the sound of someone giving up on you.
You diagnose them as narcissistic because you can't say "I'm terrified you don't see me."
They shut down because they can't say "I'm terrified I'm failing you."
The labels feel safer than the truth.
The solution isn't better diagnosis.
It's recognizing you're both trapped in the same pattern.
Both scared of the same thing.
Both desperately trying to protect yourselves from the same wound.
The moment you can look at each other and say "We're both scared and we don't know how to stop hurting each other" — that's when the real work begins.
But first you have to put down the diagnostic manual.
And pick up a mirror.
And send yourself the kind eyes that you wish your partner could easily give you.
Almost every single piece of relationship advice you will find here on social media will give you a clever way to diagnose what's wrong with your partner.
You might need that and you might need to get away from them.
But you are going entirely in the wrong direction if you wish to learn how to heal as a couple. See less

I Give, Therefore I Deserve You
It's 5:40 in the morning and you're already in the car.
They've got a flight. You offered before they finished the sentence about the flight. Didn't even think about it, your mouth just did it.
And on the way to the airport you're running the list. They mentioned their apartment's a wreck, so Saturday's gone now. Their mom's birthday is in three weeks and you've already got the gift narrowed down to two options, which is two more options than they've thought about.
You handle things. That's the word people use about you.
So helpful. So generous. He'd do anything for you.
Now go back through the last several relationships and look at how each one started.
Not how it ended. How it started.
If the opening move was you being useful, every single time, that's worth sitting with for a minute.
Because that's not generosity. Generosity is something you can turn off.
Somewhere back there you worked out an equation, and it wasn't in words. It was in temperature.
Warmth showed up when you were easy. When you helped with dinner, when you were no trouble, when you handled your own bad day quietly and didn't make it anybody's problem.
And the warmth went somewhere else when you needed something. Not cruel. Not loud. Just gone, like a room where the heat kicked off.
You were young and you got good at reading it fast, and you did what any kid does. You figured out which version of yourself kept the heat on, and you became that one full time.
Maybe it wasn't a parent, either. I've sat with people where it was a friend group at fifteen. You were the one who planned everything, remembered everything, held the whole thing together. And one time you got tired and stopped texting first.
The friendship didn't blow up. Nothing dramatic happened at all.
It just got thin. And you found out real quick what had been holding it up, and it wasn't you.
Carl Rogers had a name for this. Conditions of worth. The terms you learn early about what you have to be to get let in.
You picked yours up before you ever went on a date. And it's been sitting in the passenger seat of every relationship since.
So here's what's actually happening three weeks into something new.
You've memorized their schedule. You know the Thursday meeting runs long, so you text after. You noticed they've been skipping lunch, so food shows up.
They didn't ask. You got there first. You always get there first.
And every time you do it, you feel a little safer, because necessary is close enough to loved that it scratches the itch.
But look at what's happening on their end, because it's not what you think.
They're not falling for the person who shows up with solutions. They're just settling into an arrangement where you give and they take. And they're not villains for it. You built the thing. You wrote the terms. They just moved in.
The version of you they know is the one that's always on. Always scanning, always three steps ahead of whatever they might need.
They've never met the other one. The one who needs something back. You've kept that guy in the trunk this whole time.
And then comes the week.
You get sick, or you hit some wall, or you're just flat empty. And you show up with nothing. No plan, no food, no anticipating. You sit on the couch and you want somebody to ask about your day first, one time, before you ask about theirs.
And the room gets strange.
They're not being mean. Watch their face, they're genuinely lost. Because the person who handles things isn't handling anything, and what's sitting on that couch is somebody they've never been introduced to.
And you lie there running the tape, trying to find what you did wrong.
You didn't do anything wrong. You built a whole relationship on a belief about yourself that was never true, and the week you couldn't perform, you got to see the foundation.
Now I want to be careful here, because the helping isn't the problem.
That instinct saved you. It worked. It kept you connected to people you needed when you were way too small to have any other options. That's not a defect, that's an adaptation, and it did its job for years.
The lie isn't in the helping. The lie is underneath it. It's the part that says you have to earn the chair you're sitting in. That rest doesn't count. That needing something makes you a burden and being a burden is how you lose people.
You absorbed that. It didn't come with you.
And the people worth having are not staying because you remembered the birthday or fixed the thing or made the week run smooth.
They're staying because they like being in a room with you while you do absolutely nothing.
So here's what I'd try, and it's gonna feel awful, which is how you know it's the right one.
Next time somebody offers you something, let them. Don't counter-offer. Don't even out the ledger. Just say thank you and sit there in the discomfort of owing somebody, which is gonna feel roughly like a wool sweater on a sunburn.
And then, at some point, say the line you've never said:
"I don't need anything fixed. I just want to be around you tonight. I don't have much to bring."
Then watch what happens next. That's the whole test right there.
Some people will get uncomfortable and reach for the door, and it's gonna hurt like hell, and it's information you needed years ago.
And somebody's gonna say, good, come over.
That's the one. That's the whole thing you've been trying to earn since you were nine years old, and it turns out it was never for sale in the first place.
So what's the last thing you let someone do for you without paying it back? See less

You were young and you got good at reading it fast, and you did what any kid does. You figured out which version of yourself kept the heat on, and you became that one full time.

Maybe it wasn't a parent, either. I've sat with people where it was a friend group at fifteen. You were the one who planned everything, remembered everything, held the whole thing together. And one time you got tired and stopped texting first.

The friendship didn't blow up. Nothing dramatic happened at all.

It just got thin. And you found out real quick what had been holding it up, and it wasn't you.

Carl Rogers had a name for this. Conditions of worth. The terms you learn early about what you have to be to get let in.

You picked yours up before you ever went on a date. And it's been sitting in the passenger seat of every relationship since.

So here's what's actually happening three weeks into something new.

You've memorized their schedule. You know the Thursday meeting runs long, so you text after. You noticed they've been skipping lunch, so food shows up.

They didn't ask. You got there first. You always get there first.

And every time you do it, you feel a little safer, because necessary is close enough to loved that it scratches the itch.

But look at what's happening on their end, because it's not what you think.

They're not falling for the person who shows up with solutions. They're just settling into an arrangement where you give and they take. And they're not villains for it. You built the thing. You wrote the terms. They just moved in.

The version of you they know is the one that's always on. Always scanning, always three steps ahead of whatever they might need.

They've never met the other one. The one who needs something back. You've kept that guy in the trunk this whole time.

And then comes the week.

You get sick, or you hit some wall, or you're just flat empty. And you show up with nothing. No plan, no food, no anticipating. You sit on the couch and you want somebody to ask about your day first, one time, before you ask about theirs.

And the room gets strange.

They're not being mean. Watch their face, they're genuinely lost. Because the person who handles things isn't handling anything, and what's sitting on that couch is somebody they've never been introduced to.

And you lie there running the tape, trying to find what you did wrong.

You didn't do anything wrong. You built a whole relationship on a belief about yourself that was never true, and the week you couldn't perform, you got to see the foundation.

Now I want to be careful here, because the helping isn't the problem.

That instinct saved you. It worked. It kept you connected to people you needed when you were way too small to have any other options. That's not a defect, that's an adaptation, and it did its job for years.

The lie isn't in the helping. The lie is underneath it. It's the part that says you have to earn the chair you're sitting in. That rest doesn't count. That needing something makes you a burden and being a burden is how you lose people.

You absorbed that. It didn't come with you.

And the people worth having are not staying because you remembered the birthday or fixed the thing or made the week run smooth.

They're staying because they like being in a room with you while you do absolutely nothing.

So here's what I'd try, and it's gonna feel awful, which is how you know it's the right one.

Next time somebody offers you something, let them. Don't counter-offer. Don't even out the ledger. Just say thank you and sit there in the discomfort of owing somebody, which is gonna feel roughly like a wool sweater on a sunburn.

And then, at some point, say the line you've never said:

"I don't need anything fixed. I just want to be around you tonight. I don't have much to bring."

Then watch what happens next. That's the whole test right there.

Some people will get uncomfortable and reach for the door, and it's gonna hurt like hell, and it's information you needed years ago.

And somebody's gonna say, good, come over.

That's the one. That's the whole thing you've been trying to earn since you were nine years old, and it turns out it was never for sale in the first place.

So what's the last thing you let someone do for you without paying it back? See less

Their marriage almost disappeared in the ten seconds between a glance that didn’t happen and a sentence neither of them could take back.
They’d gone to a crowded birthday dinner with his family.
He spent most of the night moving around the room.
Getting drinks.
Checking on his father.
Making sure his brother didn’t start another argument.
Changing the subject whenever the conversation became tense.
He thought he was taking care of everyone.
She sat near the end of the table and kept looking for him.
Not because she needed him beside her every second.
She wanted one glance.
One small look across the room that said:
*I know you’re here.*
*We’re in this together.*
*I haven’t forgotten about us.*
The glance never came.
On the drive home, she waited almost fifteen minutes before saying anything.
Then she said:
“You left me alone in there.”
He looked over at her.
“I was five feet away from you the entire night.”
He wasn’t trying to be cruel.
He believed he was correcting something inaccurate.
She said he’d left her alone.
He hadn’t.
Technically.
But something happened inside her when he answered.
Her shoulders pulled in.
Her face turned toward the window.
“That’s exactly what I mean,” she said.
Now he felt accused of something he couldn’t understand.
“No, it’s not. You said I left you alone. I didn’t leave you alone.”
He wanted her to recognize the facts.
She wanted him to recognize her.
They were already losing each other.
She tried again.
“I kept looking for you.”
“I was busy making sure the night didn’t turn into a disaster.”
“I know. You were available to everybody except me.”
That one landed hard.
He’d spent the evening trying to keep things peaceful. He’d watched his father’s face. He’d headed off tension with his brother. He’d made sure nobody drank too much. He’d done everything he knew how to do to protect the evening.
And now the woman he loved was telling him he hadn’t been there.
“You make everything into proof that I don’t care about you.”
He said it because he felt hopeless.
She heard it as contempt.
She went quiet.
He experienced the quiet as punishment.
She experienced the quiet as the only place left where she couldn’t be corrected.
By the time they got home, neither one was speaking.
He went to bed thinking:
*Nothing I do is ever enough for her.*
She stayed awake thinking:
*I could disappear right in front of him and he’d explain why I hadn’t.*
They came into my office carrying two completely different versions of the same evening.
He told me how hard he’d worked to hold his family together.
She told me how alone she’d felt while he did it.
They both had evidence.
They both remembered the night clearly.
They were both telling the truth.
And neither person’s truth had any room for the other.
He thought care meant preventing chaos.
She thought care meant finding each other inside it.
He’d been offering care all night.
She hadn’t felt cared for once.
I asked them to stop explaining the dinner.
Just for a moment.
I looked at her.
“What were you hoping would happen when you looked across the room?”
Her answer came quietly.
“I wanted him to see me.”
He started to respond.
I asked him to wait.
She continued.
“I didn’t need him to come sit beside me. I just wanted one look that told me I still mattered to him while he was taking care of everyone else.”
His face changed.
Not dramatically.
His jaw loosened.
His eyes softened.
For the first time, he wasn’t hearing a criticism of how he’d behaved at the party.
He was seeing the woman who’d been searching the room for him.
Then I looked at him.
“What did you want her to understand about you that night?”
He took a breath.
“I was trying so hard.”
She looked at him.
He continued.
“My family can turn on each other so quickly. I was watching everything. I thought if I could keep the night calm, I was taking care of us too.”
Now her face changed.
She hadn’t known that.
She’d seen a man who had attention for everyone but her.
He’d experienced himself as a man trying to protect the room they were both standing in.
Neither one had been pretending.
Neither one had stopped caring.
But their care had been translated into something unrecognizable by the time it reached the other person.
Her loneliness arrived as an accusation.
His effort arrived as emotional absence.
Her protest made him feel unseen.
His explanation made her feel even more alone.
This is how couples push each other away without wanting distance.
They don’t usually begin with cruelty.
They begin with pain.
Then they use the other person to explain that pain.
“You left me.”
“You never appreciate anything I do.”
“You’re available to everybody except me.”
“You make everything into proof that I don’t care.”
Every sentence contains something true.
And every sentence makes the partner responsible for carrying the truth while recovering from the injury wrapped around it.
That night wasn’t really about a birthday dinner.
It wasn’t even about the glance.
It was about two people standing inside the same room, both asking to be seen, and both expressing it in a way the other person could only experience as blame.
He wasn’t cold.
She wasn’t needy.
They were both alone inside the same evening.
The love was there the entire time.
It just didn’t get through.
**

27 things people say when they’re coping instead of saying what they really want to say
Most couples don’t lose each other because they have nothing vulnerable to say.
They lose each other because vulnerability gets translated into protection before it ever leaves the mouth.
The longing comes out as criticism.
The fear comes out as anger.
The hurt comes out as indifference.
The wish to be understood comes out as an explanation.
And suddenly two people who desperately want to reach each other are having an argument neither of them actually wants to be having.
Listen underneath some of the things people say:
1. “You never listen to me.”
What I may really want to say:
“Please let me matter to you right now.”
2. “I don’t care anymore.”
“I care so much that I don’t know what to do with how much this hurts.”
3. “Whatever.”
“I don’t think I can keep trying to explain myself and survive feeling misunderstood again.”
4. “You’re impossible to talk to.”
“I don’t know how to reach you.”
5. “Why do I have to tell you everything?”
“I want you to notice me without my having to beg to be noticed.”
6. “Nothing I do is ever good enough for you.”
“I want to know that you can still see the good in me.”
7. “You’re overreacting.”
“Your feelings are getting big, and I’m scared I won’t know what to do with them.”
8. “Calm down.”
“I’m getting overwhelmed, and I don’t know how to stay connected to you while this is happening.”
9. “I was only trying to help.”
“Please don’t see me as someone who wanted to hurt you.”
10. “That’s not what happened.”
“I’m afraid that if your version is true, I become the bad person.”
11. “That’s not what I meant.”
“Please know my heart before you judge my mistake.”
12. “You always make everything about you.”
“Is there room for my pain too?”
13. “Fine. I just won’t say anything anymore.”
“I don’t know how to speak without making this worse.”
14. “Leave me alone.”
“I need the intensity to stop, but I don’t necessarily want to lose you.”
15. “Why are you always criticizing me?”
“I need to know you still like me.”
16. “You obviously don’t care.”
“Please show me that I matter.”
17. “I shouldn’t have to ask.”
“I want to feel known by you.”
18. “You’re just like your mother.”
“Something is happening between us that I’ve felt before, and it scares me.”
19. “Forget it.”
“I wanted you to understand without my having to expose how much I needed you.”
20. “I’m fine.”
“I’m not ready to show you what’s happening inside me.”
21. “You’re too sensitive.”
“I’m afraid your hurt means I’ve done something terrible.”
22. “Can we not do this right now?”
“I don’t have enough inside me right now to do this well.”
23. “All you ever want to do is fight.”
“I miss feeling safe with you.”
24. “You only think about yourself.”
“I want to feel considered.”
25. “Why can’t you just admit you’re wrong?”
“I need some sign that you understand what this was like for me.”
26. “I’m done.”
Sometimes it really does mean, “I’m done.”
But sometimes it means:
“I cannot keep hurting like this.”
And maybe one of the most important ones:
27. “You don’t love me.”
Often underneath that sentence is something much more frightening to say:
“I love you, and right now I can’t feel you loving me back.”
That’s the part couples so often miss.
We listen to the coping and respond to the coping.
We defend against the accusation.
Correct the facts.
Explain our intention.
Point out the exaggeration.
Prove that never isn’t actually never and always isn’t actually always.
And we may be completely right.
But being technically right doesn’t create repair.
Because underneath the sentence we’re arguing with, there is often another sentence.
A softer one.
A scarier one.
A sentence that sounds much more like:
Do I matter to you?
Can you see me?
Are you still here?
Do you understand why this hurt?
Can I need you without losing you?
Am I safe showing you how much I care?
That is the conversation hiding inside so many of our arguments.
And learning to hear that conversation can change everything.
And a bonus.

Trauma is complex because it has no timeline.
It doesn't let you off the hook often enough.
It forces painful emotion to come through you as you witness the rest of the world seeming to be happy more often.
When you feel the ecstasy of loving somebody, you often simultaneously feel the pain of losing them.
And they're doing great.
Don't even have a cold or a fever.
And you anticipate their loss... now.
And this difficulty enters your relationship.
You want to connect and have a responsive partner.
And somewhere in you... you don't believe you deserve a responsive partner.
I'm not talking about the intellectual version of this, where right now, you might say you believe you deserve that.
I'm saying you were conditioned as a child not to be worthy of predictable, loving attention when you were hurting.
This stays stuck in a loop in your mind.
So the confusing sabotage is choosing a partner who perfectly mirrors your inherited nervous system.
You chose them because they fit.
You did not choose them because they are a notch beyond what fits.
You're not ready yet.
--
Until.
Life brings some really difficult moments.
It hurts so deeply that you wake up.
You find a far deeper set of validations that you didn't know you needed.
A loss of a relationship partner, a loss of what you hoped life would be.
A coming out of denial.
And you rise up again.
And still wishing there weren't so many continuous things in this world that show us how mean people are to each other.
And still wishing you didn't have to feel it so deeply.
And one day you find that you are the one giving yourself the deepest validation.
The validation you needed.
That you indeed feel this deeply.
And that is never going away.
And then...
--
You can learn to use this for a more joyful life.
You stop accusing a partner of their avoidance.
You learn how to show them, and others, your pain.
You learn that the path to being happier is revealing how much it hurts.
And showing that it hurts.
And recognizing who will not walk away from you.
Then you're ready.
To step into being you.
The one WE ALL NEED.
Yes.
You're up.
Your true frustration with how a life that requires healing almost takes you out at times.
But you're not gonna give up.
Not because it's the right thing to do.
Because you now understand that the revealing of your pain is what others need to see to reveal theirs.
Because sometimes you're one step ahead of them.
And they need your help.
And you are rewarded when you see your pain turned into something that helps another.
Your pain shrinks.
Their pain shrinks.
The permanence of trauma from the past does not go away.
But what it means for you, and how it directs you, is a gift you can seek out if you wish.
And then.
One day.
For a minute.
For an hour.
For a whole day.
You will forget about trauma because you're busy enjoying a sunset within your own skin.

One day.

For a whole day.

Criticism doesn’t usually begin with cruelty.
It begins with hurt.
You feel ignored.
Unimportant.
Lonely.
Disappointed.
Scared that something between you is slipping away.

“Why do I always have to ask you?”
“You never think about me.”
“You’re always on your phone.”
“I can’t count on you.”
And here’s the part most couples miss:
The fight may already be changing direction before the argument even begins.
You say something that makes perfect sense from inside your experience.
Your partner’s face changes.
Their body tightens.
They hear something underneath your words that you may never have intended:
You’re selfish.
You’re failing me.
You’re the problem.
And now they protect themselves.
They explain.
They defend.
They correct you.
They go quiet.
They push back.
And within seconds, two people who may actually love each other are no longer talking about the original hurt.
They’re fighting about the fight.
The part I’m most interested in is not the twenty-minute argument.
It’s the tiny moment where contact gets lost.
Because if we can see that moment, we have a chance to do something very different.

How do you really know when a relationship is over?
It’s not when the fights get loud.
It’s not when the distance grows heavy.
It’s not even when you lie awake at night wondering if you’re still compatible.
Those are signs of struggle, but struggle is not the end. Struggle can be repaired. Struggle can even bring two people closer.
The real ending happens quietly.
It happens when both people stop trying.
Because fights don’t end relationships, silence does.
It’s not the argument that breaks you, it’s what happens after.
Do you reach for each other, or do you turn away?
Do you lean in with trembling honesty, or do you retreat into silence?
A relationship starts to die the moment the desire to repair disappears. That’s when love loses its pulse.
And then something darker takes its place: resentment.
Resentment is like rust on metal. At first, it’s small, almost invisible. But once it spreads, it eats away at everything.
When resentment outweighs respect, you stop seeing your partner’s good intentions. Their words no longer sound like clumsy attempts to connect, they sound like weapons. Their quirks that once made you smile now feel like irritations you can’t stand.
Every little thing becomes evidence against them.
Healthy couples fight, but they fight from a foundation of respect. If that respect erodes completely, the ground beneath the relationship collapses.
And when respect is gone, emotional safety disappears with it.
You stop sharing what you feel. You stop being vulnerable. You stop turning to your partner for comfort. And eventually, you stop turning toward them at all.
You find yourself editing your truth, guarding your heart, carrying your pain alone because it no longer feels safe to let them see it. And once emotional safety is gone, trust follows.
That’s when the bond breaks.
So how do you know when a relationship is truly over? It’s not when you no longer love them. It’s when neither of you is willing to reach for each other anymore.
Because the end of a relationship is not about the absence of love. It’s about the absence of effort.
And yet, here’s the quiet hope no one talks about.
If even a small part of you is still willing to lean in, if even a piece of your heart is still willing to try, then the story isn’t finished. Because relationships don’t end with conflict, they end with indifference.
The real question is not, “Do you still love each other?”
The real question is, “Are you still willing to fight for each other?” See less

The moment you truly understand how terrified your partner gets when you're angry... everything changes.
Most people think anger is just anger.
But your partner experiences it as danger.
When you raise your voice, here's what's happening in their body:
Their nervous system is screaming: "THREAT. THREAT. THREAT."
Their heart rate spikes. Their breathing gets shallow. Their brain goes into survival mode.
They're not thinking about resolving the issue anymore.
They're thinking about how to make you stop being scary.
You think you're just "expressing frustration."
They experience it as being under attack.
Even if you've never laid a hand on them. Even if you "would never hurt them."
Your anger feels like violence to their nervous system.
The game-changer realization:
When you can hold space for how frightening you become when you're angry...
When you can see their fear instead of just your frustration...
When you realize they're not "being dramatic" - they're genuinely scared...
Everything about how you handle conflict will shift.
Instead of: "You're too sensitive!"
Try: "I can see I scared you. That wasn't my intention. Let me take a breath."
Instead of: "I wasn't even that angry!"
Try: "Your fear matters more than my intention. How can I do this differently?"
Instead of: "You should know I'd never hurt you!"
Try: "I want you to feel safe with me, especially when we disagree."
This isn't about never feeling angry.
It's about understanding the impact of your anger on someone you love.
It's about taking responsibility for the energy you bring into the room.
It's about caring more about their safety than your right to be loud.
The beautiful thing that happens when you get this:
Your partner starts feeling safe enough to actually communicate with you instead of just surviving you.
They stop walking on eggshells. They stop shutting down. They stop agreeing just to make you calm down.
Real intimacy becomes possible when fear leaves the room.
Love isn't just about how you feel about your partner.
It's about how safe they feel with you when you're upset.
That's where real care lives. See less

The Uncomfortable Truth About Why We Fall in Love
Your brain is playing tricks on you.
Every single day of your childhood, your nervous system was taking detailed notes.
Not about your parents specifically.
Not about you.
About how reality itself operates.
Emotionally unavailable mom? → The world withholds love until you prove yourself worthy.
Explosive dad? → Pain is how people show they care about getting through to you.
These aren't conscious thoughts.
They're hardwired survival maps that live in your body.
And then you grow up and wonder why you keep attracting the same type of person.
Here's the plot twist nobody talks about:
You don't fall in love with someone because they make you happy.
You fall in love with someone because they feel like home.
And "home" feels like whatever chaos, neglect, or conditional love you learned to navigate as a kid.
Your unconscious mind isn't looking for someone who treats you well.
It's looking for someone who recreates the familiar wound so you can finally, FINALLY heal it.
"If I can just get THIS person to stop abandoning me, then I'll prove I was always loveable."
"If I can just get THIS person to stop criticizing me, then I'll finally feel good enough."
You're not choosing a partner.
You're choosing a healing project.
The brutal reality:
The more traumatic your childhood, the more "sophisticated" your self-sabotage becomes.
You'll unconsciously reject the person who wants to treat you with genuine care because kindness feels foreign and unsafe.
Your nervous system literally interprets healthy love as boring, suspicious, or "too good to be true."
Meanwhile, the person who triggers your deepest wounds? Electric. Addictive. "This must be real love because it hurts so good."
Breaking the cycle requires feeling the discomfort of the unfamiliar:
• Learning to sit with someone's consistency instead of chasing their attention
• Allowing yourself to be seen without performing or fixing anything
• Tolerating the "boring" safety of someone who doesn't need you to save them
• Discovering what your own preferences actually are when you're not in survival mode
Most people will spend 10+ years trying to turn the wrong person into the right person instead of doing the harder work of rewiring what "love" feels like in their body.
The person who feels "too easy" might actually be exactly what your nervous system needs to learn that love doesn't have to hurt to be real.
Sometimes "falling in love" is really just falling into the desperate hope that this time, you can rewrite your origin story.
But healing happens when you stop trying to fix the past through other people and start learning to give yourself what you needed all along.

Most of the time the question about getting back with an ex comes out wrong.
Has he changed. Is she different now. Nine months go by, you bump into 'em somewhere and they seem softer, calmer, and you start doing the math on it.
But you were never in a relationship with a person. You were in a relationship with whatever happened between the two of you.
That's a different animal. And that's the thing that ended you.
Think back on the last stretch of it. There was a move you made when you got scared. Maybe you pushed harder. Needed an answer right then, couldn't let it sit overnight. And there was a move they made back. Went flat. Went quiet. Went out to the garage.
And your move made theirs worse, and theirs made yours worse, and round and round it went 'til one of you got tired enough to leave.
That's what you broke up with. Not them.
So here's the question that actually matters. Does either one of you know how to do it differently now?
And I don't mean intentions. Intentions are gorgeous in month one, they cost nothing. I'm talking about 10:40 at night when something lands sideways and you feel the old thing come up in your chest. In that second, do you have any idea what to do besides exactly what you did last time?
If the answer's no, you're not getting back with a person. You're getting back into a pattern. And that pattern's undefeated.
Now, I've watched couples do this and have it work. It happens. Just never the way it gets pictured.
It doesn't work 'cause time went by. Time doesn't heal a pattern, it just gives you a breather from running it.
It doesn't work 'cause somebody promised. Promises get made by the calm version of a person, and the calm version isn't who shows up at 10:40.
The ones I've seen make it, something actually got learned in the gap. Usually by both of 'em, sometimes just one. Somebody figured out how to say the scared thing straight instead of firing off the protected version. Somebody learned to stay in the room instead of disappearing for three days. Then they got back together, and the old moment showed up right on schedule, 'cause it always does, and this time one of 'em did something different with it.
That's the whole gap between a second chance and a rerun.
There's another version of this, though, and I gotta name it, 'cause a lot of you are sitting in it right now.
Sometimes you don't miss them. You miss not being alone. You miss knowing what Saturday looks like. You miss having somebody who knows how you take your coffee and which sister to call first when something goes wrong.
That ache is real and it deserves respect. It's just not information about them. It's information about how loud the quiet's gotten.
And your body will lie to you about which one it is. Especially around 11 at night. Especially that first winter.
So if you're standing at this crossroads right now, here's what I'd ask, and it's not "would we be happy."
Can you both name the pattern out loud? Not their part. Yours. Can you say the specific thing you did when you got scared, without one single word about what they did first?
If neither of you can do that, nothing's changed yet. Doesn't mean it can't. Means it hasn't.
And if you can, if you can both put it on the table plain and then say what you'd wanna do instead, that's not nostalgia talking. That's two people who learned something.
The relationship didn't fall apart 'cause you were incompatible.
It fell apart 'cause neither one of you was ever shown what to do in the moment it went sideways.
So be honest with you.
You want them back?
If so, you want a new version of the relationship, perhaps one with boundaries that you overrode before?
If so, you want a new version of the relationship, perhaps one with boundaries that you didn't set before?
If so, you want a new version of the relationship, perhaps one that has less affection, the truth for one partner?
If so, you want a new version of the relationship, perhaps one that has more affection, the truth for one partner? See less

Then they got back together, and the old moment showed up right on schedule, 'cause it always does, and this time one of 'em did something different with it.

That's the whole gap between a second chance and a rerun.

There's another version of this, though, and I gotta name it, 'cause a lot of you are sitting in it right now.

Sometimes you don't miss them. You miss not being alone. You miss knowing what Saturday looks like. You miss having somebody who knows how you take your coffee and which sister to call first when something goes wrong.

That ache is real and it deserves respect. It's just not information about them. It's information about how loud the quiet's gotten.

And your body will lie to you about which one it is. Especially around 11 at night. Especially that first winter.

So if you're standing at this crossroads right now, here's what I'd ask, and it's not "would we be happy."

Can you both name the pattern out loud? Not their part. Yours. Can you say the specific thing you did when you got scared, without one single word about what they did first?

If neither of you can do that, nothing's changed yet. Doesn't mean it can't. Means it hasn't.

And if you can, if you can both put it on the table plain and then say what you'd wanna do instead, that's not nostalgia talking. That's two people who learned something.

The relationship didn't fall apart 'cause you were incompatible.

It fell apart 'cause neither one of you was ever shown what to do in the moment it went sideways.

So be honest with you.

You want them back?

Most couples therapy fails.
You sit down on the couch and you tell the therapist what you're frustrated about. Which is mostly what you don't like in your partner. They don't pay attention enough to you. They don't treat you like you matter. You feel dismissed when you tell them something important.
Every single part of that explanation is true when you’re in distress.
You don’t like them.
You get annoyed when you see them talk kindly to others. Doesn’t happen with you. You hear them on the phone being reasonable and open with somebody else. More reason your frustration increases.
No matter what you do in this scenario, no matter how you tell them, it will not change it. Because you’ve worn out the good will of being able to listen to each other’s frustrations about each other.
You can describe your partner accurately for a year of sessions. Every complaint verified. Every example real. And nothing changes, because describing your partner was never the work. It's actually the thing that keeps you safe from the work.
Nobody tells most of us what the work is.
It’s unclear. Books try to explain it, but they fall short because they’re focused on what to do or what to say.
Won’t change it. You’ve tried a thousand times.
Change only becomes possible when someone points you inward. Away from your partner's behavior, toward what's underneath your complaint. Not just naming your emotion. Making contact with it, in front of your partner.

You don’t need more information. You need to watch the transformation happen in real time. That’s how you will know the steps to repair the continuous lack of emotional safety in your relationship.

MARRIAGE VOWS
-
ANXIOUS PARTNER FREDDIE:
I vow to love you with my whole heart, and to check approximately every ninety minutes that you still love me back, using a rotating system of tests you will never be told you are taking.
I vow to hear you sigh from three rooms away and arrive within seconds, like an emotionally available smoke detector, asking what's wrong, whether it's me, whether you're sure, and whether you're sure you're sure.
I vow to read your text messages the way scholars read ancient scrolls. A period where an exclamation point used to be will trigger a full investigation. The letter "k" arriving alone may require me to sit down.
I vow to text you a paragraph, then a second paragraph apologizing for the first paragraph, then "lol anyway" to make the whole thing seem breezy. It will not seem breezy.
I vow that when you ask for a little space, I will say "of course, take all the time you need" in my most emotionally secure voice, and then appear in eleven minutes holding a snack I will claim I was already making.
I vow to ask "what are you thinking about" during movies, during dinner, and once, memorably, while you are asleep.
I vow to know the exact number of hours since you last said I love you first, unprompted. There is a running tally. It has never once been shared with the committee, but the committee meets nightly.
And here are the vows I am actually working on. I vow to learn, slowly, that your silence is not a verdict. That when you go quiet, you have not left, you have gone inside, and there is a difference, and I am allowed to breathe while you are in there.
I vow to take one breath before I follow you down the hallway. Then, on my best days, a second breath instead of the hallway at all.
I vow to tell you "I am scared right now" instead of presenting you with a list of your crimes, because I finally understand those were always the same sentence, and only one of them ever worked.
-
AVOIDANT PARTNER WENDY:
I vow to love you deeply, constantly, and at a volume you may occasionally need special equipment to detect.
I vow to answer "what are you thinking about" with "nothing," while inside my head three civilizations rise and fall, two of them because of you.
I vow to say "I'm fine" fluently in fourteen dialects, including the one where I say it while reorganizing the garage at eleven at night with the focus of a man defusing a bomb.
I vow that when you say "we need to talk," some ancient part of me will immediately begin pricing land in Montana. I vow to stay anyway. I want that vow in writing. Someone please write that one down.
I vow to love you in my native language, which is acts. I will fix the squeaky door you mentioned once, in passing, eight months ago. I will put air in your tires without being asked. When you find your car mysteriously full of gas, that was a love letter. I am asking you to learn to read them, because I have thousands more.
I vow to hug you back with one arm while holding something in the other, because a full two-arm hug with nothing in my hands is scheduled for later, and later is a place I keep many things.
I vow to miss you most when you are in the next room, and to tell you about it roughly never, and I am also working on that one.
And here are my real vows. I vow to learn that being needed is not being swallowed. That your reach toward me was never an audit. You were not checking my work. You were checking if I was there, and I vow to start answering the actual question.
I vow to stay ninety more seconds than my body wants to. Then, on my best days, to stay in the room entirely, and to say the thirteen hardest words I know: "I am overwhelmed and I am not going anywhere. Give me a minute."
I vow that when I do need to step away, I will leave you a return time, and I will keep it, because I finally understand that my open-ended exits were writing stories in you that I never meant to write.
-
TOGETHER:
We vow to stop asking which one of us is broken, because the answer was always neither, and the answer was always both, and the real answer is that one of us learned early to reach loudly and one of us learned early to disappear quietly, and then we found each other, the way we always find each other, and built a dance out of it.
We vow to fight the pattern and not each other.
We vow to get it wrong constantly, repair it clumsily, and trust the repair more than we fear the rupture.
You may now both take one deep breath.
You may kiss the person who is going to trigger you for the rest of your beautiful life. See less

They met at a party neither of them wanted to be at.
She noticed him because he was the only one not performing. He noticed her because she laughed with her whole body.
They stayed up until 4am that first night, talking. That became their thing. Long drives to nowhere, talking until the sky got light. Conversations that wandered from childhood to what they were most afraid of. She told him things she'd never said out loud. He cried in front of her once, early, and she didn't flinch, and he thought: this one. This is the one person I don't have to hide from.
They got married in a backyard. They couldn't afford anything better and they didn't care. During the vows, he forgot his lines because he was looking at her.
Nobody warns you that marriages rarely end in an explosion.
They end politely.
Here's how it actually happened.
Year three, she came home from the worst day of her working life and started to tell him about it. He was tired. He half listened, offered a fix, went back to his phone. Small thing. Forgivable thing. She told herself it was nothing.
But something in her took a note.
Year five, he reached for her in the dark and she rolled away. Exhausted, touched-out, nothing personal. He lay there staring at the ceiling and told himself it was nothing.
Something in him took a note too.
That's all it is, in the beginning. Notes. Little pieces of evidence, filed away in silence. It's not safe to need her at midnight. It's not worth telling him about my day.
Nobody fought. That's the part people get wrong. There was no affair, no thrown plates, no screaming in the driveway. There were just two people slowly learning, missed reach by missed reach, that the real stuff went badly when you brought it.
So they stopped bringing it.
They brought other things instead. The kids. The schedule. The gutter that needed fixing. They became excellent coworkers running a small family business called their life.
By year twelve, they had the choreography down. Moving around each other in the kitchen without touching. Timing their bedtimes so they wouldn't have to lie there awake together. At dinner parties they still told the story of how they met, taking turns with the good lines, and everyone laughed, and on the drive home neither of them said one word.
She sat in the driveway some nights, an extra minute before walking in. She couldn't have told you why.
He started staying up late for no reason. Just to be in a room where nobody was disappointed in him.
And here's what neither of them could see:
Every night, lying inches apart, both of them were rehearsing the same conversation. The real one. She wrote him whole speeches in her head. He composed apologies he never sent. Two people, six inches of mattress between them, each one certain they were the only one still awake, each one a hundred miles alone.
They didn't stop fighting because things got better.
They stopped fighting because fighting takes hope.
You have to believe someone will finally hear you in order to raise your voice one more time. Somewhere around year eight, they'd both quietly run out.
The night it almost ended wasn't dramatic either. She said, at the kitchen sink, not even angry, just flat: "I think we're done, aren't we." Not a question. An observation, the way you'd notice it started raining.
And he surprised them both.
He didn't defend. He didn't list his contributions or bring up her coldness or reach for any weapon in the arsenal they'd both been quietly stocking for a decade.
He put down the towel. He said the thing under the thing.
"I've missed you for nine years and I never once said it out loud. I thought you stopped wanting me, so I hid. I'm still hiding right now. I don't know how to stop."
Silence. But a different kind. Not the empty kind that had filled their house for years.
This silence was full.
It was holding every conversation they never finished. Every reach that got missed. Every "do I still matter to you" that had spent a decade hiding inside arguments about dishes and money and whose turn it was.
She looked at him. Actually looked, for the first time in longer than either could measure. And what she saw wasn't the coworker, or the roommate, or the man on his phone.
She saw the guy from the party. Scared. Not performing. Asking, underneath everything: is it safe to be seen by you?
She started to cry. Not about the marriage.
About how long they'd both been so alone, two feet apart.
"I write you speeches," she said. "In my head. Every night. I've been talking to you for years and you never heard any of it."
"Me too," he said. "Every night."
Ten minutes. That's all it was. After nine years of silence, ten minutes of the real conversation, and they were looking at each other tenderly across the kitchen like something had been unlocked. Because it had.
Nothing was fixed that night. The distance took years to build. It doesn't come down in an evening.
But here's what's true:
They were never two people who stopped loving each other.
They were two people who stopped feeling safe enough to be seen. Filing notes. Building the case for silence. Falling out of contact while sleeping in the same bed.
Underneath every quiet marriage there's a conversation like theirs, intact, patient, waiting. It doesn't die. It just waits for one of two people to find the courage to go first.
Not with a technique.
With the truth. See less

There’s no such thing as rebuilding trust.
At least not in the way many of us think about it.
We say trust is broken when a partner follows an ex, gets a little too close to a coworker, hides a conversation, crosses a line emotionally, or blows past it physically. We all know what someone means when they say, “I don’t trust you anymore.” That part makes sense. The pain is real. The betrayal is real.
Not a lotta places that explain how trust actually comes back.
Because the way we try to rebuild it is doomed from the start. Ain't gonna happen.
We try to rebuild trust with behavior.
Transparency.
Rules.
Passwords.
Location sharing.
Checking in.
Proving.
Explaining.
Reassuring.
Doing everything “right” for long enough.
Sure you can see my phone (after I erase my history - incognito expert)
Here's my text messages sweetheart
And here’s the deal:
If someone has been betrayed, every “right” behavior happens inside doubt.
Every text sent on time is questioned.
Every night home early is monitored.
Every reassurance is measured.
Every good moment is followed by, “But what if it’s happening again?”
So how long does it take?
How many months?
How many perfect choices?
How many thousands of correct behaviors does it take to rebuild trust?
The honest answer is: it will never be enough.
Not because the betrayed partner is cruel.
Not because they won’t forgive.
But because betrayal doesn’t live in behavior.
It lives in the body.
Trust is not a behavior problem.
Trust is not an agreement problem.
Trust is not a compliance problem.
Trust is a nervous system injury.
When trust breaks, something collapses inside the betrayed person. Their sense of safety. Their sense of reality. Their ability to relax in your presence. Their ability to look at you without bracing. Their ability to know what’s real.
And when that’s broken, no amount of “doing the right thing” can fix it on its own.

Forgiveness is a concept.

99 Things You Have To Give Up To Have Secure Attachment
Everyone wants secure attachment.
Everyone wants to feel calm in love.
Everyone wants to trust that the person they love will stay, listen, and care.
But getting there isn’t about learning more.
It’s not about more skills, more therapy, or more self-awareness.
It’s about letting go.
Because secure attachment isn’t built by adding things.
It’s built by releasing what keeps you in defense.
It’s what happens when your nervous system no longer has to grip every moment for control.
It’s when you stop fighting to be right and start wanting to be connected.
Here are 99 things you have to give up to create the kind of love that actually feels safe.

39. Making assumptions instead of asking questions
40. Using withdrawal to feel safe
41. Using anger to feel powerful
42. Using sex to avoid talking
43. Using silence to feel superior
44. Using logic to avoid emotion
45. Interrupting before they finish
46. Listening to rebut instead of understand
47. Expecting repair to erase the pain instantly
48. Thinking forgiveness means forgetting
49. Holding grudges as proof you were wronged
50. Waiting to feel safe before showing your truth
51. Using humor to dodge intimacy
52. Using work to avoid closeness
53. Believing vulnerability makes you weak
54. Pretending you don’t care
55. Minimizing your pain
56. Minimizing theirs
57. Withholding affection when you’re mad
58. Testing love instead of trusting it
59. Reading their mood instead of asking
60. Avoiding eye contact during conflict
61. Comparing your relationship to others
62. Telling yourself love shouldn’t take this much work
63. Expecting repair to look like your version of it
64. Talking about change without practicing it
65. Saying “I’m trying” while repeating the same defense
66. Expecting understanding without giving it
67. Holding your love hostage until you feel safe
68. Assuming the worst
69. Believing love means agreement
70. Ignoring small hurts until they become big ones
71. Refusing to admit when you’re scared
72. Thinking your partner is the enemy
73. Believing your partner should heal your past
74. Confusing self-protection with strength
75. Using emotional shutdown as self-care
76. Hiding behind intellect
77. Correcting your partner’s language instead of hearing their pain
78. Pretending you don’t need anyone
79. Treating emotional repair like a negotiation
80. Believing peace means silence
81. Labeling your partner with diagnoses instead of empathy
82. Trying to solve emotions with logic
83. Demanding emotional safety while offering none
84. Avoiding small repairs until resentment builds
85. Waiting to feel loved before giving love
86. Repeating patterns without noticing them
87. Assuming your version of the story is the whole truth
88. Believing conflict means failure
89. Believing calm means disconnection
90. Thinking your partner’s pain diminishes yours
91. Mistaking emotional intensity for closeness
92. Thinking surrender means losing power
93. Using your childhood as an excuse to stay closed
94. Thinking awareness equals healing
95. Waiting for your partner to lead
96. Believing comfort means control
97. Trying to finish the argument instead of pausing it
98. Forgetting that repair happens in small gestures

You get it by letting go of everything that keeps you unreachable.

Before you send a REEL to your romantic partner, ask:
1) Am I sending this because it's endearing and I want to show my person something special.
2) Am I sending this because I want to explain something to them that is continuously concerning to me, and this is my indirect way of not knowing how to repair this in my relationship with them.

Before you send a REEL to your romantic partner, ask:

1) Am I sending this because it's endearing and I want to show my person something special.

2) Am I sending this because I want to explain something to them that is continuously concerning to me, and this is my indirect way of not knowing how to repair this in my relationship with them.

I promise you this. When you enter romantic argument, at least one of you did not reveal what you just got scared about.
Here's what actually happens:
She says "You never help with the dishes."
He hears: "You're a bad husband who doesn't care."
His nervous system goes to war. He defends. Counterattacks. Lists everything he DID do.
Now they're screaming about housework for two hours.
But that's not what happened.
What happened was: She walked into the kitchen, saw the dishes still there, and got scared.
Scared that she's invisible. Scared that her exhaustion doesn't matter. Scared that she's going to spend the next 20 years being the only one who sees what needs to be done.
She didn't say "I'm scared you don't see how tired I am."
She said "You never help."
And he got scared too.
Scared that nothing he does is ever good enough. Scared that she thinks he's failing as a partner. Scared that he's becoming his father who could never make his mother happy.
He didn't say "I'm scared I'm disappointing you."
He said "I do plenty around here."
Now you have two terrified people fighting about everything except what scared them.
She's not really angry about dishes. She's terrified of being unseen.
He's not really defensive about chores. He's terrified of being inadequate.
But scared people don't say "I'm scared." They attack or defend.
Fear comes out as criticism: "You always..." "You never..."
Fear comes out as defensiveness: "That's not true!" "What about when I..."
Fear comes out as silence: Walking away. Shutting down. Disappearing.
The cruelest part? They're both scared of the same thing.
She's scared she doesn't matter to him.
He's scared he doesn't matter to her.
Two people drowning in the same ocean, pushing each other underwater trying to survive.
Here's what changes everything:
Next time you feel the urge to criticize, stop. Ask yourself: "What am I scared of right now?"
Instead of "You never listen to me," try "I'm scared that what I'm saying doesn't matter to you."
Instead of "You're being dramatic," try "I'm scared that nothing I do makes you happy."
Instead of "Fine, whatever," try "I'm scared that if I keep talking, I'll say something that hurts us both."
Watch what happens when you lead with fear instead of blame.
Fear is disarming. Fear invites care instead of defense.
Fear says "I need you" instead of "You're wrong."
Your partner can't argue with your fear. They can only help with it or ignore it.
Most of the time, they'll help with it. Because underneath their defensiveness, they've been scared too.
Scared of the same things you are.
The next time you start to fight, remember this:
You're not enemies. You're two scared people who forgot how to say "I'm afraid" instead of "You always."
The couples who make it aren't the ones who never get scared. They're the ones who learned to be scared out loud, together.
Because the opposite of fear isn't courage. It's intimacy.
And intimacy is just two people saying "I'm scared" at the same time and choosing to stay. See less

I have been asked over 25,000 questions about relationships.
A client today asked me if I had to give one answer to all of those questions, if I had only one chance to answer all 25,000 questions, what would be my answer?
Here's my answer.
"Become more aware of what is happening inside you, your body, your sensations, your emotions, your stories. Challenge all that you believe about our World.
Know that all distress, all trauma... comes from not understanding how your history, when unsafe, made you adjust and over-compensate, and you developed coping strategies with your imperfect parents.
Those coping strategies now mean that you cannot connect the dots between the current moment, your feelings inside, what those feelings are, how they relate to this moment, and how they relate to your past.
You have had to create meaning out of all the moments, starting young, when you were let down and not satisfied with those that were supposed to be the ones that cared for you and installed in you a safe or unsafe Universe.
Without this awareness inside, you react, and you set off the alarms in the person across from you... the alarms that they have not made contact with.
In some moments it might seem like you know what your feelings are, and what needs you have, and how those needs will help you.
You are often wrong.
Knowing what we need is very difficult.
What we usually need is deep understanding at a feeling level, and to have that, both partners must know how.
And not knowing how makes us human.
So both partners have to have the intention of wanting to learn how.
That is truly what is needed to begin.
If you are fighting about your frustrations, and not in contact with a much deeper need for understanding, then the softer primary emotions, like hurt, fear, sadness, joy... are not being made contact with.
Only gentleness with the above can heal.
It's hard for me.
It's hard for you.
And the person in front of you... it's also hard for... and he/she would probably make better choices... if he/she knew how.
We must be taught this if it was skipped in childhood, with imperfect frustrated parents." See less

You're standing in the grocery store, aisle seven, and you're still mad.
Three days mad. The kind where you've been going to bed at different times and saying "fine" in that clipped little way.
And you reach up and grab the yogurt.
Not your yogurt. Theirs. The weird one. The flavor nobody else in the house eats, the one you have to hunt for because they moved it to the bottom shelf again.
You didn't decide to do that. Your hand just did it.
I want to talk about that hand for a minute.
When couples come to me in trouble, they're usually trying to answer one question, even if they never say it out loud. Do I still love this person.
And they go looking for the answer in their feelings. Which, lemme tell you, is like checking the weather by asking somebody who's been indoors for six years.
Your feelings are exhausted. They've been through it. They're not a reliable instrument right now.
So I tell 'em to look somewhere else. Look at your hands.
Your hands have been voting on this marriage the entire time. Go read the ballots.
You buy the yogurt.
You still park on the side that puts their door away from the wind.
You grab their coat when you grab yours, even on the night you're not speaking.
You hear a sound at 2 in the morning and you get up to check it. You. Every time. And you're not even brave, you're just not gonna let it be them.
You order for 'em when the waiter comes and they're in the bathroom, and you get it right, no onions, the whole thing, without a second's thought.
You take the burnt piece of toast. Twenty-six years of burnt toast, and it's never once come up out loud.
You save them the corner piece with the frosting.
You start the car early on cold mornings and don't say anything about it.
You know exactly which way the pillow has to face.
I've had people sit in front of me and swear up and down there's nothing left, it's dead, it's been dead for years, and then their partner mentions the burnt toast thing and they get real quiet.
Because a reflex can't lie for you.
You can fake a compliment. You can fake a date night, plenty of people do, they've got a standing Friday reservation and they eat in silence and call it romance. You can say I love you with absolutely nothing behind it, and honestly, some nights we all have.
But there's no audience in aisle seven. Nobody's handing out credit for it. You're not even doing it to be nice. You're doing it because some part of you built a shape around this person years ago and it never got dismantled.
That's not sentiment. That's structure.
Your mind quit. Your hands kept working.
Now I'm not gonna tell you this fixes anything. It doesn't. You can be full of these little reflexes and still be in real trouble, still be lonely as anything, and I'm not here to talk anybody into staying in something that's hurting 'em.
But if you're lying there wondering whether there's anything left under all the dust, this is where I'd look. Not at the big feelings. They're not answering the phone right now.
Look at the small automatic things your body still does for them when nobody's keeping score.
And then here's the part that actually changes something, and it's so simple it sounds dumb.
Say it out loud.

If your heart hurts in relationship and it cannot be shared with your partner, blame must and will go somewhere.
Recognize where.
You can't hold that much pain without a target.
So you aim it at yourself: "I'm too needy. Too sensitive. Too much."
Or you aim it at them: "They don't care. They're selfish. They're probably a narcissist."
Or you aim it at the relationship: "We're incompatible. This is toxic. I should leave."

The terror that your hurt doesn't matter.

So you protect yourself by making someone the villain.
Safer than discovering your heart isn't safe with the person you love most.

The heart that can't be shared becomes the heart that can't be healed.
And relationships die in that silence.
One unshared hurt at a time.
We solve that with vulnerability.
