How to Talk to Your Partner About Which Layers Are Slipping Without It Turning Into a Fight
If you've recognized that one or more layers of love have been slipping in your marriage, the next question is how to bring it up to your partner without the conversation collapsing into a fight, a list of grievances, or one of those exchanges where both of you walk away feeling worse than when you started.
Most couples get this conversation wrong. Not because they don't care. Because the impulse, when you've been carrying the awareness of a slipping layer alone for months or years, is to deliver everything you've been thinking all at once. You've been doing the noticing in private. You've built up a case. You've been mentally rehearsing how you'd explain it. And when you finally bring it up, the case comes pouring out, and your partner experiences it as an indictment instead of an invitation.
The conversation, done badly, can speed up the death of the very layer you're trying to save. Because your partner's nervous system, on the receiving end of an indictment, will go into defense, and once they're defending, they can't actually hear what you're saying. They'll respond to the attack instead of responding to the love that's underneath your concern. And the conversation will end with both of you further apart than when it started.
I want to walk you through the right way to have this conversation. Because there's a structure that works, and a structure that fails, and the difference is small but decisive.
Here's what fails first.
Don't lead with the inventory. The list of all the things you've noticed slipping. The catalog of evidence. The dates and the moments and the specific events that prove your case. Even if every item on the list is true, the list itself is the wrong vehicle for this conversation. Your partner cannot absorb a list. The list will feel like an attack. They'll start defending against the items one by one, and the conversation will become a debate about each instance instead of a conversation about the layer.
Don't open with "we need to talk." That sentence has been ruined for marriages. It carries a charge that tells your partner's nervous system to brace before you've said anything substantive. Whatever you say next will be filtered through the bracing.
Don't start with what they've stopped doing. The framing of the conversation as their failure to provide what you need will close them. Even if it's true. Even if you have legitimate concerns about something they used to do and stopped. Leading with their failure is the fastest way to ensure you don't get the layer back.
Don't have this conversation when you're activated. If you're feeling lonely or hurt or angry in the moment, do not bring it up in that moment. Wait until you're regulated. Until you can speak about the layer without the heat of the immediate disappointment driving the words.
Now here's what works.
You start by naming what you've been noticing in yourself, not in them.
That's the key move. You're going to talk about what you've been experiencing, not about what they've been doing. The conversation is going to be about your interior life and what you've noticed about your own state inside the marriage. They're going to be invited to listen to that, and then to share their own.
Here's the opener.
"There's something I've been noticing about myself lately, and I want to talk about it. Not as a complaint. As a thing I've been working on understanding. Can you give me about ten minutes to walk through it?"
That's the whole opener.
Notice what it does. It signals that you're bringing something thoughtful, not reactive. It tells them this isn't a fight. It asks for their attention rather than demanding it. It promises a contained conversation, not an open-ended one. And it puts the focus on you, not them, which gives their nervous system permission to relax.
If they say yes, you move into the substance.
The substance is a careful description of what you've been feeling about a specific layer, framed as something you've been observing in yourself.
You can say something like, "I've been noticing that I've been missing something in our relationship. I don't fully know how to name it yet, but I think it has to do with romance. With the small acts of pursuit we used to do for each other. I've been feeling the absence of that, and I've been wondering when it stopped, and I've been wondering whether that's something we could think about together."
Read that paragraph carefully. Notice what it doesn't do.
It doesn't blame them.
It doesn't list their failures.
It doesn't compare them to who they used to be.
It doesn't accuse them of anything.
It just describes what you've been feeling, names the layer in soft language, and invites them into a shared exploration.
The phrase "thinking about it together" is doing a lot of work. It tells them this isn't a problem you're handing them to fix. It's a question you're inviting them to consider with you. They're a collaborator, not a defendant.
Now, after you've said your piece, here's the next critical move.
You stop talking.
You don't fill the silence. You don't add caveats. You don't rephrase. You don't soften it further. You let the words you said sit in the air and give them time to respond.
Whatever they say next is data. Track it carefully.
If they say something receptive, like, "I think I've been feeling that too," or, "I didn't realize you were noticing that," or, "Tell me more about what you mean," then the conversation can deepen. Take the opening. Continue gently. Tell them more.
If they say something defensive, like, "What do you want from me," or, "I do plenty for you," or, "Is this about the thing last week," that's information too. They're not ready to hear it as an exploration. They're hearing it as an accusation, even though you didn't make one. Don't argue. Don't double down. Just say, "I'm not accusing you. I'm sharing something I've been feeling. I don't need you to fix it right now. I just wanted you to know what's been going on inside me."
That sentence, repeated calmly, is the de-escalator. It returns the conversation to the original frame. It tells their nervous system that the threat they're sensing isn't actually there.
If they still can't receive it, end the conversation.
You can say, "I think we can come back to this another time. I just wanted to put it in front of you. Thanks for hearing me."
Then drop it. Don't bring it up again that night. Don't bring it up the next day. Let what you said sit in their body for a few days without you adding anything to it.
Most of the time, even with a defensive partner, the words land. Just not in the moment you said them. They land later, when your partner is alone, driving, doing dishes, lying in bed. Their nervous system has had time to disarm. They can finally consider what you said without having to defend against it. And they often come back to you, sometimes a few days later, with their own version of the conversation. "I've been thinking about what you said."
That's the moment the real conversation happens.
Now here's the part most couples don't do, and it's the part that turns this into a real exchange instead of a one-sided complaint.
After you've shared what you've been feeling, you ask them what they've been feeling.
Not in a transactional way. Not in a "now it's your turn" way. You ask because you genuinely want to know.
You can say, "I've been telling you what's been going on in me. I want to know if there's something you've been noticing about yourself or about us that I haven't been tracking. I might be missing something on your side that's just as real."
This is the move that prevents the conversation from being one-directional. It signals to your partner that you understand they have an experience of the marriage too. That you don't think you're the only one with insight about what's happening between you. That you're inviting them to be in the same conversation, not just to react to yours.
Most partners, when invited this way, will say something. Maybe not immediately. Maybe they'll need a minute. But the invitation opens space for them to bring something they've been carrying that you haven't seen.
And whatever they say, you receive it.
You don't argue. You don't dismiss. You don't compare it to what you said. You don't tell them their concern is smaller than yours.
You receive it. You let it be real. You sit with it the same way you wanted them to sit with what you said.
That's what makes the conversation a real one instead of a delivery.
Two people sharing what they've been carrying. Both being heard. Both being taken seriously. Both willing to look at the marriage as something that has multiple dimensions and that requires both of them to participate in tending.
Now the final piece.
End the conversation without trying to solve everything.
The conversation about a slipping layer is not supposed to produce a solution that night. The conversation is supposed to open the topic. To name what's been quiet. To get both of you on record about what you've been feeling.
The solutions, the rebuilding, the small acts of revival, those happen over weeks and months, not in a single conversation.
So when the conversation has run its course, you can close it with something simple.
"I'm glad we talked. I want to keep talking about this over the coming weeks. We don't have to figure it all out tonight. I just wanted to start the conversation."
Then you stop. You don't try to schedule the next conversation. You don't make it a project. You let it be what it is. A first opening. A signal to both of you that the marriage is being attended to in a new way.
Couples who have this conversation correctly often describe a small but distinct shift in the days that follow. The air feels different. Both of you are watching each other more carefully. Both of you are trying to do small things to address what you said. Neither of you is announcing the trying. The trying is just happening.
That's how a marriage starts to come back.
Through one careful conversation that names what's been slipping, asks the partner about their own experience, and ends without trying to solve the whole thing.
That conversation is available to you tonight.
You don't have to wait for the right moment. The right moment is whenever both of you are not actively in another conflict. Whenever the day has settled. Whenever you're alone in a room together and there's space.
Use the opener I gave you.
Trust the structure.
Trust the silence after you've spoken.
Trust your partner enough to invite them into the conversation rather than presenting them with a verdict.
This is how marriages are saved. Not by grand gestures. Not by ultimatums. Not by sweeping declarations.
By careful conversations that name what's been quiet and invite both people to look at the marriage together.
Have the conversation.
Tonight, if you can.
It will probably be one of the most important things you do for your marriage this year.

What to Do When You and Your Partner Are Losing Different Layers at Different Speeds
There's a dynamic in long-term relationships that nobody warns you about, and it's one of the most painful and confusing things two people can live through together without naming it.
You and your partner are losing different layers of love at different speeds.
You might be in the early stages of losing romantic love while your partner is still fine on that layer but losing intellectual love. Or you might still feel emotionally connected while your partner is quietly losing the committed layer. Or you might be feeling the death of s*xual love while your partner thinks the marriage is fine because the layers they care about are still alive.
This is happening in most marriages. And almost nobody sees it for what it is.
What people see, instead, is that they and their partner are out of sync. They're having different experiences of the same marriage. One of them feels like things are okay. The other one feels like something is wrong. They argue about who's right. They argue about whether there's a problem. They argue about what the problem is. There's a Thing Called Pre-Couples Work, and Most Couples Have Never Heard of It
When couples come to me after tens of thousands of dollars of counseling somewhere else, I tell them something in the first session that surprises almost all of them.
I tell them they haven't actually started couples work yet.
They look at me like I've said something offensive. They've been in counseling for two years. Three. Sometimes longer. They've sat through more sessions than they can count. They've done the worksheets. They've read the books. They've followed every protocol their previous counselor offered.
And I'm telling them they haven't started.
So they ask me, reasonably, what I mean.
I tell them they've been in pre-couples work the whole time.
And until they understand the difference between pre-couples work and actual couples work, they're going to keep paying for sessions that aren't going to move them anywhere. Because pre-couples work is real, and it's necessary, and it has its own goals, but if neither the couple nor the counselor knows that's the phase they're in, they're going to confuse motion for progress and keep doing the same things forever.
Let me explain.
Couples work, the real thing, happens when I can bring two people close enough to each other in the room that I can show them how to open up to each other and they follow me there. The work is collaborative. The work is delicate. The work depends on both people being willing and able to do something specific, which is to drop their defenses, even briefly, in the presence of someone they've been hurting and someone who's been hurting them.
If both people can do that, even imperfectly, even with shaking hands, the work moves fast. Faster than people expect. Couples work, when it's possible, is some of the most beautiful work I get to do.
But couples work isn't always possible.
A lot of couples who come to me are nowhere near being able to do that yet. They're not close enough. The defenses are too high. The pain is too fresh, or too buried, or too unequal between them. Their nervous systems are still in too much war with each other to drop into anything intimate.
If I try to do real couples work with these couples, it doesn't take. They can't follow me there. The exercises I might use with a couple who's ready don't land. The questions don't open them. The closeness I'm trying to invite them into bounces off the wall they're each protecting.
If I push past their readiness, I make things worse. I create the appearance of progress that isn't actual progress. I produce sessions that feel meaningful in the moment and then evaporate the second they get back into their car.
So I don't push. I name what's happening. I tell them they're in pre-couples work, and I describe what that phase requires.
There are several things that signal a couple is in pre-couples work, but I want to talk about just one of them today, because it's the one that catches most people off guard.
It's whether they have anything resembling a shared narrative about what's happened in their marriage.
Let me explain what I mean.
A couple ready for couples work has something in common in how they understand their story. Not full agreement. They might disagree about details. They might disagree about who's more responsible for what. They might disagree about how they got here. But the basic shape of what's happened, the events, the harms, the losses, the meaning of the major moments, those are roughly aligned. They might be standing on opposite sides of the same room, but they're in the same room.
A couple in pre-couples work isn't in the same room. They're in two completely different houses. Their narratives about what's happened don't even overlap. The major events of their marriage are remembered differently, weighted differently, framed differently. They could each describe the last five years of their relationship and you would think they were describing two different marriages.
Here's an example, simplified, but it shows the shape.
A couple comes to me after an affair. They both agree the affair happened. They agree on the basic facts. He had an affair. She found out. They came to counseling.
That's where the agreement ends.
He arrives in the session full of guilt. He's been carrying the weight of what he did for months. He wakes up in the middle of the night thinking about it. He can barely look at her without his chest collapsing. And underneath the guilt, there's a layer of defensiveness he can barely contain, because every time she brings it up, he feels accused of something he's already accusing himself of, and the accusation makes him want to disappear.
She arrives in the session not actually feeling the pain yet. Not really. She's still in the part of the trauma where her body hasn't caught up to what happened. She's intellectually furious, but her grief hasn't landed. She's functional in a way that worries me. She's organized. She has a list of questions. She wants the timeline. She wants the details. She wants to understand what she's looking at, because her body hasn't yet allowed her to feel what she's looking at.
So I have a husband drowning in shame and defensiveness and a wife operating in cognitive overdrive while her actual feelings are still in shock.
These two people are not in the same room.
They're not even close.
If I try to do couples work with them in this state, it fails. He can't be in the room with her without flinching from his own shame. She can't be in the room with him without managing herself instead of feeling herself. Whatever closeness I try to invite gets blocked on both sides by completely different mechanisms.
This is pre-couples work.
In pre-couples work, my job isn't to bring them close to each other. My job is to help them each get into a state where being close to each other might eventually be possible. That work is real. It's necessary. It can take months. Sometimes longer. And during that time, I'm not running couples therapy. I'm running parallel individual processes inside a couples format, helping each of them get to the threshold where actual couples work becomes possible.
That's a completely different kind of session than what most people picture when they hear couples counseling.
In pre-couples work, the goals aren't the counselor's goals. The goals belong to the couple. And one of the most important things I do is help them figure out what their goals actually are.
Here's what most people don't realize about goals in this kind of work.
There's a default assumption in our culture that the goal of couples counseling is to make the couple as close and intimate and vulnerable as possible. That's not always the goal. That's the counselor's goal, sometimes, for a couple that doesn't share it. And when that mismatch happens, the work fails because the couple is being pulled toward something they didn't actually ask for.
Some couples come to me and they don't want to be deeply intimate. They want to be functional roommates who don't fight. That's their goal. They've decided that's what they can do, and they want to do it well. My job is to help them do that well. Not to push them toward something else.
Some couples come to me and they want to figure out whether to stay together. Not whether to be close. Whether to stay. That's their goal. The work I do with them is different from the work I'd do with a couple who's already committed and just needs help getting there.
Some couples come to me wanting full intimacy and depth and rebuilding everything. Great. That work has its own shape.
The point is that the goals belong to the couple. And in pre-couples work, defining those goals carefully, with them, is a huge part of what we're doing. Because if we don't define them, we'll be wandering. The couple will be confused about what they're trying to build. And we'll do session after session without any clear sense of what success would even look like.
A couple knowing they're in pre-couples work is vital. Because it changes everything about how they measure progress.
Let me give you an example of how this plays out badly when they don't know.
A couple in pre-couples work has a session. In the session, they manage one conflict pretty well. They listen to each other. They get a little vulnerable. They leave feeling closer than they have in months.
If they don't know they're in pre-couples work, they think the marriage is fixed. The one good moment in the session becomes the proof point. They cancel the next appointment. They go home riding the high of a single hour where things went well.
A few weeks later, the same dynamics are back. The fights are back. The distance is back. And now they're confused. Because they thought it was working.
It wasn't working in the way they thought. They had one good hour. That's not the same thing as being out of pre-couples work. They were still in the early phase. The real work hadn't even started. And by leaving early, they went home with the inflated belief that they'd done the thing, when actually they had taken one small step toward maybe being able to do the thing eventually.
A practitioner who doesn't help a couple understand this is, in my opinion, just taking money for an hour. Nothing long-term good is happening. The couple is paying for the experience of feeling temporarily better, not the actual work of building something durable.
It's not that the temporary feeling-better is fake. It's real. It just isn't the goal. The goal is to bring them to the place where they can do real couples work. And then to do that work. And then to bring them through it. That arc takes time. Pre-couples work is the bridge that gets them to the entry point.
If you're a couple reading this, I want you to consider something honestly.
If you've been in counseling for a while and don't feel like the marriage is fundamentally different than when you started, you might not be in failed couples therapy. You might be in pre-couples work that nobody named for you.
That's not a failure of your marriage.
It's a misunderstanding of what phase you've been in.
And the question for you isn't whether the work is failing. The question is whether your counselor is helping you see that you're in the bridge phase, defining your goals there, and gradually moving you toward the place where real couples work becomes possible.
If they are, stay in it. Pre-couples work is real and it's worth doing.
If they're not, if every session feels like the same hour repeated forever, if neither of you knows what you're working toward, if the small wins keep evaporating, you might need a counselor who can name the phase you're in and help you understand what kind of work you're actually doing.
Sometimes the most important thing a counselor can give you isn't a technique or a framework.
It's an honest description of where you are.
And if where you are is pre-couples work, you deserve to know that, so you can do that phase well, and so you can recognize when you finally cross over into actual couples work, and so you can stop expecting from one phase what only the other phase can deliver.
Most couples don't know any of this exists.
Now you do.

When couples come to me after tens of thousands of dollars of counseling somewhere else, I tell them something in the first session that surprises almost all of them.

I tell them they haven't actually started couples work yet.

They look at me like I've said something offensive. They've been in counseling for two years. Three. Sometimes longer. They've sat through more sessions than they can count. They've done the worksheets. They've read the books. They've followed every protocol their previous counselor offered.

And I'm telling them they haven't started.

So they ask me, reasonably, what I mean.

I tell them they've been in pre-couples work the whole time.

And until they understand the difference between pre-couples work and actual couples work, they're going to keep paying for sessions that aren't going to move them anywhere. Because pre-couples work is real, and it's necessary, and it has its own goals, but if neither the couple nor the counselor knows that's the phase they're in, they're going to confuse motion for progress and keep doing the same things forever.

Let me explain.

Couples work, the real thing, happens when I can bring two people close enough to each other in the room that I can show them how to open up to each other and they follow me there. The work is collaborative. The work is delicate. The work depends on both people being willing and able to do something specific, which is to drop their defenses, even briefly, in the presence of someone they've been hurting and someone who's been hurting them.

If both people can do that, even imperfectly, even with shaking hands, the work moves fast. Faster than people expect. Couples work, when it's possible, is some of the most beautiful work I get to do.

But couples work isn't always possible.

A lot of couples who come to me are nowhere near being able to do that yet. They're not close enough. The defenses are too high. The pain is too fresh, or too buried, or too unequal between them. Their nervous systems are still in too much war with each other to drop into anything intimate.

If I try to do real couples work with these couples, it doesn't take. They can't follow me there. The exercises I might use with a couple who's ready don't land. The questions don't open them. The closeness I'm trying to invite them into bounces off the wall they're each protecting.

If I push past their readiness, I make things worse. I create the appearance of progress that isn't actual progress. I produce sessions that feel meaningful in the moment and then evaporate the second they get back into their car.

So I don't push. I name what's happening. I tell them they're in pre-couples work, and I describe what that phase requires.

There are several things that signal a couple is in pre-couples work, but I want to talk about just one of them today, because it's the one that catches most people off guard.

It's whether they have anything resembling a shared narrative about what's happened in their marriage.

Let me explain what I mean.

A couple ready for couples work has something in common in how they understand their story. Not full agreement. They might disagree about details. They might disagree about who's more responsible for what. They might disagree about how they got here. But the basic shape of what's happened, the events, the harms, the losses, the meaning of the major moments, those are roughly aligned. They might be standing on opposite sides of the same room, but they're in the same room.

A couple in pre-couples work isn't in the same room. They're in two completely different houses. Their narratives about what's happened don't even overlap. The major events of their marriage are remembered differently, weighted differently, framed differently. They could each describe the last five years of their relationship and you would think they were describing two different marriages.

Here's an example, simplified, but it shows the shape.

A couple comes to me after an affair. They both agree the affair happened. They agree on the basic facts. He had an affair. She found out. They came to counseling.

That's where the agreement ends.

He arrives in the session full of guilt. He's been carrying the weight of what he did for months. He wakes up in the middle of the night thinking about it. He can barely look at her without his chest collapsing. And underneath the guilt, there's a layer of defensiveness he can barely contain, because every time she brings it up, he feels accused of something he's already accusing himself of, and the accusation makes him want to disappear.

She arrives in the session not actually feeling the pain yet. Not really. She's still in the part of the trauma where her body hasn't caught up to what happened. She's intellectually furious, but her grief hasn't landed. She's functional in a way that worries me. She's organized. She has a list of questions. She wants the timeline. She wants the details. She wants to understand what she's looking at, because her body hasn't yet allowed her to feel what she's looking at.

So I have a husband drowning in shame and defensiveness and a wife operating in cognitive overdrive while her actual feelings are still in shock.

These two people are not in the same room.

They're not even close.

If I try to do couples work with them in this state, it fails. He can't be in the room with her without flinching from his own shame. She can't be in the room with him without managing herself instead of feeling herself. Whatever closeness I try to invite gets blocked on both sides by completely different mechanisms.

This is pre-couples work.

In pre-couples work, my job isn't to bring them close to each other. My job is to help them each get into a state where being close to each other might eventually be possible. That work is real. It's necessary. It can take months. Sometimes longer. And during that time, I'm not running couples therapy. I'm running parallel individual processes inside a couples format, helping each of them get to the threshold where actual couples work becomes possible.

That's a completely different kind of session than what most people picture when they hear couples counseling.

In pre-couples work, the goals aren't the counselor's goals. The goals belong to the couple. And one of the most important things I do is help them figure out what their goals actually are.

Here's what most people don't realize about goals in this kind of work.

There's a default assumption in our culture that the goal of couples counseling is to make the couple as close and intimate and vulnerable as possible. That's not always the goal. That's the counselor's goal, sometimes, for a couple that doesn't share it. And when that mismatch happens, the work fails because the couple is being pulled toward something they didn't actually ask for.

Some couples come to me and they don't want to be deeply intimate. They want to be functional roommates who don't fight. That's their goal. They've decided that's what they can do, and they want to do it well. My job is to help them do that well. Not to push them toward something else.

Some couples come to me and they want to figure out whether to stay together. Not whether to be close. Whether to stay. That's their goal. The work I do with them is different from the work I'd do with a couple who's already committed and just needs help getting there.

Some couples come to me wanting full intimacy and depth and rebuilding everything. Great. That work has its own shape.

The point is that the goals belong to the couple. And in pre-couples work, defining those goals carefully, with them, is a huge part of what we're doing. Because if we don't define them, we'll be wandering. The couple will be confused about what they're trying to build. And we'll do session after session without any clear sense of what success would even look like.

A couple knowing they're in pre-couples work is vital. Because it changes everything about how they measure progress.

Let me give you an example of how this plays out badly when they don't know.

A couple in pre-couples work has a session. In the session, they manage one conflict pretty well. They listen to each other. They get a little vulnerable. They leave feeling closer than they have in months.

If they don't know they're in pre-couples work, they think the marriage is fixed. The one good moment in the session becomes the proof point. They cancel the next appointment. They go home riding the high of a single hour where things went well.

A few weeks later, the same dynamics are back. The fights are back. The distance is back. And now they're confused. Because they thought it was working.

It wasn't working in the way they thought. They had one good hour. That's not the same thing as being out of pre-couples work. They were still in the early phase. The real work hadn't even started. And by leaving early, they went home with the inflated belief that they'd done the thing, when actually they had taken one small step toward maybe being able to do the thing eventually.

A practitioner who doesn't help a couple understand this is, in my opinion, just taking money for an hour. Nothing long-term good is happening. The couple is paying for the experience of feeling temporarily better, not the actual work of building something durable.

It's not that the temporary feeling-better is fake. It's real. It just isn't the goal. The goal is to bring them to the place where they can do real couples work. And then to do that work. And then to bring them through it. That arc takes time. Pre-couples work is the bridge that gets them to the entry point.

If you're a couple reading this, I want you to consider something honestly.

If you've been in counseling for a while and don't feel like the marriage is fundamentally different than when you started, you might not be in failed couples therapy. You might be in pre-couples work that nobody named for you.

That's not a failure of your marriage.

It's a misunderstanding of what phase you've been in.

And the question for you isn't whether the work is failing. The question is whether your counselor is helping you see that you're in the bridge phase, defining your goals there, and gradually moving you toward the place where real couples work becomes possible.

If they are, stay in it. Pre-couples work is real and it's worth doing.

If they're not, if every session feels like the same hour repeated forever, if neither of you knows what you're working toward, if the small wins keep evaporating, you might need a counselor who can name the phase you're in and help you understand what kind of work you're actually doing.

Sometimes the most important thing a counselor can give you isn't a technique or a framework.

It's an honest description of where you are.

And if where you are is pre-couples work, you deserve to know that, so you can do that phase well, and so you can recognize when you finally cross over into actual couples work, and so you can stop expecting from one phase what only the other phase can deliver.

Most couples don't know any of this exists.

Now you do.

The Three Things Couples Counseling Is Actually For
When I sit with a couple, almost everything I'm trying to do, in any given session, comes down to three things.
Increase safety.
Decrease tension.
Increase moments of reaching and responding to each other.
That's it.
Everything else, every framework, every technique, every exercise, every homework assignment, every theory I've ever read, is in service of those three movements. If those three things start happening between two people, the marriage is healing. If those three things stop happening, no amount of technique is going to save the marriage, because technique without those three things is just polished disconnection.
I want to walk you through what each one actually looks like. Inside the body. In the room. In the marriage. Because I think most couples have never had these named for them, and once you can see them, you can start to track whether they're happening in your own home.
Safety.
I want to talk about what it means to not have safety in a marriage, because most people who don't have it don't know they don't have it. They think they do. They think safety means nobody's hitting them. They think safety means the relationship isn't violent. They think safety means the lights are on and the bills are paid and there's no infidelity.
That's not what I mean by safety.
The safety I'm talking about is the experience of being able to say something true to your partner without your nervous system having to brace for what comes next.
Most people in struggling marriages don't have this. They don't know they don't have it. The bracing has become so automatic that they don't register it as bracing anymore. They register it as just how they are.
Here's what the absence of safety looks like.
It looks like you rehearsing what you're going to say to your partner before you say it. Not for emphasis. For survival. You're calculating in advance how the sentence might land. You're editing the words. You're choosing your tone. You're planning your timing. The conversation hasn't even started, and you've already worked harder than most people work in their entire week, just to figure out how to say a normal thing to the person you live with.
It looks like you waiting for the right moment. The right mood. The right Tuesday. The right hour after dinner when they've eaten enough and watched enough TV and unwound enough that maybe, possibly, they can hear what you need to say. You've been carrying this thing for three weeks waiting for the moment, and the moment never quite arrives, and the thing you needed to say goes back into the drawer where it lives with all the other unsaid things.
It looks like you swallowing what you were about to say and saying nothing instead. Or saying a softer, smaller, less true version. Or saying it in a way that's so coded and indirect that your partner couldn't possibly understand what you actually meant. You've translated yourself into a language that doesn't communicate, just to avoid the cost of being clear.
It looks like you scanning their face when you bring something up, monitoring their micro-expressions, watching for the first signs that they're about to react in the way you've been bracing for. The scanning is constant. The scanning is exhausting. The scanning is one of the loneliest things a married person can do, because the person you're scanning is supposed to be the safest person in the world to you, and instead, they're the person whose face you have to read like an enemy.
It looks like you having entire conversations with them in your head that you never have out loud. The articulate, true, devastating versions of what you actually want to say. They live inside you. They don't get out. Because the cost of letting them out is higher than the cost of carrying them silently.
It looks like your body settling slightly when they leave the house and tightening slightly when you hear them come back. Not because you don't love them. Because being in their presence requires a kind of vigilance that being alone doesn't.
If any of this is true for you, you don't have safety in your marriage.
You have a marriage. But you don't have safety inside it.
And without safety, every other layer of the relationship is compromised. Because the things you'd need to talk about to keep the marriage alive can't get said. They get rehearsed and edited and translated and swallowed, and the marriage starts to be made up of all the things both of you didn't say.
Now here's what safety looks like when it's present.
It looks like you saying something hard without rehearsing it for three weeks first. Just saying it. Knowing your partner will be able to hear it. Knowing the saying of it isn't going to start a war.
It looks like your body relaxing in their presence. Not bracing. Resting. Because their nervous system isn't a threat to yours.
It looks like your face showing what you're actually feeling instead of managing what you're feeling for their comfort.
It looks like silences that aren't loaded. Where you can be in a room with them and not say anything and the silence is just silence, not a referendum on the marriage.
It looks like you being able to tell them when you're sad and not having to defend the sadness. Not having to explain it. Not having to make sure it's not their fault. Just being sad, in front of them, and having the sadness be allowed to exist.
That's safety.
That's the first thing I'm working on with every couple. Not because the other things don't matter. Because nothing else can grow if safety isn't there.
Tension.
Now I want to talk about tension. Because tension and the absence of safety are related but not the same.
Tension is what builds up in a marriage when problems don't get repaired. Every fight that doesn't end well leaves a residue. Every misunderstanding that doesn't get cleared up leaves a residue. Every small wound that doesn't get tended to leaves a residue. The residue accumulates. And after enough years, the residue is the marriage. The actual relationship is buried under so much accumulated tension that the people inside it can't even remember what it felt like before the residue was there.
Here's what high tension looks like.
It looks like you having the same fight over and over again, with slight variations, and never resolving it. The fight has been happening, in some form, for years. The specifics change. The structure doesn't. Both of you can predict, by the third sentence, exactly how the fight is going to unfold. And it does. And it ends the same way it always ends. And the residue gets a little thicker.
It looks like you both getting reactive faster than you used to. Things that wouldn't have caused a fight a few years ago now cause one. Not because the things are bigger. Because the residue is bigger. The threshold for activation has been lowered by years of unrepaired moments stacking on top of each other.
It looks like you both bringing up old fights inside new fights. The fight from years ago. The fight from before the kids. The fight from his mother's birthday. The fights are all live. None of them got buried properly, so they all keep showing up to the new ones.
It looks like the air being different in the house even when nothing is happening. There's a low-grade hum of pressure. Both of you can feel it. Neither of you names it. You walk through the house carrying it, and your bodies are tired in a way you can't trace to anything specific because the fatigue is the cumulative cost of living inside that hum.
It looks like s*x going cold, even when desire is technically still there. Bodies don't open under high tension. They might function. They don't open. And the absence of opening, over time, becomes its own additional layer of tension.
It looks like both of you flinching at small things. A tone of voice. A sigh. A door closing. A specific look. Your nervous systems have been trained to detect threat in subtle signals, because the subtle signals have, in the past, escalated into something painful.
It looks like you secretly counting how many days you can go without the next blowup. Like you're tracking the weather. Like you live in a place where storms come, and you've learned to read the sky.
If this is what your home feels like, you have high tension.
And the work isn't to resolve every individual fight. The work is to lower the overall pressure in the room so that the fights stop firing as easily, and the ones that do happen can actually be repaired.
Here's what low tension looks like when it's been built.
It looks like the air in the house being quiet. Just quiet. Not silent in a watchful way. Quiet in a settled way. Both of you walking through the rooms without bracing. Both of your bodies running at a lower baseline.
It looks like fights being shorter. Not because you're avoiding them. Because they don't have years of unrepaired tension fueling them anymore. The fight is just about the thing it's about. It ends when the thing is addressed. It doesn't sprawl into a referendum on the entire marriage.
It looks like both of you being able to apologize without choking on it. Because apology, when there's low tension, is just information. It doesn't require you to give up ground you can't afford to give up.
It looks like the small irritations of daily life staying small. The traffic. The dishwasher. The thing the kid forgot. None of it escalates. None of it becomes a fight about something else.
It looks like your bodies finding each other again. S*x. Touch. Closeness. Because bodies open in low tension and close in high tension, and a marriage that has lowered its tension is a marriage where the physical dimension comes back online without anyone having to schedule it.
That's what I'm working on, alongside safety. Lowering the tension in the room until both bodies remember what it felt like to live without bracing.
Reaching and Responding.
Now the third thing. The one I think is the most beautiful, and the one most couples don't know they've stopped doing until I name it for them.
Reaching and responding.
This is the actual lifeblood of a relationship. The small daily moments where one of you reaches for the other one, in any of a thousand quiet ways, and the other one responds.
Most couples in trouble have stopped reaching, or stopped responding, or both. They don't know they've stopped. The reaching and the responding became so unreliable for so long that both of them learned to operate without it. Each of them is now functioning as a solo agent inside a shared house, occupying overlapping logistics but no longer reaching toward each other and no longer responding when reached for.
Here's what the absence of reaching and responding looks like.
It looks like you walking into the room where they are, and them not looking up. Not because they're angry. Because they've learned not to track your entrance anymore. The tracking didn't lead anywhere. The reaching was met with too many missed responses. The reaching just stopped.
It looks like you saying something small at dinner and watching it fall into the air without being received. They heard the words. They didn't reach back. The sentence just hung there until the conversation moved on.
It looks like one of you having a hard day and not telling the other one, because the other one isn't a place where hard days get held. So the hard day gets carried solo. And the next one. And the next one. Until both of you are carrying full lives inside a shared house and neither of you is sharing the carrying.
It looks like the texts during the day stopping. The "thinking of you" stopping. The "how are you" stopping. The small contact through screens that used to keep you tethered when you were physically apart fades to nothing. And neither of you mourns the fading, because you stopped expecting it years ago.
It looks like sleeping in the same bed and not touching. Not even reaching across the small space between you. The space stays. The bodies stay separate. You wake up alone in a bed with another person.
If you're living inside a marriage where reaching and responding has died, you might not know it. You might just feel a low-grade chronic loneliness that you can't trace to anything specific. The marriage looks fine. You function together. The kids are okay. The bills get paid. And underneath, you're alone next to a person who's also alone next to you, and neither of you is reaching anymore, and neither of you would notice if the reaching disappeared completely, because it disappeared a long time ago.
Now here's what reaching and responding looks like when it's alive.
It looks like you walking into the room and them looking up. Just that. They look up. Their face changes a little. They acknowledge you crossed the threshold.
It looks like one of you saying something small and the other one receiving it. "I had a weird thing happen at work today." And the other one says, "Tell me." And then listens.
It looks like a hand on a back as you pass each other in the kitchen. A shoulder squeeze. A hair brush. A small daily physical contact that keeps the bodies tethered.
It looks like a text in the middle of a Wednesday afternoon that has nothing to do with logistics. "I was thinking about you." For no reason. Just because you crossed their mind.
It looks like one of you saying you're tired and the other one bringing you a cup of tea without being asked.
It looks like a question you didn't expect to be asked. "What's something you've been thinking about lately?"
It looks like both of you crying at a movie, and one of you reaching for the other one's hand without looking, and the hand being there, and meeting yours, and staying.
That's what I'm building toward. That third thing. The thing that's the actual texture of intimacy.
Couples don't fall apart because they fight too much. Couples fall apart because they stopped reaching for each other and nobody noticed when the reaching stopped.
So here's what I want you to take from this.
If you're in a marriage that's in trouble, the work isn't fancy. It isn't communication training. It isn't any of the elaborate frameworks you've heard about.
The work is three things.
Make the room safe enough that both of you can say true things without bracing.
Lower the tension in the air enough that small irritations stay small and bodies stop having to operate at constant alert.
Start reaching for each other again. And start responding when you're reached for.
Those three movements, repeated daily, slowly, patiently, are what brings a marriage back to life.
Everything else is in service of those three.
Don't get lost in the techniques. Don't get lost in the books. Don't get lost in the worksheets.
Make it safe.
Lower the tension.
Reach. And respond.
That's the whole work.
And if you can do those three things, even imperfectly, even slowly, even in small daily increments, you can rebuild a marriage you thought was gone.
I've watched it happen too many times to doubt it.
It works.
It just requires you to stop looking for the complicated answer and start doing the simple one.

The structure doesn't. Both of you can predict, by the third sentence, exactly how the fight is going to unfold. And it does. And it ends the same way it always ends. And the residue gets a little thicker.

It looks like you both getting reactive faster than you used to. Things that wouldn't have caused a fight a few years ago now cause one. Not because the things are bigger. Because the residue is bigger. The threshold for activation has been lowered by years of unrepaired moments stacking on top of each other.

It looks like you both bringing up old fights inside new fights. The fight from years ago. The fight from before the kids. The fight from his mother's birthday. The fights are all live. None of them got buried properly, so they all keep showing up to the new ones.

It looks like the air being different in the house even when nothing is happening. There's a low-grade hum of pressure. Both of you can feel it. Neither of you names it. You walk through the house carrying it, and your bodies are tired in a way you can't trace to anything specific because the fatigue is the cumulative cost of living inside that hum.

It looks like s*x going cold, even when desire is technically still there. Bodies don't open under high tension. They might function. They don't open. And the absence of opening, over time, becomes its own additional layer of tension.

It looks like both of you flinching at small things. A tone of voice. A sigh. A door closing. A specific look. Your nervous systems have been trained to detect threat in subtle signals, because the subtle signals have, in the past, escalated into something painful.

It looks like you secretly counting how many days you can go without the next blowup. Like you're tracking the weather. Like you live in a place where storms come, and you've learned to read the sky.

If this is what your home feels like, you have high tension.

And the work isn't to resolve every individual fight. The work is to lower the overall pressure in the room so that the fights stop firing as easily, and the ones that do happen can actually be repaired.

Here's what low tension looks like when it's been built.

It looks like the air in the house being quiet. Just quiet. Not silent in a watchful way. Quiet in a settled way. Both of you walking through the rooms without bracing. Both of your bodies running at a lower baseline.

It looks like fights being shorter. Not because you're avoiding them. Because they don't have years of unrepaired tension fueling them anymore. The fight is just about the thing it's about. It ends when the thing is addressed. It doesn't sprawl into a referendum on the entire marriage.

It looks like both of you being able to apologize without choking on it. Because apology, when there's low tension, is just information. It doesn't require you to give up ground you can't afford to give up.

It looks like the small irritations of daily life staying small. The traffic. The dishwasher. The thing the kid forgot. None of it escalates. None of it becomes a fight about something else.

It looks like your bodies finding each other again. S*x. Touch. Closeness. Because bodies open in low tension and close in high tension, and a marriage that has lowered its tension is a marriage where the physical dimension comes back online without anyone having to schedule it.

That's what I'm working on, alongside safety. Lowering the tension in the room until both bodies remember what it felt like to live without bracing.

Reaching and Responding.

Now the third thing. The one I think is the most beautiful, and the one most couples don't know they've stopped doing until I name it for them.

Reaching and responding.

This is the actual lifeblood of a relationship. The small daily moments where one of you reaches for the other one, in any of a thousand quiet ways, and the other one responds.

Most couples in trouble have stopped reaching, or stopped responding, or both. They don't know they've stopped. The reaching and the responding became so unreliable for so long that both of them learned to operate without it. Each of them is now functioning as a solo agent inside a shared house, occupying overlapping logistics but no longer reaching toward each other and no longer responding when reached for.

Here's what the absence of reaching and responding looks like.

It looks like you walking into the room where they are, and them not looking up. Not because they're angry. Because they've learned not to track your entrance anymore. The tracking didn't lead anywhere. The reaching was met with too many missed responses. The reaching just stopped.

It looks like you saying something small at dinner and watching it fall into the air without being received. They heard the words. They didn't reach back. The sentence just hung there until the conversation moved on.

It looks like one of you having a hard day and not telling the other one, because the other one isn't a place where hard days get held. So the hard day gets carried solo. And the next one. And the next one. Until both of you are carrying full lives inside a shared house and neither of you is sharing the carrying.

It looks like the texts during the day stopping. The "thinking of you" stopping. The "how are you" stopping. The small contact through screens that used to keep you tethered when you were physically apart fades to nothing. And neither of you mourns the fading, because you stopped expecting it years ago.

It looks like sleeping in the same bed and not touching. Not even reaching across the small space between you. The space stays. The bodies stay separate. You wake up alone in a bed with another person.

If you're living inside a marriage where reaching and responding has died, you might not know it. You might just feel a low-grade chronic loneliness that you can't trace to anything specific. The marriage looks fine. You function together. The kids are okay. The bills get paid. And underneath, you're alone next to a person who's also alone next to you, and neither of you is reaching anymore, and neither of you would notice if the reaching disappeared completely, because it disappeared a long time ago.

Now here's what reaching and responding looks like when it's alive.

It looks like you walking into the room and them looking up. Just that. They look up. Their face changes a little. They acknowledge you crossed the threshold.

It looks like one of you saying something small and the other one receiving it. "I had a weird thing happen at work today." And the other one says, "Tell me." And then listens.

It looks like a hand on a back as you pass each other in the kitchen. A shoulder squeeze. A hair brush. A small daily physical contact that keeps the bodies tethered.

It looks like a text in the middle of a Wednesday afternoon that has nothing to do with logistics. "I was thinking about you." For no reason. Just because you crossed their mind.

It looks like one of you saying you're tired and the other one bringing you a cup of tea without being asked.

It looks like a question you didn't expect to be asked. "What's something you've been thinking about lately?"

It looks like both of you crying at a movie, and one of you reaching for the other one's hand without looking, and the hand being there, and meeting yours, and staying.

That's what I'm building toward. That third thing. The thing that's the actual texture of intimacy.

Couples don't fall apart because they fight too much. Couples fall apart because they stopped reaching for each other and nobody noticed when the reaching stopped.

So here's what I want you to take from this.

If you're in a marriage that's in trouble, the work isn't fancy. It isn't communication training. It isn't any of the elaborate frameworks you've heard about.

The work is three things.

Make the room safe enough that both of you can say true things without bracing.

Lower the tension in the air enough that small irritations stay small and bodies stop having to operate at constant alert.

Start reaching for each other again. And start responding when you're reached for.

Those three movements, repeated daily, slowly, patiently, are what brings a marriage back to life.

Everything else is in service of those three.

Don't get lost in the techniques. Don't get lost in the books. Don't get lost in the worksheets.

Make it safe.

Lower the tension.

Reach. And respond.

That's the whole work.

And if you can do those three things, even imperfectly, even slowly, even in small daily increments, you can rebuild a marriage you thought was gone.

I've watched it happen too many times to doubt it.

It works.

It just requires you to stop looking for the complicated answer and start doing the simple one.

100 Ways Couples Lose Each Other Slowly Without Anyone Noticing
The Slow Loss of Curiosity
1. You stop asking what they're thinking about.
2. You stop wondering who they're becoming.
3. You assume you already know the answer.
4. You finish their thought without checking if you got it right.
5. You stop reading the things they're reading.
6. You stop listening to the music they're loving.
7. You stop asking about the friend they've been spending time with.
8. You stop asking what made them laugh today.
9. You stop noticing what's new in their inner world.
10. You start treating them like a finished book instead of an unfolding one.
The Slow Loss of Attention
11. You half-listen while looking at your phone.
12. You wait for them to finish so you can talk.
13. You miss the small thing they said that mattered.
14. You stop noticing when they walk into the room.
15. You stop noticing when they leave it.
16. You stop registering their tone changes.
17. You miss the look they gave you across the table.
18. You stop catching their bids for connection.
19. You stop watching them when they're not watching you.
20. You stop seeing them at all, even when they're right there.
The Slow Loss of Touch
21. The kiss goodbye gets shorter.
22. The hand on the back gets rarer.
23. The hug becomes a pat.
24. You stop reaching for them in your sleep.
25. You stop sitting close on the couch.
26. You stop touching them when you walk past.
27. The body language stops saying "I'm here."
28. The body language starts saying "Don't."
29. The space between you on the bed gets wider.
30. You forget what their skin feels like.
The Slow Loss of Words
31. "I love you" becomes a sign-off instead of a statement.
32. "Thank you" gets dropped from the small things.
33. "I'm sorry" gets shortened or skipped.
34. Compliments get rationed.
35. Pet names disappear without a ceremony.
36. The inside jokes go cold.
37. You stop telling them about your day.
38. You stop telling them what you noticed about them.
39. The good morning text becomes a logistics text.
40. You forget the last actual conversation you had.
The Slow Loss of Time
41. You stop protecting time together.
42. The work calendar wins every week.
43. The kids' calendar wins the rest.
44. Date night becomes a quarterly event.
45. Weekends become a checklist.
46. You scroll instead of turn toward them.
47. Bedtime becomes a relay race past each other.
48. Vacations turn into managed logistics.
49. You stop having unstructured time together.
50. You forget what it feels like to be bored together.
The Slow Loss of Repair
51. A small hurt goes unrepaired and gets filed.
52. A misunderstanding gets explained away instead of resolved.
53. The apology gets skipped because "they know."
54. The follow-up conversation never happens.
55. A pattern shows up and you both pretend not to see it.
56. The fight ends without resolution and you call it peace.
57. Resentment gets dressed up as preference.
58. You start avoiding the topic instead of addressing it.
59. The repair attempts get fewer and fewer.
60. The damage starts compounding silently.
The Slow Loss of Sex
61. You stop initiating because the answer might be no.
62. They stop initiating because it always feels like a request.
63. The window of opportunity gets shorter every month.
64. You stop flirting because it feels like work.
65. You stop being naked together casually.
66. You stop changing in the same room.
67. You stop talking about what you want.
68. You stop talking about what's changed.
69. The desire dies of neglect, not absence.
70. You become roommates with a shared past.
The Slow Loss of Friendship
71. You stop being each other's first call.
72. You stop telling them the small things first.
73. You stop laughing together.
74. You stop sharing the article, the meme, the moment.
75. You stop being a team in front of other people.
76. You stop defending each other behind closed doors.
77. You stop missing each other when you're apart.
78. You stop celebrating each other's wins.
79. You stop confiding.
80. You stop liking them, even though you still love them.
The Slow Loss of Self Inside the Relationship
81. You shrink to keep the peace.
82. You hide the parts of yourself that don't fit anymore.
83. You stop asking for what you need because asking takes too much.
84. You start calling your needs "too much."
85. You stop dreaming out loud.
86. You stop telling them when something hurts.
87. You stop expecting them to know.
88. You start performing instead of being.
89. You stop feeling like yourself when you're with them.
90. You forget who you were before this dynamic shaped you.
The Slow Loss That Becomes the End
91. You stop hoping it'll get better.
92. You start fantasizing about an exit you'd never take.
93. You start measuring time in years left, not years together.
94. You start saying "we" with quotation marks around it.
95. You start telling friends it's "fine" with a tone they catch.
96. You stop fighting because you stop caring enough to fight.
97. You stop feeling anything when they walk in.
98. You stop feeling anything when they walk out.
99. You wake up next to them and feel nothing.
100. You realize you didn't lose them in a moment. You lost them in a thousand mornings just like this one.

Here's what's happening in both bodies during that window.
The day is over. Whatever was going to get done has either been done or hasn't, and either way, it's too late to fix it now. The kids are asleep. The phones are usually starting to go away, or should be. The household is quiet. The lights are lower. The body is moving from vertical to horizontal, which is a significant physiological shift that affects the entire nervous system in ways most people don't consciously register.
And here's the key thing. Both people's defenses are down.
All day long, both of you have been carrying various forms of armor. Work armor. Parent armor. Public-facing armor. Social armor. The armor you wear to handle whatever the world throws at you. By the time you're brushing your teeth next to each other at 10:47pm, the armor is off. It's been off for a while. There's nothing left to perform for. Nobody is watching except each other, and after a certain number of years together, even that stops being a performance.
You are, in those fifteen minutes, more yourself than at any other time in the day.
And so is your partner.
Which means those fifteen minutes are the single highest-quality window for real contact between two adults who share a life, because both of them are operating without defenses, without performance, and without the noise of everything else.
And most couples are wasting them on their phones.
Or on logistics. "Did you remember to put the garbage out." "What time is your thing tomorrow." "Did you pay the electric bill."
Or on silence that isn't the connecting kind of silence. The transactional kind. The kind where two people are in the same bathroom but might as well be in different countries.

Use it tonight.

I have never, in fourteen years, planned something that was just for him. Just because I was thinking about him. Just because he crossed my mind and I wanted him to know."

Does he need to be planned for too?
Does the man who's been asked to show more initiative also need to be on the receiving end of initiative?

I was really choked up with my client. And I need to be honest with you about something before I tell you what it was. I almost didn't share this part of the story. Because it's the part that made me emotional on camera in front of clients. And counselors aren't supposed to do that. We're supposed to hold the room. We're supposed to be the steady thing. I am the steady thing. I have been the steady thing for thousands of couples across thousands of sessions.

But I am also human. And Tuesday got to me.

Because this woman did something for her husband that cracked him open in a way I've never witnessed a man crack open on screen. And what came out of him is the thing I need every woman in a long-term relationship to hear.

Here's what happened.

This couple had been doing real work. The sticky note on the refrigerator. "He shows. She receives. No grading." He'd been showing up. Cooking. Planning. Initiating. She'd been receiving differently. The marriage was moving. Not performing recovery. Actually moving. I could feel it through the screen every Tuesday.

And somewhere in the middle of all that movement, something shifted inside her that she didn't fully understand until she tried to describe it to me.

She said, "I've been so focused on receiving his effort differently that I didn't notice something obvious."

I said, "What's that?"

She said, "He's been planning things for me for three weeks. And in our entire marriage, I have never once planned something for him."

She let that sentence sit.

"Never. Not once. I've planned his birthday parties. But those are obligations. I've organized family vacations. But those are logistics. I have never, in fourteen years, planned something that was just for him. Just because I was thinking about him. Just because he crossed my mind and I wanted him to know."

She said, "I've spent so many years being the one who plans that it never occurred to me that he might need to be planned for too."

And when she said that on our Zoom call, I watched something move across her face that I can only describe as the expression of a woman who just realized she's been starving someone without knowing he was hungry.

Because here's the thing about this particular dynamic that nobody talks about.

We talk about men who stop initiating. We talk about women who carry the emotional load. We talk about the planning gap and the initiative gap and the mental load gap. And all of that is real and all of it matters.

But nobody asks the question she just asked.

Does he need to be planned for too?

Does the man who's been asked to show more initiative also need to be on the receiving end of initiative?

Does the person who's learning to show up also need to experience what it feels like to be shown up for?

The answer is yes. And it's a yes that almost nobody in the relationship conversation is saying out loud.

Because the narrative is one-directional. He needs to try harder. He needs to plan more. He needs to initiate. He needs to pursue.

And all of that is true.

But pursuit is not supposed to be a one-way street.

And this woman realized on a random Wednesday afternoon that her husband has been the object of exactly zero pursuit for fourteen years.

Zero.

She told me, "He has never been surprised by me. He has never come home to something I built for him. He has never been the one who gets to walk through the door and feel like someone was thinking about him while he was gone."

She said, "I've been so busy being the one who isn't pursued that I never realized he isn't pursued either. By anyone. Ever. Nobody in his life is planning things for him. Not his friends. Not his family. And definitely not me."

She said, "I don't think anyone has ever planned something for this man just because they wanted to see his face when he walked into it."

And then she said, "I want to do that. Before our next session. I want him to know what it feels like."

I said, "What are you thinking?"

She said, "I don't know yet. But I want it to be something that tells him I see him. Not the version of him that's been showing up for me. The version of him that exists when he's not performing husband. The version of him that nobody in this marriage has paid attention to in a very long time."

She said, "I want to plan something for the person he is. Not the person I need him to be."

That sentence gutted me.

Because that's the sentence that's been missing from this entire story.

He's been learning to show up as the husband she needs.

And she just realized she's never shown up for the person he actually is.

Not the husband. The person.

The man underneath the role.

The man who has interests she stopped asking about. Passions she stopped noticing. A whole interior world that she used to be curious about when they were dating and gradually stopped exploring once the marriage became about logistics and kids and the operational running of a shared life.

She didn't even have to tell me what she was going to plan. The fact that she was thinking about it this way told me something had fundamentally shifted inside her. She wasn't planning a date night. She wasn't booking a restaurant. She wasn't organizing an experience that she would also enjoy.

She was building something entirely for him.

About him.

Around who he is when he's not being a husband or a father or a provider.

She spent three days on it.

She told me later she almost gave up twice because she kept defaulting to things she would enjoy and then catching herself and saying, "No. This isn't about me. This is about him."

She said that was the hardest part. Realizing how many years she'd spent at the center of her own planning that she didn't know how to plan from someone else's center.

Saturday came.

She told him that morning to be free at two o'clock. Don't ask questions. Just be ready.

She said his face did something she'd never seen before. Not the nervousness she'd been watching for weeks while he planned things for her. Something else. Confusion. Like a man who just heard a sentence in a language he doesn't speak. He didn't know what to do with "I planned something for you." He had no category for it. No file. No precedent. She told me he stood in the kitchen holding his coffee and said, "For me?" like she'd just told him he won something he didn't enter.

For me?

Two words. And those two words told her everything about how long it had been since anyone in his life had built anything in his direction.

At two o'clock she drove. He sat in the passenger seat. She told me he was fidgeting the way she fidgets when she doesn't know what's coming. She'd never seen him fidget before. She realized she'd never seen him in the position of not being in control of the plan. He's either the one planning or the one who didn't plan. He's never the one being planned for. He didn't know where to put his hands.

She took him to a place about forty minutes outside of town. A buddy of his from college owns property out there. She'd called the buddy three days earlier and asked if they could use it for the afternoon. The buddy said yes. She asked the buddy what her husband used to love doing in college before life got practical and mortgages got real and hobbies became things other people have.

The buddy told her.

And she built the afternoon around it.

I'm not going to share the specific details of what she planned because it's personal to them and the details aren't the point. The point is what the afternoon represented.

She'd called his oldest friend. She'd asked what her husband used to love. She'd built an experience around a version of him that existed before she met him. A version she'd heard stories about but never pursued. A version that got buried under fourteen years of being a responsible adult who provides and shows up and handles things.

She planned an afternoon for the man he was before the marriage made him into the man she needed him to be.

And when they pulled up and he realized what she'd done and who she'd called and what this was about, he didn't say anything.

He got out of the car.

He stood in the driveway.

And he cried.

Not the way he'd cried before. Not the quiet eyes-wet thing that happens when something tender lands on him unexpectedly. Not the jaw-unclench exhale of a man whose effort just got received.

He put his hands over his face and he cried the way men cry when something reaches a part of them that hasn't been touched in so long they forgot it existed.

She stood next to him and she didn't say anything. She didn't comfort him. She didn't ask what was wrong. She let it happen. Because she knew, finally, after everything they'd been through, that this wasn't a cry that needed to be managed. This was a cry that needed to be witnessed.

He cried because someone planned something for him.

That's it.

That's the whole reason.

Not the activity. Not the location. Not the thoughtfulness of calling his college buddy. Not the effort she put in or the three days of planning or the forty-minute drive.

Because someone, for the first time in as long as he can remember, put him at the center of something.

Not as a provider. Not as a husband. Not as a father. Not as the person responsible for making sure everyone else's life works.

As him.

The him that existed before all the roles.

The him that nobody had pursued or planned for or been curious about in so long that he'd stopped expecting it.

She told me on our Zoom call, "He stood in that driveway and I watched him realize that nobody has done this for him in our entire marriage. And I watched him realize that he'd stopped believing anyone ever would."

And then she said the sentence that broke me on camera.

She said, "I've been so angry for so many years that he wasn't pursuing me. And I just found out that he's been just as unpursued as I was. He just never said anything. Because men don't say anything. They just stop expecting."

He just never said anything.

Because men don't say anything.

They just stop expecting.

I had to look away from the screen for a second when she said that. Because she just described about eighty percent of the men I've worked with in 36 years and she did it in three sentences.

Men stop expecting to be planned for.

Men stop expecting to be pursued.

Men stop expecting to be the center of someone's effort and attention and curiosity.

And they stop so quietly and so gradually that nobody notices. Not even them. They just slowly accept that their role in the relationship is to provide and to show up and to initiate and to try. And the trying flows in one direction. And they adjust to that direction so completely that when someone turns the current around and tries in their direction, they stand in a driveway with their hands over their face because they forgot what it feels like to be the destination instead of the vehicle.

That's what she gave him on a Saturday afternoon.

The experience of being the destination.

And he wept.

Not because he's weak. Because the destination had been closed for so long that the arrival of someone at its door was overwhelming. The door hadn't opened in years. And when it opened, everything behind it came flooding out.

They spent the afternoon together. Doing something he loved. Something she'd never asked about because she'd been so consumed with what she needed from him that she stopped being curious about what he needed from life.

She told me they drove home and he held her hand for forty minutes without letting go. He wasn't performing connection. He was holding onto someone who'd just seen him. Not the husband version of him. The real one. The one underneath.

And on our Zoom call that Tuesday, when I asked him how the weekend was, he said the thing I've never heard a man say in 36 years.

He said, "I've been married for fourteen years and Saturday was the first time I felt like my wife knows who I am."

Not loves me.

Knows who I am.

Those are different things.

You can love someone for decades without ever knowing who they are underneath the role they play in your life.

And you can know someone in a single afternoon if you're willing to stop needing them long enough to see them.

She saw him.

Not the husband.

Him.

And he felt it.

For the first time.

In fourteen years.

She said, "I didn't know what I was missing by never planning for him. I thought the imbalance in our marriage was that he didn't plan enough for me. The real imbalance was that neither of us was planning for each other. He just started first."

She said, "And when I finally did it, when I finally pursued him the way I've been begging him to pursue me, I understood something I've never understood before."

She said, "Initiative is terrifying. Building something for someone you love and not knowing if it will land is the most vulnerable thing I've ever done. And he's been doing it for three weeks. Every time he plans something for me, he is doing the scariest thing I've ever done once. And I've been grading it."

That's when I had to look away from the screen.

Because that's the sentence.

That's the sentence that could save every marriage that's stuck in the planning gap.

If the person who's been demanding more initiative would try initiating once, just once, they'd understand what it costs. And they'd never grade it again.

She understands now.

Not because I told her.

Because she felt it in her own body.

The terror of building something for someone you love and standing in a driveway watching their face to see if it lands.

That's what he's been feeling every time.

And now she knows.

And she will never grade his effort the same way.

Not because of a sticky note.

Because she finally stood where he's been standing.

And it changed everything.
