I watched a man at Starbucks today at 515am spend 85 minutes with over 25 suggestions trying to fix his wife's pain.
She failed the bar exam.
He had no idea how to be with her.
So I refilled my already too strong cold brew and began:
You think the greatest relationship skill is knowing what to say.
It is not.
The greatest skill you will ever learn in love is this:
To sit with another human’s pain
and not try to fix it.
To stay.
To listen.
To let their feelings exist in the room without rushing to control them.
Most of us were never taught how to do this.
We were taught to offer solutions.
We were taught to cheer people up.
We were taught to say, “Look on the bright side,” or “At least it’s not worse,” or “You just need to…”
That is not connection.
That is management.
When your partner is hurting, your nervous system feels it as danger.
Their tears, their sadness, their anger, their confusion, all of it lights up your body.
You feel blamed, even when they never said the words.
You feel accused, even if they are just talking about their day.
You feel like you are failing, just because their eyes look heavy.
So you do the fastest thing you know.
You fix.
You explain.
You defend.
You give advice.
You interrupt.
You say, “You know what you should do…”
You say, “You are taking it too personally…”
You say, “You always do this…”
You think you are helping, and something deep inside you really is trying to help,
but what your partner’s nervous system hears is:
“I cannot hold your pain.”
“Your feelings are too much.”
“Please stop being how you are in front of me.”
So they shut down.
Or they get louder.
Or they get harsh.
Or they go numb.
And both of you are now in pain,
but neither of you feels understood.
Listening to pain without fixing is not passive.
It is one of the most intense things you will ever do.
It means you let their feelings touch you.
It means you let your heart be moved by what happened to them,
even if you do not agree with every detail.
It means you are willing to feel uncomfortable,
so they do not have to feel alone.
That is the whole point.
Your partner does not need a judge.
They need a witness.
Someone who can say, with their eyes and their voice and their silence:
“I see that this hurts.”
“I can feel that this matters to you.”
“I am not going anywhere while you feel this.”
Why fixing does not work:
Fixing puts the spotlight back on you, your ideas, your logic. Their experience disappears.
Fixing moves too fast. Pain needs to be seen before it can move.
Fixing is usually your way of escaping your own discomfort, not their suffering.
Fixing often sounds like criticism, even when you think it sounds like wisdom.
Fixing tells their nervous system, “Your feeling is a problem to solve,” not “Your feeling is welcome here.”
When you learn how to be with pain instead of fixing it, everything changes.
Imagine this:
Your partner comes home, eyes tired, and says, “I feel like nobody hears me at work. I feel invisible.”
Old habit:
You say, “Just speak up more,” or “You are overthinking it,” or “You hate that job anyway.”
Their body hears: “You are wrong to feel this. You should already know how to fix it.”
New skill:
You pause.
You soften your face.
You let your shoulders drop.
You look right at them and say,
“Tell me more.”
“Where did you feel that the most today.”
“I can see how defeated you look. That hurts to see.”
“I want to understand what this feels like inside you.”
You have not solved anything yet.
You have done something far more important.
You have made their inner world a place that is allowed to exist in front of you.
You have told their nervous system,
“You are not alone inside this feeling.”
That is what heals.
Sometimes your partner will talk for five minutes and then say,
“I feel better. I just needed to say it out loud.”
You did nothing, and you did everything.
You did not argue with reality.
You did not edit their story.
You did not rush them out of their own heart.
You stayed.
This is why listening to pain is the greatest relationship skill you will ever learn:
Because pain is the doorway to the real relationship.
When somebody shows you where they ache,
they are handing you the map to their history,
their childhood,
their past betrayals,
their deepest fears.
If you can hold that map with care,
they will hand it to you again.
If you fold that map up and tell them to stop being dramatic,
they will learn to hide it from you.
Over time, the couples who thrive are not the ones who avoid pain.
They are the ones who have built a shared ritual around it.
The ritual goes something like this:
One person says,
“Something in me is really hurting right now.”
The other answers,
“I am listening. I want to understand.”
Then the hard part.
You let there be silence.
You let them search for words.
You let them stammer, or cry, or get confused.
You do not rush in with a lesson.
You stay curious, not corrective.
You can ask questions, if they are gentle questions:
“What was the hardest moment today.”
“What did you tell yourself about you when that happened.”
“Where do you feel it in your body right now.”
Questions that deepen, not questions that debate.
And when they are done, you do not grade their feelings.
You do not evaluate if they are “fair.”
You do not compare it to your own.
You say things like:
“I did not realize it hurt that much.”
“I get why that would feel awful.”
“It makes sense your body reacts that way.”
“Thank you for trusting me with this.”
That is emotional resonance.
My nervous system meets your nervous system in the exact place that is hurting.
No fixing.
No lecturing.
No performance.
Just two humans, both a little softer,
both a little less alone.
Will there be a time for problem solving. Of course.
But problem solving only works after pain has been held.
If you skip that part, every solution will feel like a rejection.
If you include that part, even imperfect solutions will feel like love.
So if you want one sentence to carry into your relationship, let it be this:
“When you hurt, my job is not to fix you, my job is to stay with you.”
Learn that, practice that, live that,
and your relationship will change in ways no technique book can touch. See less

Not because you’re fragile.
Not because you’re lacking emotional strength or stability.

It touches belonging.
It touches safety.
It touches survival.

It isn’t just “a feeling.”
It’s a full-body experience.
It tightens the chest.
It shortens the breath.
It floods the body with adrenaline.
It wakes up grief that’s been asleep for years.
It makes your mind spin and your heart ache and your body brace for emotional impact.
Especially when the rejection comes from someone you love.
Because this isn’t just anyone rejecting you.
This is the person your nervous system has marked as home.
This is the person your body relaxes around (or desperately wants to).
This is the person you leaned toward with hope.
And when home feels like “no,” everything inside you revolts.
But this is where things get deeply misunderstood.
Most of the world tries to teach you to outrun rejection.
Detach.
Act unbothered.
Be proud.
Be strong.
Convince yourself you don’t need what you desperately need.
Pop psychology gives you walls disguised as wisdom: “It’s their problem.”
“It doesn’t matter what they think.”
“Don’t let them have power over you.”
Those ideas sound empowering.
But what they really teach you is to numb instead of heal.
To disconnect instead of understand.
To shut down instead of soften.
They teach you to be less human, not more whole.
Because rejection doesn’t hurt because you’re weak.
Rejection hurts because you’re wired for love.
And love is supposed to matter.

They experience rejection in totally different universes.

They feel erased.
Their brain doesn’t say: “They’re busy.”
Their brain says: “I don’t matter. I’m alone again. I’ll disappear if I don’t fight for love.”
The body remembers every moment in life where closeness slipped away: Parents who weren’t emotionally available.

Moments they were told they were “too much.”
Moments they begged for connection and didn’t get it.
So when rejection shows up, it doesn’t feel like “today.”
It feels like a lifetime storm waking back up.
So they don’t quietly sit with pain.
They escalate.
They repeat themselves.
They text again.
They explain harder.
They talk faster.
They plead.
They chase.
It’s not obsession.
It’s not emotional immaturity.
It’s survival trying to stay alive.

But theirs happens in silence.
They don’t erupt.
They implode.

It sounds like failure.

“I’m never enough.”
“No matter what I do, it isn’t right.”
“There must be something wrong with me.”

That being vulnerable meant being hurt, overwhelmed, shamed, or invaded.

They don’t escalate.
They withdraw.
Not because they don’t care.

They shrink their needs to survive.

They disconnect to survive.

They’re flooded.
They’re overwhelmed.
They’re scared.

One who disappears to stop hurting.

Nobody taught you that rejection needs two nervous systems breathing together, not two egos defending themselves.

It becomes hopelessness.
It becomes shutdown.

When rejection is softened, connection grows.

It’s to slow your reach so your nervous system doesn’t overwhelm the very closeness you’re fighting for.

It hurts because you attach.
It hurts because love matters to you.

Not shameful.
Not weak.
Human.

Don’t seek your intellectual equal.
Seek your emotional equal.
It sounds romantic to say you want someone who can “keep up with you.”
Someone sharp. Someone brilliant. Someone who can think fast, argue well, analyze deeply.
But here’s what we rarely talk about:
When the relationship hurts,
when your heart’s aching,
when your nervous system’s trembling,
intellect doesn’t save you.
It often hurts you more.
Because the person who matches you intellectually can debate your pain so convincingly
that you start doubting your own inner world.
You say, “That hurt me.”
They say, “Here’s why it shouldn’t have.”
You say, “I feel alone with you.”
They say, “I’ve been present. You’re just misinterpreting.”
You say, “My body feels anxious when this happens.”
They say, “Calm down. That reaction isn’t logical.”
Now your feelings aren’t feelings anymore.
They’re arguments to dismantle.
Your heart’s now a thesis.
Your pain’s now a courtroom.
And suddenly you’re defending your humanity instead of being held in it.
That’s what happens when you choose intellect over emotional maturity.
An intellectual equal can win the argument.
An emotional equal can keep your soul intact.
And when your soul’s at risk, it doesn’t care how clever the dialogue is.
Look for the person who can feel you.
The one who notices the tremble in your voice before you name your sadness.
The one who says, “Wait… something just shifted in you,” instead of pushing forward.
The one who values your nervous system more than their need to be right.
Look for the one who says:
“I believe you.”
“Your feelings make sense here.”
“I care more about your heart than about being correct.”
That’s emotional intelligence.
Not fixing.
Not analyzing.
Not turning your suffering into a problem set to solve.
Emotional maturity is the ability to:
Sit beside pain without needing to control it.
Hold tenderness without shaming it.
See hurting without minimizing it.
And here’s the part most people don’t understand:
An emotionally mature partner doesn’t dismiss your intellect.
They honor it by making your emotional world safe enough for your intellect to exist freely.
Because only when you feel safe do your ideas flow openly.
Only when you feel understood do your thoughts come alive.
Only when your heart can breathe do your insights deepen.
Emotional safety isn’t a luxury in love.
It’s the foundation.
If your nervous system’s constantly defending itself,
your mind can’t ever fully relax.
And if your mind can’t relax,
there’s no intimacy… only negotiation.
Don’t fall for “impressive.”
Fall for “present.”
Not the partner who always has the perfect reasoning,
but the one who reaches for your hand when your voice cracks.
Not the partner who explains away your tears,
but the one who lets their chest ache because you’re hurting.
Not the partner who teaches you why you shouldn’t feel what you feel,
but the one who finds reverence in the fact that you feel deeply at all.
Because love isn’t about who wins.
Love’s about who stays.
Who stays curious.
Who stays tender.
Who stays with your humanity when it’d be easier to disappear into logic.
The right partner will still challenge your thinking.
But they’ll never debate your existence.
They won’t argue your pain.
They’ll honor it.
Don’t just choose someone who matches your mind.
Choose someone who protects your heart.
Regulates with your nervous system.
Meets your vulnerability as a privilege, not a burden.
Your true equal isn’t the one who thinks as brilliantly as you do.
It’s the one who can sit in the fire of emotion with you
without trying to extinguish it immediately.
The partner who makes your nervous system feel like home
will always take you farther than the partner who only makes your mind feel entertained.
That’s the difference.
That’s emotional equality.
And that’s where love lives. See less

If you’re building your relationship on rules, agreements, and conditions… you’re in more trouble than you think.
If you’re sitting at the kitchen table having the conversation that sounds like:
“From now on, we’re going to…”
“Let’s agree that next time you’ll…”
“Can we promise that we’ll always…”
“Let’s make a rule about how we handle this in the future…”
I want you to pause.
Those conversations don’t mean you’re wise, mature, disciplined, or “doing the work.”
They mean something much more painful.
They mean you hurt each other…
and you don’t know what to do with the pain.
Rules in romantic relationships don’t get created out of emotional safety.
They get created out of emotional fear.
A rule is almost always born at the exact moment you don’t know how to love each other through a wound.
You didn’t know what to do with the hurt.
You didn’t know how to stay with the pain.
You didn’t know how to slow down and feel what happened between you.
So your brain did what the brain does when the heart has no map.
It built one.
Not one for closeness.
One for protection.
And protection feels like structure.
Protection feels like order.
Protection feels like “Now we have a plan.”
But let’s tell the truth:
Rules are coping strategies dressed up as maturity.
They say:
“I don’t trust your nervous system not to hurt me again.”
“I don’t trust my nervous system to handle your reaction.”
“I don’t trust us to stay connected when we’re in pain.”
So instead of learning how to repair…
instead of learning how to be with hurt in real time…
instead of learning how to meet vulnerability with tenderness…
You build a fence around the next time.
“We’ll handle it better next time.”
“If this comes up again, we’ll do it differently.”
“Let’s have a plan so this never happens again.”
But here’s the problem:
Romantic love isn’t a policy manual.
It isn’t a behavioral training program.
It isn’t a performance agreement.
It’s two nervous systems, two histories, two attachment templates crashing into each other…
and trying desperately to feel safe.
When you build rules instead of learning repair, you’re not healing anything.
You’re building a fragile structure on top of an untreated wound.
And do you know what happens?
You follow the rule… until the nervous system gets scared again.
You follow the agreement… until your trauma gets activated.
You follow the plan… until the part of you that’s hurting is louder than the part of you that promised.
Then the rule breaks.
And when the rule breaks, the hurt is even worse.
Not only did you get hurt again…
Now there’s shame.
Now there’s failure.
Now there’s “You promised.”
Now there’s, “We agreed.”
Now there’s, “See, nothing changes.”
Rules don’t create safety.
Emotional connection does.
Rules don’t heal betrayal.
Repair does.
Rules don’t build trust.
Feeling seen, felt, and held does.
If your relationship needs a rulebook to function, it means the actual skill you need has never been learned:
How to sit inside a rupture.
How to stay with each other when the pain shows up.
How to slow the moment down enough to feel what happened.
How to reveal what’s hurting instead of defending what’s right.
How to move toward each other instead of away.
A healthy relationship doesn’t run on rules.
It runs on emotional responsiveness.
It runs on:
“I hurt you. I see it. Stay with me.”
“I’m scared. Don’t solve it. Just be here.”
“I didn’t mean to, but the impact matters. I care.”
“Let’s repair this, not police it.”
If you find yourself constantly negotiating “how to behave,”
it’s not because you’re disciplined or thoughtful.
It’s because your heart is starving and your nervous system is terrified.
Don’t build a structure over the wound.
Learn to be with the wound.
That’s where real intimacy begins.

50 Relationship “Rules” That Won’t Save You (and usually make things worse)

2. “We’ll never raise our voices again.”
3. “We’ll always use calm tones, no matter what.”
4. “We’ll wait 24 hours before talking when we’re upset.”
5. “We’ll schedule every hard conversation.”
6. “We’ll never go to bed upset.”
7. “We’ll never argue in front of the kids.”
8. “We’ll always see things from each other’s perspective before responding.”
9. “We’ll only talk about feelings when we’re both emotionally regulated.”
10. “We’ll only discuss conflict at the perfect time.”
11. “We’ll have weekly relationship check-ins and fix everything there.”
12. “We’ll never bring up the past again.”
13. “We’ll only focus on the future.”
14. “We’ll forgive and forget.”
15. “We’ll just move forward.”
16. “We’ll create boundaries so this never happens again.”
17. “We’ll just try harder next time.”
18. “We’ll be more mindful.”
19. “We’ll give each other grace.”
20. “We’ll just choose love.”
21. “We’ll stay positive and avoid negativity.”
22. “We’ll take turns being the strong one.”
23. “We’ll keep things light to avoid conflict.”
24. “We’ll focus on gratitude instead of problems.”
25. “We’ll be more intentional.”
26. “We’ll never use certain words again.”
27. “We’ll use time-outs when things feel intense.”
28. “We’ll follow the ‘rules of communication’ perfectly.”
29. “We’ll always speak respectfully.”
30. “We’ll only talk when we’re calm.”
31. “We’ll assume positive intent every time.”
32. “We’ll always remember we love each other.”
33. “We’ll remind ourselves it’s just our trauma.”
34. “We’ll try to be more understanding.”
35. “We’ll just trust each other more.”
36. “We’ll commit to growing together.”
37. “We’ll recommit to the relationship.”
38. “We’ll stop criticizing.”
39. “We’ll practice appreciation.”
40. “We’ll never threaten to leave.”
41. “We’ll never say hurtful things.”
42. “We’ll set boundaries around conflict.”
43. “We’ll avoid triggering topics.”
44. “We’ll stay curious, not furious.”
45. “We’ll just communicate better.”
46. “We’ll love each other more intentionally.”
47. “We’ll remember we’re on the same team.”
48. “We’ll stay solution-focused.”
49. “We’ll be adults about it.”
50. “We’ll just be better for each other.”
All of these sound wise.
They sound mature. They sound conscious. They sound emotionally evolved.
But they’re missing the only ingredient that actually heals:
The ability to sit with pain together, respond to it with tenderness, and repair in real time.
If you don’t learn repair…
You’ll build rules instead of connection. You’ll build structure instead of safety. You’ll build agreements instead of intimacy.
And you’ll still be hurting.
Because healing doesn’t come from better choreography.
It comes from being able to hold each other when it hurts. See less

Here are the top 7 phrases that sound sincere but often contain hidden criticism in troubled relationships:
1.
"I'm just trying to help"
Often used to justify unwanted advice or control, implying the partner is incapable of handling things themselves
2.
"I'm sorry you feel that way"
Appears apologetic but actually deflects responsibility and subtly suggests the partner's feelings are the problem, not the speaker's actions
3.
"We need to talk"
While seemingly promoting communication, this phrase frequently signals incoming criticism and creates immediate anxiety
4.
"I'm not mad"
Usually said when clearly upset, this contradicts obvious emotional cues and makes the partner feel crazy for perceiving the anger that's actually present
5.
"I don't want to fight about this"
Appears conflict-avoidant but often serves to shut down legitimate concerns and prevent necessary discussions
6.
"You always say that"
Presents as pattern recognition but actually dismisses the current concern by generalizing and exaggerating, making the partner feel unheard
7.
"I love you, but..."
The "but" negates the love statement and signals incoming criticism, creating a painful association between love and correction See less

Emotional intelligence isn’t about sounding enlightened, staying calm under pressure, or always knowing what to say.
It’s the courage to recognize something most people don’t want to admit:
The past isn’t “gone” if it hasn’t been repaired yet.
It still lives in the nervous system.
It still echoes in the body.
It still pulls at the heart when love feels risky.
When someone gets triggered, they aren’t being dramatic.
They aren’t being weak.
They aren’t “dwelling” on things they should’ve let go of.
Their body’s remembering where connection broke.
Their nervous system’s remembering where trust collapsed.
Their heart’s remembering the moment it didn’t feel held, protected, or chosen.
Emotional intelligence is the ability to see that what you call “overreacting” is often just a wound trying to find safety.
It’s understanding that your partner isn’t fighting you because they want conflict.
They’re reacting because something inside them didn’t get comfort, reassurance, or repair when it desperately needed it.
The moment wasn’t cleaned up.
The conversation never finished.
The hurt got buried… but it never actually healed.
And buried pain doesn’t disappear.
It hardens.
It tightens.
It waits for the next moment that feels even remotely similar, and then it rushes back like it never left.
This is why people shut down.
This is why people get angry so fast.
This is why people become guarded, defensive, withdrawn, anxious, avoidant, or “too emotional.”
They weren’t taught to let go.
They were forced to survive.
So emotional intelligence isn’t telling someone: “Just move on.”
“Stop bringing it up.”
“That was years ago.”
“You’re living in the past.”
Emotional intelligence sounds more like: “I can see this still hurts.”
“I didn’t realize how deeply this landed in you.”
“Let’s slow down… I want to understand.”
“You shouldn’t have had to hold that alone.”
“If it still lives in you, then it still matters.”
Because the truth is simple: If love broke you, love needs to help heal you.
If connection caused the wound, connection is what repairs it.
Healing isn’t pretending the past didn’t happen.
Healing is letting it finally be cared for.
Stop asking people to forget pain their nervous system’s still carrying.
Stop dismissing what shaped the way they trust, attach, love, and protect themselves.
If something still hurts, it isn’t “the past.”
It’s the present asking to be honored, repaired, and finally made safe.
That’s emotional intelligence. See less

I got your back little guy, always.

The only way I truly know I’m in contact with you
is when I can see a little bit of my suffering living inside you.
Not because I want you to hurt.
Not because I need you to collapse with me.
Not because I crave drama, intensity, or emotional chaos.
It is because if I am in pain and you stay perfectly untouched by it…
I don’t experience you as “strong.”
I experience you as **far away.**
If I am breaking
and you remain emotionally neutral, composed, analytical, or “calm,”
I don’t feel held.
I feel *alone in your presence.*
And being alone next to the person I love
hurts worse than being alone by myself.
I don’t need you to fix me.
I don’t need you to rescue me.
I don’t need a solution, a lesson, a perspective shift, or a lecture.
What I need is contact.
Human contact.
Emotional contact.
I need to know that my sadness actually touches you.
That my fear doesn’t bounce off you.
That my grief lands in your nervous system somewhere.
I need to see in your eyes that there is a soft ache there.
A gentle tenderness.
A slight heaviness.
A shift in your breathing, your posture, your face.
Something that wordlessly says:
“I feel that this hurts you.
And because I love you…
it matters to me enough that I can feel a little of it too.”
That is contact.
Contact is when I don’t feel like I’m performing pain in front of an audience.
Contact is when I don’t feel like a case study you’re evaluating.
Contact is when I do not feel like a problem you’re trying to stabilize.
Contact is when I feel joined instead of observed.
Felt instead of managed.
Met instead of handled.
We talk endlessly about independence, emotional regulation, staying calm, being strong, “not taking things personally,” and “not letting someone else’s emotions destabilize you.”
But here is the truth our bodies know even when our minds deny it:
We are built to be felt.
The nervous system does not relax because someone near us is calm.
It relaxes because someone near us **cares**.
It relaxes because someone’s heart bends toward us instead of staying rigid.
It relaxes because love shows up not intellectually…
but emotionally.
If I am drowning
and you stand on the shore shouting instructions about breathing techniques,

Or do they disappear?

in the moment you expose your vulnerability
and watch what the other person does with it.

“I’m hurting”
“I feel far from you”

and the other person stays present, soft, emotionally available,

“I’m hurting”
“I feel far from you”
“I need you right now”
and the other person:

gets irritated
turns defensive
gets logical
minimizes
withdraws
attacks
or makes it about them…
your nervous system says:
“This is dangerous.”

“I should be able to self-regulate.”

Disconnection destroys it.
Every time.
So stop telling hurting people:
“Find safety inside yourself.”
Ask a better question:
“When you reach for the person you love,
do they meet you there…
or do they vanish?”
Because that answer is where safety lives. See less

When I’m busy drowning in shame… beating myself up… tearing myself apart inside... I have almost no capacity to truly be there for you.
Not because I don’t care.
Not because I don’t love you.
Not because your pain isn’t real or deserving.
But because shame is a full-body hostage situation.
When shame takes over, my nervous system collapses inward.
I stop being in the room with you.
I disappear into myself.
My mind becomes a courtroom where I am the only defendant…
and the verdict is already guilty.
“I failed.”
“I’m the problem.”
“I ruin everything.”
“I’m not enough.”
“I’m what hurts people.”
And when my brain is screaming those kinds of sentences at my nervous system,
I don’t have bandwidth left to attune to you.
You see someone who looks distant, reactive, numb, defended, cold, dismissive, unavailable.
But what you don’t see is the emotional bloodbath happening on the inside.
Shame hijacks empathy, not because I don’t feel,
but because there is no oxygen left for anything beyond survival.
Shame converts your pain into proof of my inadequacy.
Your tears become reminders that I am failing you.
Your upset becomes confirmation that I’m not good enough.
So instead of leaning toward you,
I retreat into myself trying desperately to survive the internal beating.
And then I do things that confuse and hurt you:
I defend.
I argue.
I explain.
I shut down.
I withdraw.
I get logical.
I minimize.
I disappear emotionally.
And to you it looks like I don’t care.
But the truth is, I’m not ignoring your pain.
I’m drowning.
And drowning people can’t swim for two.
Shame is not sadness.
Shame is not regret.
Shame is not accountability.
Shame is annihilation.
It is the belief that *I* am the problem, not my behavior.
It is the internal collapse that says, “You’d be better off without me.”
It is the silent self-hatred that convinces me I deserve to be punished, not forgiven.
And when I’m trapped in that state,
I don’t abandon you because you aren’t important.
I abandon you because my nervous system thinks *I am collapsing as a person*.
One of the most misunderstood realities in relationships is this:
Sometimes I can’t show up for your emotions
because I haven’t learned how to treat myself gently enough to survive mine.
If you want me available,
I have to learn to stop destroying myself inside first.
Because when I’m not at war with myself,
I have space for your pain instead of reacting to it.
When I am not shaming myself,
I am able to say, “I hurt you. I care. I’m here,”
instead of disappearing into self-defense.
When I am not bleeding on the inside,
I can actually hold you instead of trying to outrun my own emotional collapse.
This is why shame is so devastating in love.
You don’t just lose connection with me.
I lose connection with myself.
And once I lose myself, I can’t bring myself to you.
Healing isn’t about “being better” at comforting others.
It’s about learning how to be kinder to ourselves
so compassion has room to exist in the first place.
Because when I stop tearing myself apart…
I finally have enough emotional breath to stay present.
I finally have the strength to say, “Tell me. I’m listening.”
I finally have the capacity to sit in the fire with you without disappearing.
And then I’m not just physically there.
I’m emotionally there.
Fully there.
Humanly there.
With you. See less

Avoidant = adj. Distant and cold in manner. stand-offish. aloof.
The avoidant personality type had to develop ways to not feel.
To feel was to be judged, or worse, punished, annihilated.
A clever set of pre-verbal strategies were developed, far before speech, to minimize sensations and emotions inside.

The other half, the anxious person who screams from the rooftops what they are feeling while being simultaneously addicted to not being heard, will be discussed another time.
The avoidant has now grown into somebody that is a good person.
They rarely have intentions of hurting another.

They are running from how painful it is to feel.

Here’s the truth almost nobody wants to face about romantic conflict:
Your grammar school teacher on the playground was right.
It really doesn’t matter who “started it.”
Because in adult romantic love, the fight never actually starts where you think it starts.
By the time one partner finally says something critical… By the time someone blurts, “You always…” By the time someone snaps, sighs, withdraws, or raises their voice…
That argument is already hours old.
Sometimes days old.
Sometimes years old.
The first words of a fight are never the beginning.
They’re just the moment the volcano finally cracks the surface.
What couples don’t understand is that arguments don’t live in conversations.
They live in the nervous system.
They live in the quiet resentments you didn’t resolve.
They live in the nights you went to bed hurt but silent.
They live in the mornings you acted “fine” when your body wasn’t fine at all.
When a relationship is distressed, the fight runs like background software.
It follows you to work.
It lives in your chest while you’re grocery shopping.
It’s there when you laugh with friends.
It’s there when you’re pretending everything’s okay.
So when couples say things like: “We’ve only fought twice this month.”
That isn’t actually what’s happening.
Your words only collided twice.
Your systems have been in the fight the entire month.
Your body has been bracing. Your heart has been guarded. Your mind has been rehearsing the next round without you even realizing it.
This is why distressed love is so exhausting. It doesn’t clock in and out. It doesn’t wait for “big” conversations. It lives inside you.
So when you argue and immediately say: “Well YOU started it…” You’re missing the real problem.
The moment you enter the fight… You’re already part of the pattern.
Because this isn’t about a single sentence spoken too sharply. It’s not about the tone of voice one time. It’s not about the thing that happened “right now.”
It’s about the long runway that led to that moment.
It’s about fear that hasn’t been held. Sadness that hasn’t been named. Loneliness that hasn’t been understood. Rejection that hasn’t been soothed.
If you want to heal a relationship, stop obsessing over who threw the first punch in the argument.
Start asking: How long has this fight been living in our bodies? When did we stop feeling safe together? When did we stop knowing how to repair? When did we stop reaching for each other when we were hurting?
Healing doesn’t come from proving who’s right. It doesn’t come from “winning” the conflict. It doesn’t come from better logic, better explanations, or better debate skills.
Healing starts the moment both people can say: “We’re trapped in this pattern together. We both contribute to it. And we both want out.”
Because that’s the only way forward.
The argument isn’t your enemy. The pattern is.
And the moment you stop trying to identify the villain… And start trying to understand the wound…
That’s the beginning of coming back to each other. See less

Walking on Eggshells
You say you are walking on eggshells in your relationship.
Most people mean the same thing when they say that.
It means:
One wrong word and the room explodes.
One honest feeling and the silence drops.
One attempt to say, “I am hurting,” and suddenly you are defending yourself for hours.
So you adjust.
You rehearse.
You edit.
You swallow.
You carry.
That is one kind of walking on eggshells.
That is fear.
But there is another kind that almost nobody talks about.
And if you do not learn to tell the difference, you will either stay in emotional danger far too long or you will leave a relationship that still had a chance to heal.
The first kind is what you already know.
You are not choosing your words because you want to be thoughtful.
You are choosing your words because you are terrified.
You think things like:
If I bring this up, they will roll their eyes.
If I say I am lonely, they will tell me I am too sensitive.
If I mention the past, I will be told to get over it.
If I show my tears, I will be punished for being dramatic.
That is not communication.
That is survival.
In that version of walking on eggshells, you are not learning anything new about yourself or your partner.
You are just trying not to get hit emotionally.
You are trying not to trigger the same old blow up, shutdown or stonewalling.
It is a nervous system strategy.
Your body says:
Keep the peace or you will pay for it.
Now let us talk about the other kind.
When couples come to me and they are truly ready to try again, something surprising happens.
They start walking on eggshells in a different way.
They slow down.
They pause more.
They think before they speak, but not from terror.
They are practicing something.
That something has a name:
Discernment.
Discernment is what happens when you begin to learn vulnerability and you are not good at it yet.
You are trying to:
Catch the first spark of anger before it turns into an attack.
Notice the fear under your criticism before you throw it at your partner.
Feel the lump in your throat before it becomes sarcasm or shutdown.
You are still walking carefully, but for a different reason.
You are not thinking,
“How do I keep them from getting mad at me”
You are thinking,
“How do I say what is true without hurting us both more”
That is the difference.
Fear eggshells sound like:
“I cannot say that or I will pay for it.”
Discernment eggshells sound like:
“This matters to me. I want to say it in a way that gives us a chance to stay connected while we talk about it.”
In fear eggshells, your whole body is tight.
You are small.
You are performing safety for the other person.
In discernment eggshells, your body is still nervous, but you are curious.
You are trying to stay honest and kind at the same time.
When you start learning vulnerability, you will feel awkward.
You will stumble over your words.
You will start a sentence and realize it is turning into blame.
You will stop and try again.
It will feel like:
“I am walking on eggshells, but I am doing it on purpose because I am trying not to repeat the same relational injuries.”
This kind of carefulness is not a red flag.
It is often the very first sign of growth.
The question you must ask yourself is not,
“Am I walking on eggshells”
The question is,
“Why am I walking on eggshells, and what happens when I crack one”
If you are in fear eggshells and you crack one, you get:
Rage
Mocking
Withdrawal
Cold punishment
Sarcasm
Character attacks
If you are in discernment eggshells and you crack one, it is different.
You might get:
“Ouch, that stung, can we slow down and try again”
or
“I got defensive just now, but I know you are trying, let me take a breath”
You might see your partner struggle, but still stay.
You might see them fumble, but come back and say,
“I see what you were trying to say, I lost you for a moment, let us try again.”
That is the difference between danger and growth.
You will still feel scared in both.
You will still hesitate in both.
You will still overthink in both.
But in one, your nervous system eventually learns,
“I can mess up and still be loved.”
In the other, your nervous system learns,
“I exist to manage another person’s emotional storm, and if I slip, I pay.”
So take a moment and really sit with this:
When you talk to your partner about something that matters, do you feel like you are studying them so you do not get hurt
Or do you feel like you are studying yourself so you can show what hurts without destroying the room
One is walking on eggshells to avoid eruption.
The other is walking with discernment to build something new.
If you want a simple way to tell where you are, ask yourself three questions:
1. Do I have room to be clumsy
Can I say something badly and then come back and repair without being shamed for it
2. Do I ever leave a hard conversation feeling closer
Not lighter because I stayed quiet, but closer because I told a small piece of the truth and it landed
3. Do I see my partner trying too
Not perfect, not polished, but genuinely trying to notice their own defensiveness and soften it
If the answer is no to all three, you are not in discernment.
You are in danger.
If even one of them is starting to be yes, there is something to work with.
Because vulnerability is not pretty at the beginning.
It is messy.
It is shaky.
It is full of half sentences and long pauses and eyes that suddenly look twelve years old.
It sounds like:
“I am scared to say this.”
“I do not want to attack you, but something hurts.”
“I am afraid you will hear this as blame and I am trying really hard not to do that.”
“I can feel myself getting sharp, can we slow down so I do not turn this into a criticism”
That is also walking on eggshells.
But this time you are holding the egg in your own hands.
You are protecting something fragile in you, not tiptoeing around a bomb in them.
If you recognize yourself in this, try telling the truth in one small new way:
“Right now I am not just scared of what you will say. I am also scared of what I will say. I want us to learn a different way and I am clumsy at it. Will you practice with me”
If your partner can meet that with even a little bit of softness, you are not alone on the eggshells anymore.
You are both learning discernment.
And that is the difference between a relationship you must escape
and a relationship that might finally be ready to heal. See less

This is how I help couples heal that moment when they trigger each other...
That instant...
It’s not loud. It’s not dramatic. It’s not the shouting. It’s not the withdrawal. It’s not even the fight.
It’s the moment right in between.
The moment when the critical partner fires the shot… …and immediately feels the weight of shame crash down on them.
This is the moment we rarely slow down for. This is the moment everyone misses. This is the moment that needs the most tenderness.
Because for some people, criticism isn’t cruelty. It’s self-protection.
It’s the nervous system screaming, “I can’t afford to get hurt here. I need control. I need some distance. I need to strike first so I don’t collapse.”
But right behind it? Right behind the sharp tone, the cold words, the edge in their voice…
There’s exhaustion. There’s overwhelm. There’s shame so deep it almost knocks the breath out of them.
And if we do not linger here with compassion, we’ll never understand them.
Imagine this:
You’ve spent your whole life believing you cannot afford vulnerability. Not because you don’t want it. But because life taught you it wasn’t safe.
So you build a fast-response system.
You misinterpret disappointment as danger. You misread closeness as exposure. You experience emotional uncertainty as threat.
And in one split second you protect yourself by being critical. You go sharp. You go firm. You go superior. You go “let me tell you what you did wrong.”
And two seconds later?
Shame crashes in like a tidal wave.
“Why did I say that?” “Why am I like this?” “Why can’t I just be kind?” “Why do I keep hurting the person I love?”
So now you’re not just defensive… You’re ashamed. You’re scrambling. You’re under-resourced. You’re drowning internally.
Nobody sees that part.
They just see the critical person. They just see the sharpness. They just see the blame.
They don’t see the war happening inside the person doing it.
This is why real couples healing requires gentleness.
Not softness that excuses harm. Not permissiveness. Not indulgence.
Gentleness.
The kind that says: “Oh wow. This is tender. Something inside you is trying desperately to protect you. And the cost is that it hurts the person you love. Let’s stay right here and not rush out of this moment. Let’s not shame you for protecting yourself. Let’s understand why you had to.”
When I sit with someone who does this, I don’t see a bully. I don’t see a monster. I don’t see an “emotionally immature partner.”
I see someone whose nervous system has been fighting for survival for a very, very long time.
Someone who learned early in life: “If I open, I lose.” “If I soften, I’ll break.” “If I relax, I won’t survive.”
So they built a life strategy: Be sharp. Be prepared. Be critical before anyone can criticize you.
And then they fell in love.
And that strategy… started hurting someone they care about.
That’s where the heartbreak is.
So to the critical partner: No one has probably ever lingered with you here. No one has probably ever slowed the moment down long enough to notice your shame. No one has probably ever said: “This is where you need comfort, not punishment. This is where you need support, not humiliation. This is where you need someone beside you, not against you.”
You’re not bad. You’re not broken. You’re not incapable of love.
You’re just tired of living behind armor.
And to the partners who receive the criticism: Your pain matters. Your wounds matter. The way this affects you matters deeply. But healing doesn’t come from destroying the critical person.
It comes from finally understanding the battlefield they’re standing on.
If we can learn to linger in this moment… The second after the criticism, The first second shame appears, The fragile moment where the guard is confused and the heart is exposed…
That’s where change begins.
That’s where real repair happens. That’s where compassion meets accountability. That’s where love grows its roots.
In that quiet, trembling space where someone says: “I protect myself like this because I never learned a safer way… …and I’m finally ready to try.”
We begin there.
The couple inhales my compassion for each of their specific triggers. 
Then they soon can do this without me for each other. See less

in honesty

You don’t actually know what your relationship is made of…
until life stops being polite and starts being real.
Not when it is easy to love.
Not when affection costs nothing.
Not when problems are small and solvable by a good night’s sleep.
Not when you both still have energy, patience, and hope.
You learn what your love is built from
when something hits your world so hard that your nervous system can’t pretend anymore.
When death walks into your life.
When illness steals your illusion of invincibility.
When money disappears and shame creeps in.
When your partner collapses emotionally.
When your family becomes chaos and you cannot hide from it.
When your childhood wounds come roaring back.
When their unresolved trauma surfaces and fills the room.
When the story you thought your life would be shatters in front of you.
That is when the real relationship shows up.
Because crisis strips the relationship naked.
Every coping strategy appears.
Every defense mechanism wakes up.
Every childhood strategy for survival reactivates.
Every unhealed place inside both of you starts pulsing.
You see who runs.
Who freezes.
Who numbs.
Who blames.
Who attacks.
Who disappears behind stone walls of self-protection.
You also see something else:
Who softens instead of sharpens.
Who turns toward instead of turning away.
Who can stay in the room emotionally when pain is screaming.
Who can breathe with you instead of fixing you.
Who can say, “This is terrifying… come here,” instead of, “Figure it out.”
This is the moment you discover if your relationship was built for comfort
or built for life.
Because life will ask things of you that romance never mentions.
It will ask whether your partner can hold your shaking hands.
Whether they can tolerate your grief without needing it to be quieter.
Whether they can sit with your fear without making it your flaw.
Whether they can listen when your words are messy and your heart is bleeding.
Whether they can remain human with you, instead of becoming your judge, your fixer, or your ghost.
Crisis reveals something enormous:
Do you have compassion in your relationship
or do you only have preference?
Compassion is different from being nice.
It is different from giving advice.
It is different from trying to stay “positive.”
It is different from tough love.
It is different from telling someone to focus on gratitude while they are drowning.
Compassion is the ability to let another person’s experience matter inside your body.
It is the courage to feel with them, not around them.
It is the willingness to let their pain touch your nervous system without collapsing into panic, control, or dismissal.
It is the choice to protect connection instead of protecting your comfort.
We live in a world obsessed with improvement, productivity, hacks, fixes, optimization, spiritual bypassing, and emotional shortcuts.
We have tools, apps, programs, inspirational quotes, and endless books.
But none of those things teach you how to sit beside someone who is breaking apart.
No one teaches us how to look into the eyes of the person we love
and say:
“I do not know how to fix this. But I will not leave you in it alone.”
That is a human skill.
A nervous system skill.
A love skill.
And when you do not have it, crisis exposes you.
Some people discover in crisis that their partner never learned how to care.
Not deeply.
Not with presence.
Not with emotional attunement.
They discover they have a partner who can offer solutions, logic, harsh reality, lectures, distance, silence, or irritation…
but not soothing, not tenderness, not refuge.
Others discover the opposite.
They discover that when everything collapses, they are suddenly held in a way they have never been held before.
They discover depth.
Warmth.
Stability.
A groundedness that becomes sacred.
Crisis tells the truth.
It tells you whether your relationship has just been “functional companionship”
or “true attachment.”
It tells you whether you are bonded deeply
or simply coordinated well.
And it leaves you with questions that matter:
Does your partner rise in compassion
or drown in defensiveness?
Do they step toward your pain
or try to outrun it?
Do you become safer together
or lonelier together?
And let us be honest:
It is not just about them.
Crisis will expose you too.
It will show whether you can tolerate another person’s vulnerability.
Whether you can stop needing to control.
Whether you can stay instead of disappearing emotionally.
Whether you can soften instead of criticize.
Whether you can care without needing to turn the moment into a lesson, a debate, or a self-protection exercise.
Because relationships are not truly measured in the easy years.
They are measured in the moments when someone whispers:
“I am scared.”
“I am ashamed.”
“I am lost.”
“I am hurting.”
“I do not know what happens next.”
And the other person says, not perfectly, not heroically, but sincerely:
“Then we face it together. I am here. I am not leaving your heart alone in this.”
If your relationship has this… it has something rare.
If it does not… crisis will not be kind about revealing it.
Life will bring storms no matter how hard you try to avoid them.
The question is never, “Will we face hardship?”
The question is:
When the world shakes…
do we collapse into separation…
or do we become gentler, slower, more human,
and more together than we have ever been?
When you see your partner the most scared, in the most confusing anger...
How they talk to you...

When someone cries, we rush to quiet them.
“Shh… shh… it’s ok. Calm down. Don’t cry. Take a breath. Settle. Be strong.”
We do this to children.
We do this to partners.
We do this to friends.
We do this to ourselves.
Not because we are cruel.
But because unfiltered pain makes us uncomfortable.
Because loud emotions wake up our own grief, fear, guilt, helplessness, and shame.
Because we have been trained our entire lives that big feelings are problems to control, not experiences to let exist.
But crying is not the problem.
Crying is the nervous system saying:
“This hurts.”
“This matters.”
“This is too big to hold quietly.”
“My body needs help carrying this.”
And instead of honoring that…
we teach silence.
We teach swallowing grief.
We teach numbing the scream.
We teach collapsing the sob into a tiny, acceptable whimper.
We teach emotional suffocation… and then wonder why people feel disconnected, depressed, numb, explosive, anxious, and ashamed of their own humanity.
What if we did the opposite?
What if we stopped trying to turn down the volume of pain…
and helped it release?
Instead of “shh, it’s ok,”
what if we said:
“It sounds awful. Let it out.”
“Make louder sounds.”
“Belt it. Scream it. Cry like your body is begging you to.”
“I won’t leave. I can handle your tears.”
“You don’t have to hold this alone.”
Do you know what happens when someone feels safe enough to cry fully?
Their breathing changes.
Their chest softens.
Their jaw unlocks.
Their nervous system unclenches.
Their body shakes out the trauma, instead of storing it.
Their shame melts because someone stayed with them instead of shrinking away.
Loud tears are truth finding air.
They are grief moving.
They are fear exiting the body.
They are heartbreak being honored instead of buried alive.
And yes… it’s raw.
Yes… it’s messy.
Yes… it’s uncomfortable.
Yes… it might break your heart to witness.
But this is what emotional intimacy actually is.
Not fixing.
Not managing.
Not silencing.
Not coaching someone out of their pain.
Staying.
Holding.
Hearing.
Letting the storm exist without shutting down the sky.
We don’t need quieter emotions.
We need safer spaces for louder truth.
So the next time someone cries, and you feel that instinct rise up to calm them, shrink them, tidy their grief…
Pause.
Maybe they don’t need to be calmed.
Maybe they need permission to be real. See less

17 Judgments That Make an Anxious Partner Spiral
(and Guarantee the Relationship Gets More Chaotic)
If you're anxious in love, you know exactly what it feels like to be set off by a single sentence, a single tone, a single eye roll. Your nervous system processes rejection at lightning speed. Your body reacts before your mind even understands what happened.
And if you love someone anxious, you probably have no idea how fast your words can detonate panic, shame, anger, and shutdown all at once.
Here are the 17 judgments that make an anxious partner's fear explode inside them, even if you swear you didn't mean them that way. And then I'll show you what to say instead so you don't pour gasoline on their nervous system.
1. “You're overreacting.”
What they hear:
Your feelings are wrong. You're too much. Calm down.
Inside:
Instant panic. Their body screams, “I'm alone in this.”
Say instead:
“I can see you're overwhelmed. I'm here. Let's slow down together.”
2. “I can't deal with you right now.”
What they hear:
You're too difficult to love.
Inside:
Abandonment alarm fires at full volume.
Say instead:
“I need a short pause so I can come back and be present with you.”
3. “You're always upset about something.”
What they hear:
You're exhausting. You're a problem.
Inside:
Shame mixes with desperation, and they cling harder.
Say instead:
“It seems like something's hurting. I want to understand it with you.”
4. “Here we go again.”
What they hear:
You're predictable in the worst way.
Inside:
Their stomach drops. Their chest tightens. Fight or cling.
Say instead:
“Something got activated. Let's take it slowly.”
5. “You need too much.”
What they hear:
Your needs are a burden.
Inside:
Crushing self blame mixed with terror of losing you.
Say instead:
“I want to figure out what you need and how we can do this together.”
6. “Stop being so sensitive.”
What they hear:
Your emotions are a flaw.
Inside:
They try to shut down what can't be shut down.
Say instead:
“I can see this touched something real. Talk to me.”
7. “You're imagining things.”
What they hear:
Your intuition is worthless.
Inside:
Self doubt spirals into panic.
Say instead:
“Something about this feels threatening to you. I want to understand why.”
8. “You read into everything.”
What they hear:
You're broken.
Inside:
Every painful interpretation intensifies.
Say instead:
“Your mind's working fast. Let's walk through what you're feeling.”
9. “You're making a big deal out of nothing.”
What they hear:
You're dramatic. You're wrong.
Inside:
They feel abandoned inside the pain.
Say instead:
“It's a big deal because it's hitting something important in you.”
10. “You're acting crazy.”
What they hear:
You're unlovable.
Inside:
Deep shame. Survival panic.
Say instead:
“I know you're hurting. Let's sit with it together.”
11. “You're twisting my words.”
What they hear:
You're untrustworthy.
Inside:
The fear of misunderstanding becomes unbearable.
Say instead:
“It seems like something felt off in what I said. Let's slow it down.”
12. “Don't put your emotions on me.”
What they hear:
Your feelings aren't my problem.
Inside:
Total aloneness.
Say instead:
“I want to know what's happening for you.”
13. “You always think the worst.”
What they hear:
Your fear is ridiculous.
Inside:
Fear magnifies.
Say instead:
“When fear comes up, I want to help you feel grounded.”
14. “I'm tired of comforting you.”
What they hear:
You're a burden.
Inside:
They collapse inside.
Say instead:
“I want to support you, but I need a minute to collect myself.”
15. “You never trust me.”
What they hear:
You're the reason we fail.
Inside:
Fear multiplies into guilt.
Say instead:
“I know trust is hard sometimes. I want to rebuild it with you.”
16. “You're being dramatic.”
What they hear:
Your pain is invalid.
Inside:
Pain doubles.
Say instead:
“It looks like this hit something deep. Let's slow down together.”
17. “I can't talk to you when you're like this.”
What they hear:

17 Judgments That Make an Anxious Partner Spiral

(and Guarantee the Relationship Gets More Chaotic)

If you're anxious in love, you know exactly what it feels like to be set off by a single sentence, a single tone, a single eye roll. Your nervous system processes rejection at lightning speed. Your body reacts before your mind even understands what happened.

And if you love someone anxious, you probably have no idea how fast your words can detonate panic, shame, anger, and shutdown all at once.

Here are the 17 judgments that make an anxious partner's fear explode inside them, even if you swear you didn't mean them that way. And then I'll show you what to say instead so you don't pour gasoline on their nervous system.

1. “You're overreacting.”

What they hear:

Your feelings are wrong. You're too much. Calm down.

Inside:

Instant panic. Their body screams, “I'm alone in this.”

Say instead:

“I can see you're overwhelmed. I'm here. Let's slow down together.”

2. “I can't deal with you right now.”

What they hear:

You're too difficult to love.

Inside:

Abandonment alarm fires at full volume.

Say instead:

“I need a short pause so I can come back and be present with you.”

3. “You're always upset about something.”

What they hear:

You're exhausting. You're a problem.

Inside:

Shame mixes with desperation, and they cling harder.

Say instead:

“It seems like something's hurting. I want to understand it with you.”

4. “Here we go again.”

What they hear:

You're predictable in the worst way.

Inside:

Their stomach drops. Their chest tightens. Fight or cling.

Say instead:

“Something got activated. Let's take it slowly.”

5. “You need too much.”

What they hear:

Your needs are a burden.

Inside:

Crushing self blame mixed with terror of losing you.

Say instead:

“I want to figure out what you need and how we can do this together.”

6. “Stop being so sensitive.”

What they hear:

Your emotions are a flaw.

They try to shut down what can't be shut down.

Your intuition is worthless.

Self doubt spirals into panic.

You're broken.

What Is Love Addiction Really?
We all need to be touched, loved, understood, seen... gotten.
The need is Universal.
Humans deeply need each other.
A baby that isn't touched will lose a part of his/her soul.
There are two components I want to break apart here, so you know the difference between them.
Component One: the Frozen Needs that occur when your needs are not met as a child.
Component Two: relating as adults, healing the Frozen Needs.
******************************
Frozen Needs
I consider a need to be frozen when a significant abuse or neglect happened as a child.
This need was frozen in time.
If you cried as a child, and your mother didn't have "enough" maturity to place your needs first AND understand how to tend to herself, her own needs... then she might have showed up for you, annoyed with you.
Annoyance coming at you as an infant from an unhealed mother permanently builds pathways in your brain.
You learn if you are worth being loved. Or. Not.
******************************
You Have Two Mothers
In adulthood, when you are triggered by another adult, it hurts, and it's terribly confusing.
Sometimes we blame mom (or dad, just sticking with mom for brevity).
It will help you OWN your own healing path if you know that the mom you are grieving is the one from childhood; actually about 90% of it is the first 2 years of your life.
(As a side note, in professional psychology, the debate has shifted from 6 months of age all the way up to 6 years old as the most critical years.
Currently, 6 months to 2 years is the popular opinion amongst psychologists.
It doesn't matter.
It's fucking young.)
So when I'm hurting, I think of young mom: scared, confused, not ready to be a mom.
Dealing with this directly, being hard on my mom as an adult, takes me away from owning the pain.
Leave the poor lady alone.
It's the one from childhood that hurt you, the one that set up your frozen needs.
From a different vantage point, healing the adult to adult mature relationship with your mother today can be a great path to maturity, if you're ready to learn something about her, what her struggles were as Young Mom.
I am in full agreement to spend a period of time blaming mom if you need to... young mom, old mom, all versions of mom.
But make an attempt to really get Young Mom is no longer in physical form in the way you think.
Young Mom is a neural net of pathways in your brain.
Those pathways can heal.
250,000 recovery books have made attempts to tell you how.
Very few describe vulnerability with another mature adult... I will get to that in a bit.
******************************
The Trigger Is Inside You
Mature adult love exists when giving/receiving is happening.
Without a trigger, and with present, clear, caught-up communication, you can FEEL the giving/receiving.
Triggers are faster than a speeding bullet.
When you get triggered, hurt, that's when you now have choices to make if you want to be conscious, and want people... to want to be close to you.
My favorite person talks about a "Gotsta Know Now" trigger.
If you hurt me, neglect me... it hurts, and I need to know... RIGHT NOW... how to fix it.
******************************
The Red Pill Or The Blue Pill
In my needing my immediate answer, I am hurting.
USUALLY, WELL, ALMOST ALWAYS, IF I HIT CONFUSION, I AM IN A FROZEN NEED.
What I literally need is a time machine.
I need my mom to come in and feed me while I was crying, in 1972.
I can be mad at 2021 mom, or 2002 mom, but she can't do anything.
It's mine.
If I take the Red Pill, I will stay stuck in trying to get Back To The Past.
I am in a frozen need.
Every defense from childhood, every brilliant method I created to manipulate these flawed humans to love me... I will pull out every method I can to get my needs met.
I am in emotional danger.
I will attack you back, lie, withhold the truth, not return your call, talk about you negatively to others, feel victimized... basically I will ruin my mature adult relationship if I stay in this frozen need.
I want my mommy.
I want her to change in 1972.
I will take it out on you in 2021, because you hurt my feelings.
******************************
The Blue Pill
I personally love the blue pill, because I know how to do it, it works, and it's the only thing that works.
I have spent 30 years cultivating how to grieve, feel my feelings, and take the risk to tell you that I am doing just that.
I have spent 30 years cultivating how to tell you what I did in childhood to protect myself.
In my adult mature relationships, I can detect when I am triggered, and I don't only have half the equation.
The self-help books teach how to go inside and love yourself.
It's not enough.
We need each other.
And if you were harmed in childhood like I was, you need positive feedback even more.
******************************
Falling On My Sword
Vulnerability means that I am putting myself in danger... temporarily.
It is Component Two of the equation of how to grow up.
Big people are scary.
They use big words.
It seems that if I admit something that I have done, I might be annihilated.
Yes, when you are this honest, people will respond back, and it will hurt.
That is part of your training, to detect that quickly, and eliminate them from your lives. Period.
If you want a good life, and you want the vulnerable path, you must learn to not allow people to get close to you... if they are not on that path.
You have your world of self-healing, but you also have millions and millions of souls on this planet that want closeness, that want depth.
When the brain is measured on an MRI and a person sees depth, realness, a person crying in a move, the pleasure centers light up (in addition to the pain centers).
We feel safe when we see another admit how flawed they are.
******************************
You Must Get A Microwave
When you risk sharing what you ARE ABOUT TO DO to destroy your relationship, you create safety for the other.
"I'm so embarrassed that I got so angry, and I was about to yell at you. I stopped myself. Would you hold me while I feel my anger?"
When you risk sharing your CONFUSION AND NON-CLARITY ABOUT YOUR FEELINGS, you create safety for the other.
"I want to be closer to you and I don't know how. Do you want that?"
When you risk sharing the EXACT THING THAT COMES TO YOUR MIND ABOUT WHAT YOU WISH YOU COULD SAY, you create safety for the other.
"I go all day long wishing we wouldn't argue. I feel more alone when you're in my bed than when you're not. I'm scared about that. Can we get some help?"
The only way to thaw out a frozen need is one moment at a time, one vulnerability at a time, one risk at a time.
I wish that I could help individuals heal super fast with one on one counseling with me.
What clients learn from me is how to do the above.
But nothing... nothing... nothing... will help you heal faster than a romantic partner that supports you... gently... in your continuous learning of how to move from a moment of a childhood Frozen Need... to vulnerability... a moment of sharing your coping mechanisms and your imperfections.
******************************
I love all of you that follow my posts.
And I would not say all this without having to do this myself.
Every single moment I have to do the same kind of risking, just as you do.
Every single moment I risk, I think you are going to walk away and not love me anymore.
So I go within, recognize that I have this Frozen Need, and I tell my beloved, "do you have a moment to listen to something I'm scared to say?"
If she says that she does have a moment, I might need another qualifier... "This is a deep one for me, and I'm in my fear of you going away part."
She knows not to say anything to me for a minute, because I am simply crying and struggling to say my next sentence about what I'm scared to say.
In all honesty, if I really slow down, I could stop there and sometimes not even say the next thing.
Because for that moment, adult to adult, I had a person be gentle with me, while I described my coping mechanism and my wound.
That is how to heal a Frozen Need.
It is frozen, it's really stuck in there, what happened in childhood.
For me, my wounding was very difficult.
I have come to peace that my whole life will be spent healing it.
I don't know another path other than this one.
I love it.
I get to be close to people, perhaps closer, more intense, deeper, than if I wasn't hurt in the first place.
******************************
So what is Love Addiction?
It is not understanding the above.
It is acting out too much from the Frozen Need without vulnerability.
It is having bad relationship after bad relationship and not understanding why. See less

Change is painful.
Leaving abuse is painful.
Learning to be loved instead of abused is painful.
Partner with pain instead of rejecting it.
Here’s why… 
-
 She stayed “strong” for 12 years. It cost her a decade of her life.
She told herself she was fine.
She told herself it wasn’t “that bad.”
She said she could handle it.
She swallowed tears, compartmentalized hurt, performed normal, smiled for pictures.
She said she didn’t want to “feel weak,”
so she never let herself feel *anything.*
She thought avoiding emotional pain meant she was winning.
But here’s what actually happened:
The pain didn’t disappear.
It turned into chronic anxiety.
Into migraines.
Into exhaustion.
Into numbness.
Into a marriage where she no longer recognized the person she’d become.
She finally left.
And then said the sentence that destroys me every time I hear it:
“I thought I was avoiding pain by staying.
Now I realize I spent 12 years living inside of it.”
Avoiding pain didn’t save her.
It prolonged her suffering.
-
 He said therapy “wasn’t necessary.” Then cried the first time someone loved him gently.
He grew up being yelled at and criticized.
He thought emotional toughness = emotional maturity.
He prided himself on “not being sensitive.”
He stayed in abusive environments because he didn’t know it was abuse.
He stayed in cold relationships because he thought connection was optional.
He stayed disconnected from himself because feelings felt like weakness.
Then one day, someone loved him softly.
They didn’t yell.
They didn’t belittle.
They didn’t leave when it got hard.
And his body… broke.
He cried harder than he had in 20 years.
Not because it hurt.
But because for the first time his nervous system realized:
“Oh my God… THIS is what love feels like…
What have I been surviving instead?”
Learning to be loved hurt
because it exposed how much harm he had normalized.
Pain wasn’t his enemy.
Pain was telling the truth.
-
 She didn’t want to feel grief. So she kept repeating it.
After her breakup she decided not to “fall apart.”
Not to process.
Not to grieve.
Not to be sad.
She just moved on.
Immediately into another relationship.
And the same dynamic repeated.
And again.
And again.
Different faces.
Same emotional pattern.
One day she finally said:
“I never stopped long enough to feel the pain of losing someone.
So I kept choosing people who would hurt me the same way.”
Avoiding grief didn’t make her strong.
It made her stuck.
Pain she refused to feel kept controlling her life anyway.
-
 He told himself he was “fine.” Then had a panic attack at 48 years old.
Decades of holding everything in.
Never crying.
Never asking for help.
Never breaking down.
Provider.
Protector.
Performer.
On the outside, successful.
On the inside, full of pressure.
His body finally forced a shutdown.
Doctors said nothing was physically wrong.
The problem wasn’t his heart.
It was his history.
Years of emotional suppression collapsed his nervous system.
He didn’t avoid pain.
He delayed it.
And delayed pain compounds.
-
 Here is the truth all these stories share:
When you refuse to feel emotional pain,
you do not escape it.
You marinate in it.
Unfelt sadness does not disappear.
It becomes numbness.
Unfelt anger doesn’t dissolve.
It turns into resentment and explosion.
Unfelt loneliness doesn’t fade.
It turns into self-abandonment.
Unfelt grief doesn’t weaken.
It turns into emptiness.
Avoiding pain doesn’t protect you.
It enslaves you to it.
-
 Feeling pain isn’t suffering.
Feeling pain is completing it.
Pain processed becomes wisdom.
Pain honored becomes strength.
Pain moved through becomes healing.
Leaving abuse hurts.
But staying in abuse hurts forever.

But staying with harmful love rewires your nervous system against intimacy.

But refusing to grieve costs you your future happiness.
Pain is not proof you’re failing.
Pain is proof that you finally stopped abandoning yourself.
-

Be careful about what you think you know about a person
based only on a title, a credential, a rumor, or a Google search.
There’s a conversation happening in this screenshot that speaks to something way bigger than one thread, one name, or one debate about credentials.
It reflects a world where we’ve been trained to believe the only people worth listening to are the ones with letters after their name.
And listen… I love education.
I respect training.
I honor professionals and the incredible good they do.
But here’s a truth that makes people uncomfortable:
There’s book-smart wisdom
and there’s lived-body wisdom.
They’re not the same.
Both matter.
Neither cancels the other.
What worries me isn’t disagreement.
Disagreement is healthy.
Questions are valid.
Skepticism is human.
What worries me is certainty.
Certainty that “if a person isn’t licensed, they can’t possibly know what they’re talking about.”
Certainty that the human nervous system only trusts logos, institutions, and formal authority.
Certainty that credentials automatically equal emotional attunement, relational safety, and embodied understanding.
Your nervous system doesn’t attach to paper.
It attaches to resonance.
Presence.
Safety.
Truth you can feel.
I’ve worked with people who’ve got advanced degrees who’ve never once been emotionally available.
And I’ve worked with people who’ve got no degree at all who can sit inside raw human pain with steadiness, humility, accountability, and depth textbooks can’t even describe.
If you ask your nervous system instead of your fear, it usually knows the difference.
Sit still.
Breathe.
Ask yourself:
“When I listen to this human, do I feel safer? Calmer? Seen? Stronger? More honest inside myself?”
If the answer’s yes, your body’s telling you something real.
If the answer’s no, your body’s telling you something real.
Listen to it.
Every single day people sit with licensed professionals who talk at them but never truly meet them.
And every single day people meet someone who finally looks them in the eyes, sits in the dark with them, and says:
“I’m not leaving you in this.”
That doesn’t become “less” just because it isn’t certified, laminated, and stamped.
This isn’t about defending myself.
It isn’t about dismissing education.
It isn’t about discrediting people who’ve devoted their lives to formal clinical work.
It’s about humility.
It’s about remembering you don’t know someone’s depth, integrity, or capacity simply because you know their résumé.
And it’s about reclaiming a deeply human truth:
Sometimes your nervous system recognizes safety before your intellect gives you permission to trust it.
Sometimes real leadership isn’t granted by institutions.
It’s forged in lived experience.
In tears.
In mistakes.
In accountability.
In the sacred labor of actually caring for human hearts.
Honor the professionals who change lives.
They matter.
But also honor the embodied elders.
The wounded healers.
The ones who didn’t study pain from a distance, they lived it, walked through fire, and came back carrying lanterns.
If you slow down enough to listen…
Your body knows the difference. See less

I don’t often share posts on here, but this one really spoke to me. I spent six years studying to become a doctor, and I ultimately stepped away after a devastating heartbreak. Since then, life has consistently guided me away from credentials and certifications and toward direct, lived experience.
It hasn’t been easy. Developing a grounded sense of self-conviction has been part of my path. I’ve had many, many moments where I felt less than others with the shiny letters after their names. And then I come back to the present. I notice how often people soften, brighten, tell the truth, or breathe more fully when I’m with them. In those moments, my value becomes obvious.
We’ve been trained to trust letters more than lived experience. At the same time, I’m deeply aware of the harm that can happen without proper training. Training matters. Presence matters. Something essential is lost when we elevate one and dismiss the other.
Let’s not mistake the absence of letters for the absence of depth, wisdom, or beauty. Being deeply human is a potent capacity, one that long preceded institutions and quietly shaped them.
Thank you for speaking your truth here, Derek Hart See less

The “Good Person” Trap.
You don’t yell.
You don’t cheat.
You don’t name-call.
By all traditional standards, you’re a “good” partner.
So why’s your partner still lonely?
Why’re they still angry?
Why does it feel like there’s a thousand-mile canyon between you while you’re sitting on the same couch?
Here’s the truth that’s hard to swallow:
You can be a “good person” and still be a threatening partner.
Not threatening because you’re aggressive.
Threatening because you’re unavailable.
To a human nervous system, silence isn’t “peace.”
Withdrawal isn’t “giving space.”
Emotional neutrality isn’t “being calm.”
To the person who loves you, those things feel like abandonment.
And abandonment is a threat.
When your partner brings you their hurt, and you respond with:
“I didn’t mean it that way.”
“You’re overreacting.”
“I’m a good person, I’d never try to hurt you.”
You’re defending your reputation.
You’re not defending the relationship.
While you’re busy proving your innocence, your partner’s drowning in the experience of being unseen.
They don’t need to know you’re a good person. They already know that, and that’s why they’re still there.
They need to know you’re a safe person.
Safe means:
I can tell you I’m hurt without you making it about your intentions.
I can be messy without you shutting down.
I can find you when I’m lost, instead of finding a wall.
The “real death” of a relationship isn’t always a blow-up.
It’s the slow, quiet freezing over that happens when one person decides it’s safer to be “right” than to be “connected.”
It’s when you start prioritizing your “niceness” over their “wellness.”
If you want to save your marriage, stop trying to be the “good” partner.
Start being the present one.
Stop explaining why they shouldn’t feel that way.
Start wondering what it’s like to be them.
Because love isn’t a certificate you earn for good behavior.
It’s a living, breathing practice of staying when it gets uncomfortable.
Don’t just be a good person.
Be a sanctuary. See less
