Everyone will tell you that needing someone is unhealthy.

Therapists say it. Self-help books say it. The people who've been hurt badly enough say it with real conviction. You shouldn't need anyone. You should be whole on your own. A healthy relationship is two complete people choosing each other, not two broken people clinging to each other.

It sounds right. It feels wise. It gets shared a lot.

It's also wrong in a way that has quietly damaged a generation of people who were trying to heal.

Because need isn't the problem.

Need is human. Need is biological. Need is written into your nervous system at a level so deep it predates language. You were born needing. You will die needing. Every person you've ever admired, every person who seemed the most together, the most solid, the most unshakeable, needed people. They just either had the needs met well enough that it didn't show, or they got very good at pretending they didn't.

The research on this is not ambiguous. Secure attachment, the thing everyone says they want, the thing we're all trying to heal into, is not independence. It's not self-sufficiency. It's the confident expectation that when you reach for someone, they'll be there. Secure people need. They just aren't terrified about whether the need will be met.

So the problem isn't need.

The problem is dependency. And those two things are not the same thing at all.

Here's the difference.

Need says: I want you here. I feel better when you're close. Your presence matters to me and I reach for you when I'm struggling and I feel the loss of you when you're gone.

Dependency says: I cannot function without your regulation. Your mood determines my mood. Your approval determines my worth. When you pull back I stop being able to manage myself. I need you to be okay so that I can be okay.

Need reaches for connection. Dependency requires it for survival.

Need can tolerate a no. Dependency experiences a no as a threat to its existence.

Need says I miss you. Dependency says without you there is no me.

And here's what makes this so hard to untangle in real relationships: they can look identical from the outside. The person who calls their partner when they're scared. The person who wants to spend most of their time together. The person who feels the distance acutely when there's a rupture. That could be healthy need. That could be dependency. You can't tell from the behavior alone. You have to go deeper.

You have to look at what happens in the nervous system when the need isn't met.

When a secure, attached person reaches for their partner and doesn't get what they need in that moment, they feel disappointed. Maybe sad. They feel the gap. And then they find another resource. A friend. Themselves. They hold the feeling. They come back to their partner later. They trust that one unavailability isn't abandonment.

When someone is dependent, the unavailability doesn't register as disappointment. It registers as emergency. The nervous system escalates. Because the nervous system has learned that this person is the only source of regulation available. That there's no backup. That if this person isn't there, or isn't okay, or is upset with them, there's nothing to fall back on.

That's not a character flaw. That's a nervous system that never got enough consistent, reliable care to build an internal regulation system. It had to outsource the whole function. And it outsourced it to the person who felt the safest.

Dependency isn't weakness. It's a wound wearing the shape of love.

And this is what's so cruel about the way we talk about it. When we tell people their need is the problem, we're asking them to amputate something that isn't the problem. We're asking them to become more self-sufficient before they've healed enough to be self-sufficient. We're asking them to stop needing before anyone has loved them consistently enough to show them that their needs are safe to have.

That's not healing. That's just a more sophisticated form of the original wound.

Here's what the actual path out looks like, because there is one, and it doesn't involve becoming someone who needs less:

It involves building more sources. Not pulling away from the person you depend on. Not performing independence you don't feel. But slowly, carefully, creating more places where the need can land. A friend who shows up consistently. A therapist who doesn't leave. Your own capacity to sit with feeling without immediately needing it to stop. A body practice that gives your nervous system somewhere to go when it's activated.

The goal isn't to stop reaching. The goal is to have more than one place to reach.

Because dependency isn't the same as need. But the antidote to dependency isn't needlessness.

It's a bigger net.

More hands.

More places where the reach gets met.

And slowly, as more of those places hold you, the grip loosens. Not because you've taught yourself not to need. Because your nervous system has finally accumulated enough evidence that need doesn't have to be this dangerous. That there are enough sources. That you won't disappear if one of them isn't available right now.

That's not independence.

That's what security actually feels like.

And it was built out of more need, not less.

Nobody talks about this one honestly because it makes people sound crazy.
You left the one who was good to you. You stayed with the one who wasn't. And some part of you has been trying to explain that ever since, to other people, to yourself, to the therapist who raised an eyebrow when you described what you went back to.
The explanations never quite land. Because the real answer isn't logical. It isn't about what you valued or what you deserved or what you consciously wanted.
It's about what felt like home.
And home isn't always safe. For a lot of people home was the first place they learned that love and pain come in the same package. That closeness means chaos sometimes. That the feeling of almost being loved, of reaching for someone who's sometimes there and sometimes not, is what love is supposed to feel like.
Not because they decided that. Because their nervous system learned it before they had language for any of it.
So when someone comes along who is steady and kind and consistently present, who doesn't make them chase, who doesn't create the hot and cold cycle that feels so familiar, the nervous system doesn't say finally.
It says something is wrong.
It says this is boring. This is too easy. This doesn't feel like love, it feels like something is missing. And what's missing is the anxiety. The hypervigilance. The constant low hum of are we okay, do they still want me, what did that look like mean. The reaching for someone who isn't quite there yet.
That hum, for people who grew up inside it, is what love feels like.
Its absence feels like absence.
So they leave. Not because the good relationship was actually bad. But because their nervous system couldn't read it as love. Couldn't find the familiar frequency. Couldn't settle into something that didn't require them to fight for it.
And then they go back to the one that hurts. Or they find a new version of the one that hurts. And inside that relationship, as painful as it is, something finally feels recognizable.
This is the part nobody wants to say out loud.
The bad relationship felt more like love. Not because it was love. Because it matched the template.
Here's what that template gets built from, early, before you knew you were being shaped:
A parent whose affection was unpredictable. Warm one day and distant the next, with no pattern you could ever decode. So you became an expert in reading moods. In making yourself whatever the room needed. In earning the warmth when it showed up and surviving the cold when it didn't.
A home where love came with conditions. Where you had to be good enough, quiet enough, small enough, useful enough to get it. Where the love felt real but also contingent. Where you never quite knew if you were in or out.
A caregiver who needed you to take care of them. Where your needs came second and the relationship required you to stay attuned to someone else's emotional state at the cost of your own. Where love looked like vigilance.
Any of those experiences, repeated enough times, wire the nervous system for a particular kind of intimacy. One that requires work to maintain. One that involves managing another person. One where the connection has to be earned, fought for, worried over.
And then a good partner shows up and just offers it. Freely. Without the chase.
And the nervous system doesn't trust free.
Free doesn't match the template. Free feels naive. Free feels like you're missing something. Like the other shoe is about to drop. Like this person doesn't actually know you yet because if they knew you they wouldn't just give it to you like this.
So you self-sabotage. Or you get bored. Or you pick fights to create the familiar tension. Or you simply feel nothing where you expected to feel something and you mistake that numbness for incompatibility.
And you leave.
And you go find the one who makes you work for it.
And it feels like coming alive again.
That feeling is real. It isn't love, but the feeling is real. It's your nervous system finally finding a frequency it recognizes. Finally knowing what to do. Finally back in the environment it was trained for, the one where love requires effort and uncertainty and the constant low-grade management of another person's emotional availability.
Getting out of this pattern doesn't happen through understanding it. Understanding helps, but it isn't enough. You can know all of this and still feel nothing for the steady person and everything for the one who keeps you guessing.
It happens through the body. Through slowly, carefully, with support, teaching your nervous system that steady is safe. That the absence of chaos isn't the absence of love. That the person who just shows up, without drama, without the push and pull, is offering you something real even if it doesn't feel real yet.
That process takes time. More time than most people want it to. And it requires you to stay in the discomfort of the good relationship long enough for your nervous system to recalibrate. To learn that this quiet, this reliability, this uncomplicated presence, isn't emptiness.
It's what you actually needed all along.
You just weren't raised to recognize it.

What I said to myself to explain leaving the good one:
We just didn't have chemistry. The spark wasn't there.
They were too available. It felt suffocating somehow even though they weren't doing anything wrong.
I didn't want to hurt them by staying when I wasn't feeling it.
I kept waiting to feel something more and it never came.
They were great on paper but something was just missing and I couldn't name it.
I didn't want to settle. I thought I deserved to feel more than this.
It just felt too easy. Like we never had to work for anything and that didn't feel real.
I wasn't attracted to them the way I needed to be. I told myself that was important.
They were too nice. I know how that sounds. But something about it made me pull away.
I couldn't explain it then. I still can't explain it without feeling ashamed.
-
What I told myself to explain staying in the bad one:
It's passionate. That intensity means something. That's what real love feels like.
Nobody has ever made me feel this much. That has to mean we're meant for each other.
They need me in a way the other person didn't. That feeling of being needed is love.
We have history. You can't just walk away from that much history.
They're going through something hard right now. This isn't who they really are.
When it's good it's the best thing I've ever felt. I'm staying for those moments.
I've never felt more alive than I do in this relationship, even when it's painful.
If I leave now I'll regret it forever. I'll always wonder what we could have been.
Nobody else is ever going to understand me the way they do.
I can't leave. I don't know who I am without this.
-
What my nervous system was actually doing that I didn't have words for:
Reading the steady person as boring because I was trained to read chaos as love.
Feeling nothing in the safe relationship because my system didn't know how to receive what it was being given.
Feeling everything in the painful relationship because that frequency was familiar and familiar felt like home.
Interpreting unavailability as depth. Telling myself the person who kept me guessing was more complex, more interesting, more worth having.
Mistaking anxiety for attraction. The racing heart, the preoccupation, the constant wondering was my nervous system on high alert, not my heart recognizing its match.
Feeling most like myself in relationships that required me to manage someone else, because that's the self that got built.
Getting bored the moment a relationship became secure because secure felt like nothing was happening.
Chasing the high of the reconnection after conflict because rupture and repair was the intimacy template I was raised inside.
Leaving before I could be left. Getting out of the good relationship before it had a chance to go wrong, because something going wrong was always what I was waiting for.
Confusing the absence of pain with the absence of love. Telling myself that if it didn't hurt sometimes it wasn't real.
-
Mirror meditation: For the one who has left good love and doesn't know why:
Find your mirror when you're not defending anything. Not after a conversation about this. Not when you're justifying a choice. When you're just quiet and willing.
Stand close and let your face be whatever it is.
Ask yourself, out loud if you can:
What did love feel like in the house I grew up in?
Don't answer with what it should have felt like. Answer with what it actually felt like. In your body. The texture of it. What you had to do to get it. What happened when you didn't.
Sit with that for a moment.
Then ask:
Does the relationship I stayed in feel like that?
And then:
Does the relationship I left feel like that?
Notice what comes up. Not the story about chemistry or compatibility or timing. What comes up underneath all of that.
Then ask the hardest one:
Is it possible I've been calling familiar feelings love, and calling unfamiliar safety emptiness?
You don't have to answer that quickly. It might take days to sit with it. That's okay.
This meditation isn't asking you to go back. It isn't asking you to grieve. It's asking you to get honest about the template. About what got built in you before you had any say in the building.
Because you can't choose differently until you can see clearly.
And you can't see clearly until you stop mistaking recognition for rightness.
You recognized the one that hurt.
That doesn't mean it was the one.

There's a specific kind of lonely that doesn't have a good name yet.
Not the loneliness of being alone. That one is straightforward. You're by yourself and you feel the absence of people and you know exactly what you're feeling and why.
This one is harder. This one lives inside connection. Inside a relationship where someone is present, attentive, committed, and loves you genuinely. Where by every visible measure you are not alone at all.
And yet.
There is a particular devastation in being misunderstood by someone who is certain they understand you. Who has decided, somewhere along the way, that they know who you are. Who has built a complete and coherent picture of you in their mind and now relates to that picture instead of to you.
They're not relating to a stranger. They're relating to a version of you that is close enough to be recognizable and wrong enough to be isolating.
And the wrongness is almost impossible to explain. Because they'll point to evidence. They know your history. They know your patterns. They know what you order at restaurants and how you get when you're tired and what your relationship with your mother costs you. They know things about you that nobody else knows.
And still they miss you.
Not the facts of you. The actual living interior of you. The part that is still becoming. The part that surprised even you last Tuesday. The part that doesn't fit the narrative they've built, so when it shows up they either don't see it or they explain it away with something they already know about you.
You tried to tell them something real last month and watched it land in the wrong category.
You've been trying to show them something about who you are now and they keep responding to who you were.
You said something that came from a new place in you and they nodded like they'd already known you'd say that.
And you smiled and said yes and felt the distance open up quietly between you and said nothing more about it.
Because how do you explain this without sounding like you're accusing someone who loves you of not loving you well enough. How do you say I feel unseen to someone who is looking right at you. How do you say you don't know me to someone who knows more about you than almost anyone alive.
So you don't. You manage it. You find the places in the relationship where you do feel met and you live there. You stop bringing the parts of you that don't fit the picture because bringing them just leads to the particular exhaustion of being explained back to yourself incorrectly.
And slowly, without deciding to, you start to disappear inside the relationship.
Not all of you. Just the parts that don't match the version of you they've decided on.
Which over time becomes its own kind of loss. Because you stop knowing which parts of yourself are real and which parts are just the ones that got confirmed by being received. You start to organize yourself around what lands. You become, a little, the person they think you are. And one day you look up and you're not sure where you end and their idea of you begins.
This is what long intimacy can do if it stops being curious.
It can turn the person you love into a story you tell yourself about them.
And the person inside that story, however loved, however known in all the surface ways, is alone in the specific way that only happens when you're with someone who stopped wondering about you.
Who stopped asking.
Who thinks the picture is finished.
The people who feel most known in long relationships have one thing in common. Their partner never stopped being curious about them. Never stopped treating them as someone who could still surprise them. Never stopped asking questions they didn't already know the answer to. Never stopped sitting with the discomfort of being wrong about who this person is becoming.
Curiosity is the opposite of this loneliness. Not grand gesture curiosity. Not scheduled check-in curiosity. The daily, ordinary willingness to not be sure you already know. To let the person in front of you be a little stranger than you're comfortable with. To be surprised. To be wrong. To update the picture.
That's what keeps two people actually together instead of just proximate.
Not history. Not commitment. Not love even, though love matters.
Curiosity.
The willingness to keep asking who are you now.
And meaning it.
And being willing to not already know the answer.
-
What I stop bringing because it doesn't fit the picture they have of me:
The part of me that's changed in ways I can't fully explain yet.
The opinion I have that contradicts the one they've already filed me under.
The feeling that doesn't match my pattern. The sadness when I'm supposed to be the resilient one. The anger when I'm supposed to be the calm one. The fear when I'm supposed to have worked through that already.
The new thing I'm interested in that doesn't fit who they think I am.
The version of a story that makes me look different than the character they've cast me as.
The doubt. Because they've already decided what I believe.
The growth. Because growth means the old picture was incomplete and that's uncomfortable for both of us.
The parts of me that are still becoming. Because they seem more comfortable with the parts that are already settled.
The thing I said once that they quote back to me now as if it's permanent. I've changed my mind. I don't know how to tell them without it becoming a whole thing.
The real answer when they ask how I'm doing. Because the real answer doesn't fit the version of me that functions well.
-
What I say to myself to manage the loneliness of being misread by someone who loves me:
They know me better than anyone. This is just the cost of being known for a long time.

Someone asked a question and the question itself made me feel seen before I'd answered it.

There's a specific kind of lonely that doesn't have a good name yet.

Not the loneliness of being alone. That one is straightforward. You're by yourself and you feel the absence of people and you know exactly what you're feeling and why.

This one is harder. This one lives inside connection. Inside a relationship where someone is present, attentive, committed, and loves you genuinely. Where by every visible measure you are not alone at all.

And yet.

There is a particular devastation in being misunderstood by someone who is certain they understand you. Who has decided, somewhere along the way, that they know who you are. Who has built a complete and coherent picture of you in their mind and now relates to that picture instead of to you.

They're not relating to a stranger. They're relating to a version of you that is close enough to be recognizable and wrong enough to be isolating.

And the wrongness is almost impossible to explain. Because they'll point to evidence. They know your history. They know your patterns. They know what you order at restaurants and how you get when you're tired and what your relationship with your mother costs you. They know things about you that nobody else knows.

And still they miss you.

Not the facts of you. The actual living interior of you. The part that is still becoming. The part that surprised even you last Tuesday. The part that doesn't fit the narrative they've built, so when it shows up they either don't see it or they explain it away with something they already know about you.

You tried to tell them something real last month and watched it land in the wrong category.

You've been trying to show them something about who you are now and they keep responding to who you were.

You said something that came from a new place in you and they nodded like they'd already known you'd say that.

And you smiled and said yes and felt the distance open up quietly between you and said nothing more about it.

Because how do you explain this without sounding like you're accusing someone who loves you of not loving you well enough. How do you say I feel unseen to someone who is looking right at you. How do you say you don't know me to someone who knows more about you than almost anyone alive.

So you don't. You manage it. You find the places in the relationship where you do feel met and you live there. You stop bringing the parts of you that don't fit the picture because bringing them just leads to the particular exhaustion of being explained back to yourself incorrectly.

And slowly, without deciding to, you start to disappear inside the relationship.

Not all of you. Just the parts that don't match the version of you they've decided on.

Which over time becomes its own kind of loss. Because you stop knowing which parts of yourself are real and which parts are just the ones that got confirmed by being received. You start to organize yourself around what lands. You become, a little, the person they think you are. And one day you look up and you're not sure where you end and their idea of you begins.

This is what long intimacy can do if it stops being curious.

It can turn the person you love into a story you tell yourself about them.

And the person inside that story, however loved, however known in all the surface ways, is alone in the specific way that only happens when you're with someone who stopped wondering about you.

Who stopped asking.

Who thinks the picture is finished.

The people who feel most known in long relationships have one thing in common. Their partner never stopped being curious about them. Never stopped treating them as someone who could still surprise them. Never stopped asking questions they didn't already know the answer to. Never stopped sitting with the discomfort of being wrong about who this person is becoming.

Curiosity is the opposite of this loneliness. Not grand gesture curiosity. Not scheduled check-in curiosity. The daily, ordinary willingness to not be sure you already know. To let the person in front of you be a little stranger than you're comfortable with. To be surprised. To be wrong. To update the picture.

That's what keeps two people actually together instead of just proximate.

Not history. Not commitment. Not love even, though love matters.

Curiosity.

The willingness to keep asking who are you now.

And meaning it.

And being willing to not already know the answer.

Why people confuse chemistry with compatibility and what it costs them.
Nobody warns you about this when you're young and falling for someone.
They don't tell you that the feeling you're chasing, that specific electric aliveness that happens in the presence of certain people, is not a reliable indicator of anything except that your nervous system is activated. That chemistry is real and powerful and will absolutely feel like destiny and is also completely neutral about whether the relationship will make you happy.
Chemistry doesn't know if this person is kind. Chemistry doesn't know if your values align. Chemistry doesn't know if this person is available, emotionally or otherwise. Chemistry doesn't know if the way they move through the world is going to work alongside the way you move through the world ten years from now.
Chemistry just knows that something is happening in your body when this person is near.
And your body, which has been waiting for this feeling, which has been trained by every romantic story you've ever consumed to treat this feeling as the signal, says yes. This is the one. This is what it's supposed to feel like.
And you follow it.
Sometimes that works out. Sometimes the chemistry is accompanied by everything else and you build something real and lasting on top of the electricity.
But a lot of the time it doesn't work out. A lot of the time the chemistry is the whole thing. And you spend months or years trying to build a life on top of a feeling that was never designed to hold that weight.
Here's what chemistry actually is, underneath the romance of it.
It's recognition. It's your nervous system encountering something familiar, something that matches a pattern it already knows, and lighting up in response. Which means that for a lot of people, especially people who grew up in homes where love was complicated or unpredictable or required earning, the chemistry is loudest with the people who feel the most like home.
And home, as we've talked about, isn't always safe.
The person who activates you the most might be activating something old. Something unresolved. Your nervous system isn't saying this person is good for you. It's saying this person matches a template I already have. I know what to do here. This feels familiar.
Familiar and good are not the same thing.
Compatibility is quieter than chemistry. It doesn't announce itself. It doesn't make your hands shake or your thoughts race or your whole body reorganize around another person's presence. It shows up in smaller, less cinematic ways.
It shows up in how easy it is to be yourself around them. How rarely you have to translate yourself. How conflicts resolve without leaving damage. How their version of a good life and your version of a good life are pointing in roughly the same direction. How they treat the people who can do nothing for them. How you feel in your body after a long day in their company. Not the high of the early chemistry. The quieter thing underneath it. Whether you feel more like yourself or less.
That's compatibility. And it doesn't feel like lightning. It feels like ground.
And we've been so trained to chase lightning that a lot of people sit on perfectly good ground and feel nothing and leave to go find the storm again.
The cost of this confusion is significant and it tends to compound over time.
The first cost is the relationships you leave because they didn't feel electric enough. The person who was steady and present and genuinely compatible but didn't produce the feeling you'd been taught to require. You left because the chemistry wasn't there, not knowing that the chemistry you were looking for was calibrated to something that wasn't going to make you happy.
The second cost is the years you spend in relationships held together by chemistry alone. Trying to build something stable on top of something that was only ever designed to get you in the door. Mistaking intensity for depth. Mistaking the high of reconnection after conflict for intimacy. Mistaking the anxiety of loving someone unpredictable for passion.
The third cost is the recalibration. Which is real and necessary and disorienting. Learning to feel attracted to steadiness when your whole system was trained to find steadiness boring. Learning to trust the quiet feeling. Learning to stay on the ground long enough to find out what's actually there instead of leaving the moment the lightning stops.
That recalibration is some of the most important work a person can do.
Because compatibility without chemistry is friendship. But chemistry without compatibility is suffering.
And what you actually want, what's actually available if you do the work of recalibrating, is the thing that starts as one and grows into both.
The ground that eventually, slowly, with the right person and enough time, starts to feel like home.
A home that's actually safe this time.
That's what you were looking for when you were chasing lightning.
You just didn't know yet that lightning was never going to build it.

The ground is still there.
It was always there.
You just kept leaving before you found out what was underneath it.

I'm exhausted in a way that sleep doesn't fix. I've been exhausted like this for a long time.
I'm starting to grieve it while I'm still in it. I don't know what to do with that.
I keep waiting for something to happen that makes the decision for me. A blow up. A betrayal. Something I can point to. Something clean. It's not coming. This is just a slow erosion and there's no dramatic moment to wait for.
I've started noticing other people. Not acting on it. Just noticing. I know what that means and I'm not ready to say it out loud yet.
I've told myself I'm leaving before. I'm trying to figure out if this time I mean it.
I don't want to hurt them. I keep putting it off because I don't want to hurt them. But I'm starting to understand that staying to avoid hurting them is its own kind of cruelty.
I think I already know. I think I've known for a while. I'm just working up to letting myself know that I know.

I don't miss them the way I did. I miss the feeling sometimes. Less than I used to.
I wasted time in that. Not all of it. But some of it I knew and stayed anyway.
I'm noticing I'm drawn to someone steadier now and I'm trying to stay instead of leaving when the electricity doesn't show up on day three.
The person I was in that relationship wasn't fully me. I got smaller in there. I'm still finding the parts that went quiet.

I think I'm finally ready to find out what it feels like to be loved without it costing me my nervous system.

Something is wrong and I can't keep pretending I don't know what it is.

I've had this same feeling before and talked myself out of it. I'm trying to figure out if I'm doing that again or if this time is different.

I love them. I just don't know if love is enough anymore and I hate that I'm thinking that.

I keep imagining my life without them and the imagine doesn't scare me as much as it used to. That scares me more than the image does.

I'm exhausted in a way that sleep doesn't fix. I've been exhausted like this for a long time.

I'm starting to grieve it while I'm still in it. I don't know what to do with that.

I keep waiting for something to happen that makes the decision for me. A blow up. A betrayal. Something I can point to. Something clean. It's not coming. This is just a slow erosion and there's no dramatic moment to wait for.

I've started noticing other people. Not acting on it. Just noticing. I know what that means and I'm not ready to say it out loud yet.

I've told myself I'm leaving before. I'm trying to figure out if this time I mean it.

I don't want to hurt them. I keep putting it off because I don't want to hurt them. But I'm starting to understand that staying to avoid hurting them is its own kind of cruelty.

I think I already know. I think I've known for a while. I'm just working up to letting myself know that I know.

What I probably say to myself 3 days after leaving:

I think I made a mistake. The chemistry I had with them I've never had with anyone else and I don't know if I'll find it again.

I keep checking their social media. I tell myself I'm just making sure they're okay.

Everything reminds me of them. I didn't know how much space they took up until they were gone.

I miss the feeling more than I miss them and I can't tell if that distinction matters.

I'm second guessing everything. Maybe I gave up too soon. Maybe the timing was just wrong.

I feel the absence of the intensity like a withdrawal. My body doesn't know what to do with this much quiet.

I'm starting to romanticize the good parts and compress the bad parts into something I can minimize.

I keep replaying the best moments. The worst ones are getting harder to access.

Maybe I expected too much. Maybe that kind of connection doesn't come with stability and I have to choose.

I think I just need to reach out once. Just to see.

-

What I probably say to myself one year after leaving:

I can see it now in a way I couldn't from inside it. The anxiety I was calling love. The chaos I was calling passion.

I don't miss them the way I did. I miss the feeling sometimes. Less than I used to.

I wasted time in that. Not all of it. But some of it I knew and stayed anyway.

I'm noticing I'm drawn to someone steadier now and I'm trying to stay instead of leaving when the electricity doesn't show up on day three.

The person I was in that relationship wasn't fully me. I got smaller in there. I'm still finding the parts that went quiet.

I'm angrier than I expected to be at this stage. Not at them. At the pattern. At how long I confused intensity for intimacy.

I understand the chemistry thing now in my head. My body is still learning it.

I had a moment last week where someone was kind to me in a simple way and I felt more than I expected to. I'm paying attention to that.

I don't want to do that again. I mean it this time in a way I didn't mean it the last time I said it.

I think I'm finally ready to find out what it feels like to be loved without it costing me my nervous system.

The difference between a relationship that's hard and a relationship that's wrong.
Everyone tells you relationships take work.
And they're right. They do. Anyone who's been in a real one long enough knows that the early ease gives way to something that requires more of you. More patience. More repair. More choosing each other on the days when choosing feels like effort rather than instinct.
So you do the work. You stay. You try. You go to therapy and read the books and have the hard conversations and you tell yourself this is what love looks like when it gets real. This is the work everyone said it would take.
But nobody tells you there's a difference between a relationship that's hard and a relationship that's wrong.
And that difference is everything.
A hard relationship asks something of you. A wrong relationship takes something from you.
A hard relationship stretches you in ways that, even when they're uncomfortable, leave you more yourself on the other side. A wrong relationship shrinks you. Quietly, consistently, in ways you don't always notice until you're outside of it and suddenly have room to breathe and realize how long you've been holding your breath.
A hard relationship has ruptures that get repaired. The distance opens and closes. The disconnection is painful and then it ends and you find each other again and the finding each other again is real. A wrong relationship has a distance that only ever gets managed, never actually closed. You get closer to okay. You never quite get back.
A hard relationship makes you feel like yourself on most days and challenged on some. A wrong relationship makes you feel like a problem to be managed. Like your needs are an inconvenience. Like the full version of you is too much for the container you're living inside.
A hard relationship fights and repairs and grows. A wrong relationship has the same fight so many times that you both stop expecting it to go anywhere and start just waiting for it to be over.
A hard relationship requires you to grow in ways that are uncomfortable but recognizable. You can see who you're becoming. A wrong relationship requires you to shrink in ways that are so gradual you don't see them happening until someone who knew you before looks at you with something in their eyes you can't quite read.
Here's the thing that makes this so difficult to navigate from the inside.
Hard and wrong feel almost identical when you're in them.
Both are painful. Both require effort. Both leave you exhausted sometimes. Both make you question yourself. Both have good days that make you wonder if you've been wrong about the whole thing. Both have bad days that make you wonder if you can keep going.
And the story our culture tells about relationships, the work story, the it's not supposed to be easy story, can be weaponized against you by a relationship that is simply wrong. Because every time you get close to the truth of it, every time you feel how tired you are and start to wonder if tired is a sign, you can reach for the work narrative and use it to stay longer.
Real love is hard. So this must be real love.
That's not always true.
Sometimes hard is just hard. And wrong is just wrong. And the work you've been putting in has not been building something. It's been maintaining a structure that was never going to hold the weight you needed it to hold.
So how do you tell the difference from the inside, when you're too close and too invested and too tired to see clearly.
You ask a different question than the one you've been asking.
You stop asking is this hard enough to be worth it and start asking who am I becoming inside this relationship.
Not who are you at your best. Not who do you manage to be on the good days. Who are you becoming on average, across the full texture of living inside this relationship day after day.
Are you more yourself or less. More open or more defended. More willing to be seen or more careful about what you show. More trusting of your own perceptions or more likely to doubt them when they conflict with the narrative of the relationship.
A hard relationship, however painful, tends to move you toward yourself over time.
A wrong relationship, however loving, tends to move you away.
That's the difference.
Not how much it hurts. Not how hard you've tried. Not how much you love each other.
Who you are becoming.
And whether the answer to that question, when you let yourself hear it, is something you can live with.

What I say to justify staying in something wrong by calling it hard:
Every relationship takes work. I'm not going to be someone who quits when it gets difficult.
We've been through too much together to walk away now. That history means something.
They're going through something hard right now. This isn't who they really are.
I've seen who they are at their best and that person is worth staying for.
Maybe I'm the problem. Maybe if I showed up better this would feel different.
All couples go through periods like this. We just need to get through this stretch.
I don't want to look back and know I gave up right before it turned around.
The good days are so good. I'm holding on for the good days.
Love isn't supposed to feel easy all the time. The fact that it's hard proves it's real.
I've already invested so much of myself in this. Leaving now means all of that was for nothing.

What a wrong relationship actually feels like from the inside, honestly:
I'm tired in a way that doesn't lift even on the good days.
I've stopped bringing whole parts of myself here because they don't land well.
I feel like a problem that needs managing more than a person who is loved.
I monitor their mood before I know how I'm allowed to feel in a given moment.
I can't remember the last time I felt genuinely at ease in this relationship. Not performed ease. Actual ease.
I've gotten so good at managing this that I've stopped noticing how much energy the managing takes.
The repairs happen but something doesn't quite close. We get back to okay but not back to each other.
I've started to believe that some of the things I want from love aren't actually available. That I've been expecting too much.
I don't tell people the full truth about what it's like in here because I know what they'd say.
I keep waiting to feel like myself again. I'm starting to forget what that felt like.
-
What a hard relationship feels like, for contrast, so you know the difference:
It's painful sometimes but the pain has a direction. Something is happening. We're moving through something.
After the hard conversations I feel closer to them, not more alone.
I can still feel myself in here. Stretched sometimes. Still present.
The repairs actually close something. We come back to each other, not just back to functional.
I don't always like what's being asked of me but I can see why it's being asked. It makes sense in the context of building something real.
I feel challenged by this relationship but not diminished by it.
My sense of my own perceptions is intact. When something feels wrong I can say so and be heard.
The work feels like it's building toward something. Not just maintaining something that keeps breaking.
I'm becoming more myself in here over time, not less. More honest. More open. More willing to be seen.
On the hard days I still fundamentally believe in what we're building. That belief doesn't require convincing.

Mirror meditation: For the one who doesn't know anymore if this is hard or wrong:
Find your mirror when nobody needs anything from you. When you have a moment that belongs only to you.
Stand close. Let your face be what it is without arranging it.
Take one breath and ask yourself:
Who am I becoming inside this relationship?
Not who you are on your best days. Not who you manage to be when things are going well. Who you are becoming on average, across the whole of living inside this.
Let the answer come from your body before your mind has a chance to manage it.
Then ask:
Am I more myself in here or less?
Notice what surfaces. Not the story about potential or history or how much you love each other. Just the honest answer to that question.
And then the last one:
If a close friend described their relationship using the words I would use to describe mine, what would I tell them?
You already know what you'd tell them.
You've known for a while.
This meditation isn't asking you to leave. It isn't asking you to stay. It's asking you to stop using the word hard when you might mean something else.
Because hard is survivable and worth it and builds something.
And wrong is survivable too.
But it doesn't build anything.
It just costs you.
And you deserve to know the difference. See less

Taking space is not the same thing as stonewalling.
But most couples don’t know the difference.
They think walking away means abandonment.
They think staying means maturity.
They think pushing through is strength.
It’s not.
If your nervous system is flooded, you are not present.
You are activated.
And an activated nervous system does not create repair.
It creates damage.
So yes, sometimes you need space.
But space can either protect the relationship…
or punish it.
Here’s the difference.
Stonewalling is silent withdrawal with no return.
It looks like shutting down mid-sentence.
It looks like walking away without a word.
It looks like hours of silence with no explanation.
It looks like “I’m done” and disappearing.
It looks like using distance to make the other person feel small.
It says, “You don’t get access to me.”
It leaves your partner guessing.
It leaves them bracing.
It leaves them alone.
Healthy space is different.
Healthy space is intentional.
It’s structured.
It protects both nervous systems.
It sounds like this:
You value self-regulation.
So you stop engaging when you’re flooded instead of pushing through and exploding.
You recognize when you’re too activated to talk.
You trust that pausing is better than saying something you can’t take back.
You value transparency.
So you stop disappearing without explanation.
You say, “I’m too activated to talk right now.”
You say, “I need a break.”
You say it before walking away.
You value their security.
So you stop punishing them with silence.
You give a specific return time.
“Let’s talk in 30 minutes.”
“I need an hour, then I’ll come back.”
You don’t leave it open-ended.
You value resolution.
So you stop avoiding by never coming back.
You return like you said you would.
You sit back down.
You finish the conversation.
You value the relationship.
So you stop using distance as a weapon.
You take space to calm down, not to hurt them.
You don’t make them earn your return.
You value your boundaries.
So you stop pushing through when overwhelmed.
You allow your body to settle before re-engaging.
You recognize that staying while dysregulated helps no one.
This is what mature space looks like:
Recognizing when you’re too activated to stay.
Saying it clearly instead of storming off.
Giving a specific return time.
Actually coming back.
Finishing the conversation.
Most people don’t do this.
They either explode…
or they disappear.
They say they “need space,” but what they really mean is:
“I don’t know how to regulate without shutting you out.”
Real space sounds like:
“I care about this too much to fight while I’m flooded.”
“I need 20 minutes to settle.”
“I promise I’m coming back.”
“This isn’t me leaving. It’s me preventing damage.”
And then you return.
That return is everything.
Because every time you come back like you said you would, your partner’s nervous system learns:
You may step away…
but you don’t disappear.
Stonewalling creates insecurity.
Healthy space builds trust.
Stonewalling avoids discomfort.
Healthy space manages it.
Stonewalling ends connection.
Healthy space protects it.
If you can’t communicate the pause, it’s not space.
If you can’t give a return time, it’s not space.
If you don’t come back, it’s not space.
It’s avoidance.
And couples don’t fall apart because someone needs space.
They fall apart because space becomes abandonment.
The difference is responsibility.
Taking space the right way says:
“I’m calming my body so I don’t damage us.”
And that is what safety looks like in a nervous system that knows how to pause…

What happens to children who learn that need is dangerous.
There is a lesson some children learn so early and so thoroughly that by the time they're old enough to know they learned it, it's already become the architecture of how they move through the world.
The lesson is this.
Needing things is dangerous.
Not dangerous in the way they'll later be able to articulate. Not dangerous as a concept they can examine and evaluate and decide whether to keep. Dangerous in the body. Dangerous as a reflex. Dangerous the way touching a hot stove is dangerous, something the nervous system learns to avoid before the mind has had any say in the matter.
Here's how the lesson gets taught.
Not usually through cruelty. That's the part that makes it so hard to see clearly later. Most of the parents who teach this lesson are not cruel people. They are limited people. Overwhelmed people. People who were never taught to meet need well because their own needs were never met well. People who are doing the best they can with what they have and whose best, for this particular child in this particular developmental window, is not enough.
The child reaches. Children always reach. Reaching is biological. It's the first thing a nervous system does when it needs something. It reaches toward the person it's attached to and it waits to be met.
And sometimes the reaching gets met well. And the child's nervous system learns that reaching is safe. That need produces connection. That the world is a place where you can want something and get it and survive the wanting.
And sometimes the reaching doesn't get met. Not once. Not occasionally. But consistently, in the specific way that teaches a lesson rather than just disappointing in the moment.
The parent is overwhelmed and the need feels like one more thing.
The parent is emotionally unavailable in the particular way that looks like presence but isn't.
The parent needs the child to need less because the parent's own nervous system is already at capacity.
The parent meets some needs and not others, in a pattern unpredictable enough that the child can never quite figure out which needs are safe to have.
The parent meets need with guilt. With sighing. With a kind of heaviness that teaches the child that their wanting is a burden.
The parent meets need with anger. Not always. Just enough times that the child learns to be careful.
And the child, because children are extraordinarily adaptive, because survival is the first priority of every young nervous system, begins to adjust.
They learn to need less visibly.
They learn to take care of themselves before asking.
They learn to read the room before they reach, to check whether this is a moment when reaching is likely to be safe.
They learn to meet their own needs wherever possible and to feel something close to shame about the needs they can't meet alone.
They learn that being easy is how you stay safe. That being low maintenance is how you keep love. That wanting things from people is a gamble and the odds are not always in your favor and the cost of losing is high enough that not playing starts to seem like the smarter choice.
And then they grow up.
And they bring all of that into their adult relationships.
And this is where it gets complicated. Because the strategies that kept them safe in childhood, the self-sufficiency, the room-reading, the need suppression, those strategies made sense then. They were adaptations to a real environment with real constraints. They were intelligent responses to conditions they didn't choose and couldn't change.
But the environment has changed. The adult relationship they're in is not their childhood home. The person they're with is not their parent. The conditions that made those strategies necessary no longer exist.
And the strategies remain.
So they don't ask for what they need. They wait to see if their partner notices, and feel quietly devastated when they don't, and say nothing when asked if something's wrong.
They minimize. I'm fine. It's not a big deal. I don't need anything.
They take care of everyone else's needs with attention and generosity and then feel the particular loneliness of someone who gives well and cannot receive.
They feel shame when they reach for someone and the reaching doesn't land perfectly. Not disappointment. Shame. The old lesson activating. Need is dangerous. I shouldn't have reached. I knew better.
They choose partners who confirm the lesson. People who are a little unavailable. People who require the same careful room-reading and need suppression that childhood required. Not consciously. Because unavailability feels like the known condition. Like the familiar shape of how love works.
And they stay in those relationships longer than they should because leaving would require them to believe that something different is possible. That need doesn't have to be dangerous. That reaching doesn't have to be a gamble. That there are people in the world whose response to being needed is not overwhelm or withdrawal or guilt but something closer to welcome.
That belief is the hardest one to build when you were taught the opposite before you had words.
But it can be built.
Not quickly. Not without support. Not without the specific experience of reaching and being met, repeatedly, consistently enough that the nervous system begins to update the lesson.
The lesson that need is dangerous was learned in relationship.
It can only be unlearned in relationship.

What happens to children who learn that need is dangerous.

There is a lesson some children learn so early and so thoroughly that by the time they're old enough to know they learned it, it's already become the architecture of how they move through the world.

The lesson is this.

Needing things is dangerous.

Not dangerous in the way they'll later be able to articulate. Not dangerous as a concept they can examine and evaluate and decide whether to keep. Dangerous in the body. Dangerous as a reflex. Dangerous the way touching a hot stove is dangerous, something the nervous system learns to avoid before the mind has had any say in the matter.

Here's how the lesson gets taught.

Not usually through cruelty. That's the part that makes it so hard to see clearly later. Most of the parents who teach this lesson are not cruel people. They are limited people. Overwhelmed people. People who were never taught to meet need well because their own needs were never met well. People who are doing the best they can with what they have and whose best, for this particular child in this particular developmental window, is not enough.

The child reaches. Children always reach. Reaching is biological. It's the first thing a nervous system does when it needs something. It reaches toward the person it's attached to and it waits to be met.

And sometimes the reaching gets met well. And the child's nervous system learns that reaching is safe. That need produces connection. That the world is a place where you can want something and get it and survive the wanting.

And sometimes the reaching doesn't get met. Not once. Not occasionally. But consistently, in the specific way that teaches a lesson rather than just disappointing in the moment.

The parent is overwhelmed and the need feels like one more thing.

The parent is emotionally unavailable in the particular way that looks like presence but isn't.

The parent needs the child to need less because the parent's own nervous system is already at capacity.

The parent meets some needs and not others, in a pattern unpredictable enough that the child can never quite figure out which needs are safe to have.

The parent meets need with guilt. With sighing. With a kind of heaviness that teaches the child that their wanting is a burden.

The parent meets need with anger. Not always. Just enough times that the child learns to be careful.

And the child, because children are extraordinarily adaptive, because survival is the first priority of every young nervous system, begins to adjust.

They learn to need less visibly.

They learn to take care of themselves before asking.

They learn to read the room before they reach, to check whether this is a moment when reaching is likely to be safe.

They learn to meet their own needs wherever possible and to feel something close to shame about the needs they can't meet alone.

They learn that being easy is how you stay safe. That being low maintenance is how you keep love. That wanting things from people is a gamble and the odds are not always in your favor and the cost of losing is high enough that not playing starts to seem like the smarter choice.

And then they grow up.

And they bring all of that into their adult relationships.

And this is where it gets complicated. Because the strategies that kept them safe in childhood, the self-sufficiency, the room-reading, the need suppression, those strategies made sense then. They were adaptations to a real environment with real constraints. They were intelligent responses to conditions they didn't choose and couldn't change.

But the environment has changed. The adult relationship they're in is not their childhood home. The person they're with is not their parent. The conditions that made those strategies necessary no longer exist.

And the strategies remain.

So they don't ask for what they need. They wait to see if their partner notices, and feel quietly devastated when they don't, and say nothing when asked if something's wrong.

They minimize. I'm fine. It's not a big deal. I don't need anything.

They take care of everyone else's needs with attention and generosity and then feel the particular loneliness of someone who gives well and cannot receive.

They feel shame when they reach for someone and the reaching doesn't land perfectly. Not disappointment. Shame. The old lesson activating. Need is dangerous. I shouldn't have reached. I knew better.

They choose partners who confirm the lesson. People who are a little unavailable. People who require the same careful room-reading and need suppression that childhood required. Not consciously. Because unavailability feels like the known condition. Like the familiar shape of how love works.

And they stay in those relationships longer than they should because leaving would require them to believe that something different is possible. That need doesn't have to be dangerous. That reaching doesn't have to be a gamble. That there are people in the world whose response to being needed is not overwhelm or withdrawal or guilt but something closer to welcome.

That belief is the hardest one to build when you were taught the opposite before you had words.

But it can be built.

Not quickly. Not without support. Not without the specific experience of reaching and being met, repeatedly, consistently enough that the nervous system begins to update the lesson.

The lesson that need is dangerous was learned in relationship.

It can only be unlearned in relationship.

The right kind. The kind where reaching produces connection instead of cost. Where wanting something from someone doesn't require an apology. Where being met doesn't feel so unfamiliar that you flinch away from it.

That relationship, whether it's a partner or a therapist or a friendship or all three, is not a luxury.

For the person who learned that need is dangerous, it's the whole path back.

The specific exhaustion of being the most emotionally intelligent person in your relationship.
Nobody warns you about this particular kind of tired.
It doesn't show up in the early stages. In the beginning the emotional intelligence feels like an asset. You can read the room. You can feel the shift in their energy before they've said a word. You can track the undercurrents, name what's happening, stay present when things get hard, repair faster than they can, hold more complexity than they know how to hold yet.
It feels like a gift you're bringing to the relationship.
And it is. For a while.
But gifts given consistently in one direction eventually stop feeling like gifts.
They start feeling like labor.
Here's what that labor actually looks like from the inside, in the specific texture of a day, a week, a year of being the one who sees more and feels more and understands more and therefore carries more.
You track their emotional state so automatically you don't notice you're doing it. You clock the slight tightening around their eyes when something's bothering them before they know they're bothered. You adjust your approach, your tone, your timing, without deciding to. You just do it. It's so built in by now it doesn't feel like effort. It just feels like paying attention.
Except it's not just paying attention. It's continuous emotional labor running in the background of everything else you're doing. And it costs something even when you can't feel the cost accumulating.
When something goes wrong between you, you're the one who can see what happened. You can trace the rupture back to its origin, name the dynamic, identify what each of you brought to it, hold your own part and theirs simultaneously. You can do all of that while they're still figuring out why they're upset.
So you do most of the work of understanding what happened.
And then you do most of the work of explaining it.
And then you do most of the work of repairing it.
And somewhere in there you also have to manage your own feelings about being the one who always does most of the work.
Which you often don't get to. Because by the time the repair is complete you're too tired to go back and tend to the part of you that needed tending. So you file it away. You tell yourself you're fine. You tell yourself this is just what it looks like to be with someone who's earlier in their development than you are. You tell yourself growth takes time and you have more than enough capacity for both of you while they're getting there.
And you keep going.
And the filing away accumulates.
And the tiredness underneath the competence gets heavier.
And you start to notice something you don't want to notice.
You're lonely.
Not because they're not there. They're there. They love you. They show up in the ways they know how to show up. But there's a specific loneliness that comes from never being fully met at the level where you actually live. From always being the one who reaches down to where they are rather than having someone who can reach up to where you are. From having so much capacity for depth and nuance and complexity and spending most of your relational energy in the shallower water because that's where they can swim.
You stop bringing certain things. Not because you decided to. Because you've learned through repetition that bringing them requires a level of translation that costs more than the conversation is worth. You'd have to explain the concept before you could share the feeling. You'd have to do so much groundwork to get them to the place where they could receive what you're trying to say that by the time you got there you'd have lost the thing you were trying to say.
So you keep it inside. Or you take it elsewhere. To a friend who gets it. To a therapist. To the part of yourself that has learned to be its own witness because the witness in the relationship isn't available at that resolution.
And the relationship continues. And it's not bad. It's genuinely not bad. There's love in it and history and real moments of connection. But there's also a ceiling. A place where you stop being able to go with this person because they don't have the equipment yet and you're tired of waiting at the bottom of the stairs.
Here's what makes this so hard to talk about.
Emotional intelligence is supposed to be the thing that makes relationships better. And it does. It absolutely does. But it can also become the thing that makes you indispensable in a way that quietly isolates you. The more capable you are of holding the relationship together, the more of the holding gets assigned to you, the less your partner has to develop their own capacity, and the more alone you become inside your own competence.
Your strength became the ceiling.
And you built it so well that neither of you noticed it going up.

You have one problem in your relationship, and if it's not solved, the other million problems will keep happening.
There are two separate things that might be happening, and they are outside the scope of this writing.
1) Abuse - if you feel abuse is happening, get out.
2) Compatibility - this is a topic that I spend countless hours every month helping couples sort out. If you have a compatibility problem, then you don't have a couple's problem. You have two individuals having a problem and you're attempting to be a couple. Different thing.
We are putting those two things above... aside... for now.
Couples do not consist of two communication machines that need to figure out how to say the right thing in the right order.
Couples need to grasp that they are in a bond.
A bond means that you are in an extraordinary integration of two minds. (or three if you live in San Francisco or you're in my other types of groups)
Okay back to the main point.
I said you have one problem.
That problem is what to do when you're frustrated with your partner.
By the time you've reached frustration, you are hurting.
If you've had many of these, and do not have the skill sets that I explain, then you're at the next level of frustration, which we call resentment.
There are things built into what it means to be hurting.
1) The way you've pieced together the details of your hurting don't make sense by the time you reveal them to your partner.
2) You've been alone in building the stories and meaning about those stories, so your partner has not been there along the way helping you organize what you're hurting about.
3) Just like witness testimony is unbelievably inaccurate, so is your explanation (to your partner).
4) Okay stay with #3 above for a moment longer and read again. In parentheses, I wrote "to your partner." To you the details are critical in understanding YOU. To your partner, your details are offensive and hurting them when you explain things.
5) Your partner must bring the awareness being described here or you will be further alone.
6) You must help each other understand that hurting means you will say things in an exaggerated manner, or yell, or go silent, in your strategy to desperately find a way to be heard.
7) Let's review once again that this is a bond. This is a curling up with each other, looking into each other's eyes, showing your confusion to each other. If you're not doing that, you're showing your clarity and confidence to each other... otherwise known in my work as the death of relationship.
By the time your partner expresses something to you that hurts, they might be 10 minutes into a conversation with you.
And they have not sent you clarity.
Your partner has sent you criticism.
It's true that... that has occurred.
And it's true that... your partner thinks they are communicating well and NOT being criticizing.
If you are reading this fast, I need you to slow down and read the line above again, because if you don't make contact with how much this is the exact thing that happens with 100% of the couples that come to me, you will eventually breakup, or worse, stay mad and miserable.
Couples say NO to each other in every step of relational arguments.
Let's introduce the word YES.
YES you are upset.
YES you believe I did that and then I did that and then I did that.
YES it's true that I'm offended when you think I did THAT, when I really meant to do THIS and then I mean to do THIS.
Whether you know it or not, this is the bind you are in.
It's awful.
I have more bad news.
All of the possible intimacy that would heal your life is UNDERNEATH all the things you do when you continuously tell each other NO.
Let's turn that bad news into good news.
All of the possible intimacy that would heal your life is UNDERNEATH all the things you do when you continuously tell each other NO.
Yep.
It's the same sentence.
YES, every single thing about this moment is unfair, and YES we are both hurting, and NO, we cannot use a better communication technique to solve it, because that is another coping strategy that we use because we can't stand the feeling of judgment from our partner.
Until you grasp how imperfect love is, how imperfect communication is, you will not thrive.
Until you grasp how to begin this journey, and seek the proper help to recognize if you have a partner that is capable of doing this with you, you will not thrive.
It's time to thrive.
It's time to understand how much painful feelings are part of a phenomenal relationship.
It's time to understand how to turn painful feelings into a deeper connection that day.

There's a kind of love that doesn't get talked about enough. It's not the falling-in-love part. It's not the honeymoon, the butterflies, the way someone's laugh can rearrange your whole chest. That part gets all the songs and the movies and the poetry.
I'm talking about the love that stays. The love that shows up, again and again, even when it's hard. Even when it's confusing. Even when, despite everything you pour into another person, something still feels like it isn't landing.
If you've ever loved someone deeply and still felt like they couldn't quite receive it, this is for you.
-
Here's what nobody prepares you for: you can love someone with your whole heart and still not be able to make them feel safe. You can be the most devoted, most present, most committed version of yourself and watch the person you love still flinch, still pull away, still question whether any of it is real.
And it is gutting.
Because you're not just watching them struggle. You're watching yourself struggle. You're sitting there, knowing what you feel, knowing how certain you are, knowing you'd do anything for them. And yet that certainty doesn't seem to reach them. It doesn't seem to land in the way you need it to.
So you try harder. You explain more. You show up in bigger ways and smaller ways. You say it differently. You say it again. You think if you could just find the right words, the right gesture, the right moment, they'd finally get it. They'd finally feel it the way you feel it.
And sometimes that works. And sometimes it doesn't. And when it doesn't, you're left alone with a very particular kind of ache.
-
What I want you to understand is that this isn't a reflection of the quality of your love. It isn't evidence that you're doing it wrong. It isn't a sign that the relationship is broken or that your person doesn't care or that you've somehow failed them.
It's a sign that they're human.
Every single person you will ever love is carrying something you didn't give them. A history that started long before you arrived. Wounds that were formed in childhood, in past relationships, in moments of betrayal or abandonment or neglect that had absolutely nothing to do with you. They've built systems inside themselves to survive those experiences. Walls that went up for very good reasons. Defenses that made total sense at the time.
And those systems don't just disappear because someone new comes along and loves them well. The nervous system doesn't work that way. The heart doesn't work that way. Even when someone wants to receive your love, even when they're consciously choosing you every day, the old patterns can still make it hard. The body remembers what the mind wants to forget.
This isn't an excuse. It's just the truth. And the truth is worth sitting with.
-
Now here's the part that's harder to hear, the part I want you to stay with for a moment.
When you find yourself obsessing over how to make them understand your love, when you're lying awake at night crafting the perfect speech, when you're cycling through what you should have said or what you should say next, when you're desperate to close the gap between what you feel and what they're experiencing... that desperation isn't really about them.
It's about you.
That's not a criticism. I say it with so much gentleness. But that urgent need to make them feel it, to get them to finally see it, to get the confirmation that your love has landed and is accepted and is enough... that's you trying to soothe yourself through them. That's your pain looking for relief in their recognition. That's the ache of loving someone and not being able to control how they receive it, and the desperation that comes from not knowing how to sit with that ache on your own.
We all do this. Every one of us. It's one of the most profoundly human things there is. We reach outward for what we haven't yet learned to give ourselves. We look to our partners to confirm our worth, our adequacy, our enoughness. And when they can't give us that confirmation, not because they don't love us but because they're fighting their own battles inside, we feel it as rejection. We feel it as failure. We feel it as proof of something we feared all along.
-
But here's where peace lives, if you're willing to find it.
Peace lives in acceptance. Not resignation. Not giving up. Not deciding that none of it matters. But genuine, open-handed acceptance of what is actually true: that you can love someone completely and still not be able to reach every corner of them. That love is not a guarantee of understanding. That your partner's inability to fully receive you is not the same as their unwillingness to try. That two people can be deeply committed to each other and still be, in certain moments, completely unable to meet.
That's not a tragedy. That's just love in its real, unfiltered, human form.
When you stop needing them to confirm your love by fully receiving it, something shifts. You stop performing your devotion and start simply living it. You stop measuring your love by how it lands and start trusting it because of what it is. You give without keeping score. You show up without needing it witnessed. And paradoxically, when you stop clinging so hard to the outcome, the connection often deepens. Because your partner can feel the difference between love that needs something back and love that doesn't. And love that doesn't need something back is the safest place in the world to land.
-
I also want to say something to the ones who feel unseen. The ones who are on the other side of this, who love their partner and know their partner loves them, but who still can't seem to let it all the way in. Who feel guilty about it. Who wish they could just relax into it. Who wonder what's wrong with them that they can't accept what's being offered.
Nothing is wrong with you.
You learned early that love came with conditions, or that love disappeared, or that the people who were supposed to love you hurt you instead. Your heart built a perimeter. And now someone is standing at the edge of that perimeter with their arms full and you want to let them in and a part of you is terrified. That's not failure. That's just the echo of old pain being cautious with something new.
Your partner's love is real. And you're allowed to take your time with it. You're allowed to learn, slowly and at your own pace, that this is different. That this one is safe. That you don't have to earn it or watch for the moment it gets taken away.
You're allowed to heal at the speed of trust.
-
What both of you are doing, in your different and imperfect ways, is trying. And trying, in love, is everything. It isn't always graceful. It isn't always successful. There will be moments where you miss each other completely. Where you're both reaching and neither of you finds the other's hand. Where you go to bed feeling more alone than you did before.

There's a kind of love that doesn't get talked about enough. It's not the falling-in-love part. It's not the honeymoon, the butterflies, the way someone's laugh can rearrange your whole chest. That part gets all the songs and the movies and the poetry.

I'm talking about the love that stays. The love that shows up, again and again, even when it's hard. Even when it's confusing. Even when, despite everything you pour into another person, something still feels like it isn't landing.

If you've ever loved someone deeply and still felt like they couldn't quite receive it, this is for you.

-

Here's what nobody prepares you for: you can love someone with your whole heart and still not be able to make them feel safe. You can be the most devoted, most present, most committed version of yourself and watch the person you love still flinch, still pull away, still question whether any of it is real.

And it is gutting.

Because you're not just watching them struggle. You're watching yourself struggle. You're sitting there, knowing what you feel, knowing how certain you are, knowing you'd do anything for them. And yet that certainty doesn't seem to reach them. It doesn't seem to land in the way you need it to.

So you try harder. You explain more. You show up in bigger ways and smaller ways. You say it differently. You say it again. You think if you could just find the right words, the right gesture, the right moment, they'd finally get it. They'd finally feel it the way you feel it.

And sometimes that works. And sometimes it doesn't. And when it doesn't, you're left alone with a very particular kind of ache.

-

What I want you to understand is that this isn't a reflection of the quality of your love. It isn't evidence that you're doing it wrong. It isn't a sign that the relationship is broken or that your person doesn't care or that you've somehow failed them.

It's a sign that they're human.

Every single person you will ever love is carrying something you didn't give them. A history that started long before you arrived. Wounds that were formed in childhood, in past relationships, in moments of betrayal or abandonment or neglect that had absolutely nothing to do with you. They've built systems inside themselves to survive those experiences. Walls that went up for very good reasons. Defenses that made total sense at the time.

And those systems don't just disappear because someone new comes along and loves them well. The nervous system doesn't work that way. The heart doesn't work that way. Even when someone wants to receive your love, even when they're consciously choosing you every day, the old patterns can still make it hard. The body remembers what the mind wants to forget.

This isn't an excuse. It's just the truth. And the truth is worth sitting with.

Now here's the part that's harder to hear, the part I want you to stay with for a moment.

It's about you.

That's not a criticism. I say it with so much gentleness. But that urgent need to make them feel it, to get them to finally see it, to get the confirmation that your love has landed and is accepted and is enough... that's you trying to soothe yourself through them. That's your pain looking for relief in their recognition. That's the ache of loving someone and not being able to control how they receive it, and the desperation that comes from not knowing how to sit with that ache on your own.

We all do this. Every one of us. It's one of the most profoundly human things there is. We reach outward for what we haven't yet learned to give ourselves. We look to our partners to confirm our worth, our adequacy, our enoughness. And when they can't give us that confirmation, not because they don't love us but because they're fighting their own battles inside, we feel it as rejection. We feel it as failure. We feel it as proof of something we feared all along.

But here's where peace lives, if you're willing to find it.

Peace lives in acceptance. Not resignation. Not giving up. Not deciding that none of it matters. That your partner's inability to fully receive you is not the same as their unwillingness to try. That two people can be deeply committed to each other and still be, in certain moments, completely unable to meet.

That's not a tragedy. That's just love in its real, unfiltered, human form.

When you stop needing them to confirm your love by fully receiving it, something shifts. You stop performing your devotion and start simply living it. You stop measuring your love by how it lands and start trusting it because of what it is. You give without keeping score. You show up without needing it witnessed. And paradoxically, when you stop clinging so hard to the outcome, the connection often deepens. Because your partner can feel the difference between love that needs something back and love that doesn't. And love that doesn't need something back is the safest place in the world to land.

Nothing is wrong with you.
