There's a version of the front door window that almost nobody talks about, and it's the one where everything gets reversed. The person walking in the door isn't the one who needs to land. The person who's been home all day is.

And when this reversal isn't recognized, it creates one of the most quietly destructive dynamics in a marriage. A resentment that builds so slowly neither partner can trace it back to a single moment, but that eventually poisons the entire evening and then the entire week and then the entire marriage.

Let me explain what's actually happening.

The standard front door dynamic assumes the person walking in has been out in the world and needs fifteen minutes to decompress from the external chaos of the day. The meetings. The commute. The demands. That person lands. The person at home waits for them. The reunion happens after the landing.

But there's a different version of this. And it happens in households where one partner has been home with small children, or home managing a complicated household, or home dealing with their own interior work, or home in a way that looks from the outside like rest but is actually its own form of exhaustion that the outside world doesn't recognize as exhaustion.

In those households, the person walking in the door isn't the most depleted one.

The person at home is.

And the person walking in has no idea.

Here's what the day has actually looked like for the partner who's been home with small children. They've been in a sensory environment that never stopped. The noise level has been high since 6am. The demands have been constant and nonverbal and impossible to batch. They've been interrupted every ninety seconds for eleven straight hours. They've had to be the entire emotional regulation system for a small human who doesn't yet have one of their own. They've had to make decisions about food and safety and discipline and entertainment and laundry and naps and screens and snacks and outerwear and tantrums all while being physically pulled on, literally touched, held, climbed on, for most of the waking day.

That's not rest.

That's a kind of labor that most people who've never done it full-time cannot fully comprehend.

And by the time the door opens at the end of the day, the person who's been home is not in a state of waiting for connection. They're in a state of waiting to be released. Released from the constant demand. Released from the need to be the adult in the room. Released from the sensory overload. Released from being physically touched by someone who has not stopped touching them since breakfast.

They need the fifteen minutes.

But they don't get the fifteen minutes, because the person who walks in the door is in their own transition, and the cultural script says the person coming in from the world is the one who needs to land.

So the person who's been home powers through. They hand off the child. They accept the hello. They pretend they're available. They try to be warm and welcoming and pleasant because they love their partner and they've missed their partner and they don't want to start the evening by being cold.

But their body is still in the middle of an eleven-hour workday that hasn't ended yet, and their nervous system is begging for a shutdown window that they're not being given permission to take.

This is where the resentment starts.

Not in anger. In something quieter than anger. In the small, invisible moment where one partner prioritizes the other partner's fifteen minutes over their own, and doesn't say anything, and doesn't ask for reciprocity, and starts building a silent ledger in their body that says, "I needed that window and I didn't get it."

Ten times. A hundred times. A thousand times.

And now the at-home partner is walking around the house carrying a quiet grievance they can't name, because they can't articulate it even to themselves. It sounds petty. It sounds ungrateful. It sounds like, "I'm upset because my spouse came home and wanted to decompress for fifteen minutes." Who gets to complain about that?

The assumption that being home is the rest and being out is the work. The assumption that the partner at home is the default available one and the partner coming in is the one who needs to be met where they are.

When the truth, in many households, is the opposite.

And here's the part that makes this so hard to see.

The person walking in the door genuinely has had a hard day too. Work is real. Commuting is real. The emotional residue of the workday is real. They're not making it up. They actually do need the fifteen minutes.

There are three sentences I teach couples to say to each other at the end of the fifteen-minute front door window that change everything about what happens next. They're not complicated. They're not fancy. They don't sound like therapy. They take about ninety seconds total. And almost no couple has ever been given them.
I'm going to give them to you. And I'm going to tell you why each one works, because understanding why matters almost as much as knowing what to say.
Here's the setup first, because the sentences only work in the right context.
The front door window has closed. Both of you have had your fifteen minutes to land. The person who walked in from the world has decompressed. The person who was home has had a minute to shift out of the state they were in. The kids are occupied, or settled, or momentarily not pulling on anyone. The house has a minute of breathable air in it.
That's when you use the three sentences.
Not before the window closes. Not an hour later when the moment has passed. Right at the point where both of your nervous systems have arrived in the same house at the same time and you're about to either connect or drift apart for the rest of the evening.
Sentence one.
"I'm glad you're home."
That's it. Four words. And I need you to understand why these four words do something that a thousand other sentences cannot.
"I'm glad you're home" is not a question. It doesn't require the other person to respond with information. It doesn't ask them to perform anything. It doesn't put them on the spot. It doesn't set up an expectation. It's a pure declaration of presence. It says, "Your being here matters to me. Not what you did today. Not what you're going to do tonight. The fact of your presence in this house makes me glad."
Most couples haven't said that sentence to each other in years. They say things that sound like it but aren't it. "How was your day" is not that sentence. "Did you remember to pick up the thing" is not that sentence. "Can you take the kids for a minute" is not that sentence. Those sentences assume the other person is already home and are about what comes next. "I'm glad you're home" is about the arrival itself, and it marks the arrival as something worth noting.
When you say that sentence to your partner after the landing window has closed, their nervous system registers it as a welcome. Not a welcome home in the performative sense, the "hi honey how was work" sense. A welcome in the deeper sense. "I see that you have crossed the threshold and I want you to know that your crossing mattered to me."
That welcome is something most married adults have not received from their partner in years.
And receiving it changes the way the rest of the evening feels in your body.
Sentence two.
"What was one thing from today that stuck with you."
Not "how was your day." Not "what happened at work." Not "how was it." Those questions get answers like "fine" and "good" and "the usual," and those answers are dead ends because the questions are dead ends.
"What was one thing from today that stuck with you" is a completely different question. It asks the other person to do one specific piece of interior work, which is to scan their day and identify the thing that's still sitting in their chest. Everyone has one. Nobody goes through a day without one thing that stuck. A moment. A comment. A feeling. A person. A memory. A surprise. Something that wouldn't come up if you asked a generic question but that will come up if you ask a specific one.
The reason this question works is that it's not asking about performance or logistics or summary. It's asking about residue. And residue is always real. Residue is the stuff you didn't plan to think about but that's still in you. Residue is where the actual interior life lives, and most couples have not asked each other about their actual interior lives in so long that both of them have forgotten they have one to share.
When you ask this question in the right window, right after the landing, when the other person's nervous system has just settled into being home, they will have an answer. It might take them a second. They might say, "Let me think." That's fine. Let them think. The thinking is part of the gift. They're scanning their day for you. They're doing a piece of internal work in front of you that nobody else in their life has asked them to do today.
And when they tell you the thing, you will learn something about them that you didn't know this morning. Every single time. Without exception. Because something happens to every adult every day that sticks, and if nobody asks, that thing gets buried with all the other unasked-about things, and the burial is slowly filling up a graveyard inside them that is one of the reasons they feel unknown in their own marriage.
You ask the question. They answer it. You listen.
That's sentence two.
Sentence three is the hardest one for most couples to say, because it requires a small act of vulnerability that neither of you might be used to. But it's also the one that does the most work in the shortest amount of time.
Sentence three.
"Here's something I was thinking about you today."
Stop and sit with that one.
Not, "I was thinking about you today." That's fine but incomplete. The key is "here's something," because "here's something" promises specificity. You're not just reporting that they crossed your mind. You're going to tell them the content of the thought.
And the content can be anything. It can be big. It can be small. It can be a memory. It can be something you noticed about them recently. It can be something you appreciated. It can be a concern. It can be a question that came to you while you were driving. It can be a moment from this morning that made you smile when you remembered it later. It can be almost anything, as long as it's specific and as long as it's true.
"Here's something I was thinking about you today. I remembered the way you looked at me at the grocery store last week when I said something dumb and you just smiled instead of correcting me. I've been thinking about that smile all day."
"Here's something I was thinking about you today. I realized you've been really tired lately and I haven't asked you why. I'm sorry I haven't asked. I'm asking now."
"Here's something I was thinking about you today. I was in a meeting and someone said something that reminded me of a thing you said to me five years ago that I never told you I remembered. I wanted to tell you I remembered it."
"Here's something I was thinking about you today. I'm nervous about a conversation we're going to have this weekend about your mother and I wanted you to know I've been nervous about it."
Anything. Any specific thought that had them in it. Delivered with the introduction, "here's something I was thinking about you today."
Why does this sentence work so powerfully?
Because the single most devastating feeling in a long-term marriage is the feeling that you don't cross your partner's mind when you're not in the room. That feeling is one of the deepest wounds a married person can carry, and most people carry it silently because saying it out loud feels too pitiful. "I don't think my spouse thinks about me when I'm not there" is the kind of sentence most adults will die before saying.
But they feel it.
And the cure for it isn't for their partner to tell them "I think about you all the time," which sounds like a platitude. The cure is specificity. The cure is hearing, from your partner, the exact content of one thought they had about you today. Because the content proves the thought happened. You can't make up the content of a thought you didn't have. The specificity is the evidence.
When your partner hears a specific, real thought you had about them today, their nervous system receives evidence that they exist in your interior world when they're not physically in front of you. And that evidence answers the question their body has been quietly asking for years without knowing it was asking.
Do I cross your mind?
Yes. You do. Today. Here's the thought.
That answer lands in a place that no "I love you" can reach.
Because "I love you" is abstract and love is assumed. "Here's something I was thinking about you today" is specific and thinking is not assumed. Thinking is the thing people hunger for in a long-term marriage. Not to be loved, because the love is usually there. To be thought about. To be in the other person's interior world. To take up space in their mind when they're not taking up space in their field of vision.
That's what this sentence gives.

Not a welcome home in the performative sense, the "hi honey how was work" sense. A welcome in the deeper sense. Something that wouldn't come up if you asked a generic question but that will come up if you ask a specific one.

Residue is the stuff you didn't plan to think about but that's still in you. There's one question you can ask your partner tonight that will tell you more about the state of your marriage than any conversation you've ever had about the relationship itself. It takes about fifteen seconds to ask. Your partner won't feel interrogated. They won't even realize they're telling you anything important. And their answer will show you, with almost forensic precision, how many bids you've been missing lately.
Here's the question.
"What's something small that happened to you today that you didn't tell me about?"
That's it.
Read it again, because the phrasing matters and most people will skim past it without noticing why every word is doing work.
"What's something small." Not big. Small. You're not asking for the headline of the day. You're asking for the stuff underneath the headline. The stuff that didn't make it into "how was your day" because it didn't feel important enough to report. The stuff that gets lost in the summary.
"That happened to you today." Not yesterday. Not this week. Today. Recent enough that it's still in the body. Specific enough that they can actually locate something instead of drifting into generalities.
"That you didn't tell me about." This is the key phrase. This is what makes the question work. Because you're not asking what happened. You're asking what happened that they didn't share. Which means you're asking them to identify, in real time, a bid that didn't get made. A reach they didn't reach. A moment they chose to hold back instead of offering.
The answer to that question is diagnostic.
Let me explain why.
Every single day, every adult has dozens of small moments they could tell their partner about. A funny thing a coworker said. A weird interaction at the coffee shop. A memory that surfaced. A feeling that came up and went away. A decision they made that they second-guessed. A thought they had about one of the kids. A physical sensation. A worry. A small delight. A passing sadness. A song on the radio that reminded them of something. A piece of news they read that bothered them.
Your partner is carrying a whole day's worth of small moments when they walk into the room where you're sitting.
And every one of those small moments is a potential bid.
A bid doesn't become a bid until the person decides to share it. The moment is neutral. The sharing is the reach. "A weird thing happened at the coffee shop today" is a reach. It's an invitation into their interior world. It's a small door they're opening and hoping you'll walk through.
Most people share some of their small moments and hold back others. The ones they share are the bids they made. The ones they hold back are the bids they didn't make. And the ratio between the two tells you almost everything about the state of the connection between you.
Here's what you need to understand. When someone holds back a small moment from their partner, they're not usually doing it consciously. They're not thinking, "I'm going to withhold this." The withholding happens at a lower level than thought. It happens in the body, in a reflex that has learned over time whether sharing small things with this specific person is worth the effort. If the body has learned that sharing small things gets met with engagement, the small things come out. If the body has learned that sharing small things gets met with distraction or half-attention or a quick nod and a return to whatever they were doing, the small things stop coming out.
The body stops reaching.
Not dramatically. Not all at once. Slowly. A small moment here doesn't get mentioned. A small thought there doesn't get shared. The filter between the interior world and the spoken world gets tighter and tighter, and eventually the things your partner is telling you are only the things they think are important enough to justify your attention. Which means they've started quietly doing a calculation about what deserves your attention, and the calculation almost always underestimates what you'd actually want to hear.
Your partner is probably holding back small moments right now.
Not because they don't love you. Because at some point their body learned that small moments weren't worth offering, and the learning became automatic.
This is what's really happening inside a couple who feels like they've grown apart. They haven't stopped loving each other. They've stopped offering each other the small moments, and the absence of the small moments is the thing that makes the marriage feel empty even though neither of them can explain why.
The big stuff still gets talked about. The logistics. The kids. The work situation. The calendar. Nobody is failing to communicate on the big stuff. It's the small stuff that's disappeared. And the small stuff is the fabric of intimacy. The big stuff is just the infrastructure.
Now here's why the question works.
When you ask, "What's something small that happened to you today that you didn't tell me about," you're doing something very specific. You're creating permission. You're saying, with your question, "I want the thing you were going to keep to yourself. I want the unfiltered version. I want the moment that didn't make the cut. Give it to me. I'm interested in the stuff you've been holding back."
Most partners, when asked this question, will do one of three things, and each of the three answers tells you something different about the state of the marriage.
Answer one. They pause, think for a moment, and offer something small. A specific little thing. A weird interaction. A passing thought. A feeling that came up. They answer the question literally, and they give you a real moment from their day that they hadn't shared.
If your partner does this, your marriage is in relatively good shape. It means they have small moments they hadn't yet shared, but the moments are accessible to them, and when you invite them in, the moments come out easily. You've been missing some bids but not to the point where the filter has become reflexive. You can probably repair this with thirty seconds of attention a day.
Answer two. They pause, think for a longer moment, and then say something like "I don't know, I can't think of anything," or "nothing really, just a normal day." They seem to be searching and coming up empty.
If your partner does this, your marriage is in more serious territory. It means the filter has become tight enough that when you ask for the small moments, they can't even find them in their own memory. The moments happened, but the body has stopped tagging them as shareable, so they didn't get stored as potential shares. They got stored as just random content from the day, and random content from the day is hard to retrieve on demand. When the filter gets this tight, you're in a marriage where real intimacy has started to recede and neither of you has named it.
Answer three. They pause, look at you for a second, and then give you something real. Not a small thing. Something bigger. Something they'd been sitting on. A feeling. A fear. A thought about you. A memory. Something that was not what you asked for but was what they'd been holding back at a deeper level.
If your partner does this, pay attention. Because what just happened is that your question reached past the surface filter and touched something below it, and they trusted you enough to give you the real thing instead of the technically-correct answer. This is rare. And when it happens, you've just been handed a gift. Receive it. Don't interrupt. Don't redirect. Don't try to fix. Just receive what they're giving you and let them see that you received it.
Whatever answer you get, answer one, two, or three, you will now know more about the state of your marriage than any twenty-page questionnaire could tell you. You will have a real piece of data, collected in real time, from the person whose interior life you share.
And here's the other thing the question does.
It doesn't feel like an interrogation. It doesn't feel like a relationship check-in. It doesn't feel like therapy-speak. It feels like genuine curiosity. Like you're actually interested in their day in a specific and unusual way. Which you are. And the fact that it doesn't feel like a test is precisely why it tells you the truth. People tell you the truth when they don't realize they're being measured.
Your partner won't realize they're telling you the state of your marriage.
But they will be.
And you'll know how to read the answer because you'll remember which of the three categories it fell into.
Now here's what to do with the answer.
If they answered with something small and specific, thank them. Not for the specific moment. For telling you. "I love hearing the small stuff. I don't want to miss it. Tell me more small stuff from now on." That sentence, delivered after they've just offered you a small moment, trains the filter to open a little wider next time. You're rewarding the share. Their body will remember.
If they couldn't find anything, don't push. Don't say, "Come on, there must be something." Don't make them feel like they failed a test. Instead, say something like, "That's okay. I realized I've been asking about the big stuff and not the small stuff, and I want to start asking about the small stuff more. I want to know the small things too." That sentence tells them, without accusing them, that you're going to start creating more space for the small things. And their body will start tagging small moments as shareable again, slowly, over time, as the new pattern establishes.
If they gave you something bigger than you asked for, receive it. Don't panic. Don't try to fix whatever they said. Just listen. And when they're done, you can say something simple like, "Thank you for telling me that. I'm glad you did." Nothing else required. The receiving is the response.
This question, asked once, will give you diagnostic information.
Asked regularly, it becomes the thing that actually changes the marriage.
Because the more you ask, the more your partner's body learns that small moments are wanted, the more the filter opens, the more of their interior life becomes available to you, and the more the quiet accumulation of unshared moments starts to reverse itself.
You stop losing them in small drops.
You start gaining them back in small drops.
Same mechanism. Opposite direction.
And over weeks and months, the marriage you thought was growing quiet starts getting louder again. Not louder in volume. Louder in signal. More of the real stuff coming through.
One question.
Fifteen seconds.
Tonight.
Ask it, and then listen to what the answer tells you. And then tomorrow, ask it again. And the day after that. And watch what happens to the connection between you and the person you love over the next thirty days.
Most couples will never ask this question.
You now have it.
Use it tonight.

Whatever answer you get, answer one, two, or three, you will now know more about the state of your marriage than any twenty-page questionnaire could tell you. You will have a real piece of data, collected in real time, from the person whose interior life you share.

And here's the other thing the question does.

It doesn't feel like an interrogation. It doesn't feel like a relationship check-in. It doesn't feel like therapy-speak. It feels like genuine curiosity. Like you're actually interested in their day in a specific and unusual way. Which you are. And the fact that it doesn't feel like a test is precisely why it tells you the truth. People tell you the truth when they don't realize they're being measured.

Your partner won't realize they're telling you the state of your marriage.

But they will be.

And you'll know how to read the answer because you'll remember which of the three categories it fell into.

Now here's what to do with the answer.

If they answered with something small and specific, thank them. Not for the specific moment. For telling you. "I love hearing the small stuff. I don't want to miss it. Tell me more small stuff from now on." That sentence, delivered after they've just offered you a small moment, trains the filter to open a little wider next time. You're rewarding the share. Their body will remember.

If they couldn't find anything, don't push. Don't say, "Come on, there must be something." Don't make them feel like they failed a test. Instead, say something like, "That's okay. I realized I've been asking about the big stuff and not the small stuff, and I want to start asking about the small stuff more. I want to know the small things too." That sentence tells them, without accusing them, that you're going to start creating more space for the small things. And their body will start tagging small moments as shareable again, slowly, over time, as the new pattern establishes.

If they gave you something bigger than you asked for, receive it. Don't panic. Don't try to fix whatever they said. Just listen. And when they're done, you can say something simple like, "Thank you for telling me that. I'm glad you did." Nothing else required. The receiving is the response.

This question, asked once, will give you diagnostic information.

Asked regularly, it becomes the thing that actually changes the marriage.

Because the more you ask, the more your partner's body learns that small moments are wanted, the more the filter opens, the more of their interior life becomes available to you, and the more the quiet accumulation of unshared moments starts to reverse itself.

You stop losing them in small drops.

You start gaining them back in small drops.

Same mechanism. Opposite direction.

And over weeks and months, the marriage you thought was growing quiet starts getting louder again. Not louder in volume. Louder in signal. More of the real stuff coming through.

One question.

Fifteen seconds.

Tonight.

Ask it, and then listen to what the answer tells you. And then tomorrow, ask it again. And the day after that. And watch what happens to the connection between you and the person you love over the next thirty days.

Most couples will never ask this question.

You now have it.

Use it tonight.

When Your Relationship Stopped Growing
-
When the Conversation Dies
1. You talk about logistics more than feelings.
2. "How was your day?" becomes a formality neither one actually answers.
3. You've stopped asking questions you don't already know the answer to.
4. Silence between you feels empty instead of comfortable.
5. You edit yourself before you speak - not out of kindness, but out of exhaustion.
6. You rehearse difficult conversations in your head but never actually have them.
7. You've replaced curiosity about each other with assumptions about each other.
8. You stop finishing each other's sentences - because you stop starting them.
9. The last real laugh you shared - you can't remember when it was.
10. You talk about your partner more than you talk to them.
When the Body Keeps Score
11. You flinch at their tone before they've even said anything wrong.
12. Their touch feels like obligation instead of invitation.
13. You hold your breath when they walk in the room.
14. Sex becomes a negotiation instead of a conversation.
15. You sleep on your side of the bed like it's a border.
16. Physical proximity without emotional closeness starts to feel like loneliness with company.
17. Your nervous system relaxes when they leave - and tightens when they return.
18. You can't remember the last time you reached for them without a reason.
19. Hugs get shorter. Then mechanical. Then rare.
20. You stop noticing how they smell.
When Resentment Moves In
21. You keep a mental ledger of everything you've done and everything they haven't.
22. Apologies start feeling like strategies instead of repair.
23. You bring up something from three years ago in a fight about dishes.
24. Forgiveness becomes a word you say but not something your body does.
25. You interpret neutral actions as selfish ones.
26. "Fine" becomes the most common word in your house.
27. You stop giving them the benefit of the doubt.
28. Their breathing annoys you. Literally.
29. You've started keeping score - and you're always losing.
30. Every small disappointment lands on top of the pile instead of standing on its own.
When You Stop Choosing Each Other
31. Date night becomes another task on the to-do list.
32. You plan your future without instinctively including them.
33. You'd rather scroll your phone in bed than turn toward them.
34. You stop defending them to other people.
35. Their wins don't feel like your wins anymore.
36. You fantasize - not about someone else, but about being alone.
37. You stop making bids for connection because the rejection isn't worth it.
38. You've stopped fighting for the relationship and started fighting each other.
39. Compromise feels like losing.
40. You choose convenience over closeness every single time.
When Emotional Safety Disappears
41. You cry alone in the bathroom instead of in front of them.
42. Vulnerability feels dangerous instead of connecting.
43. You've learned which parts of yourself to hide.
44. Their opinion of you matters less - not because you're secure, but because you've given up.
45. You test them with small asks to see if they'll show up - and feel nothing when they don't.
46. You protect your inner world from the person who's supposed to know it best.
47. Sharing good news with them feels risky because they might minimize it.
48. "I'm fine" becomes your permanent armor.
49. You've stopped expecting comfort. You just want to not be hurt.
50. The space between you feels negotiated, not safe.
When Growth Gets Replaced by Routine
51. You can predict every single thing they'll say in an argument.
52. Weekends look the same as they did two years ago - and neither of you chose that.
53. You've stopped introducing each other to new things.
54. The relationship feels like a lease you keep renewing out of habit.
55. You've stopped dreaming together.
56. "We should..." never turns into "We did."
57. You describe your relationship in past tense - "We used to be..."
58. Growth in one partner starts feeling threatening to the other.
59. You've both settled into roles that neither of you actually wants.
60. Change sounds exhausting. Staying the same sounds safer. Neither sounds good.
When Repair Stops Working
61. Apologies come faster but mean less.
62. You make up without ever actually resolving anything.
63. The same fight happens on a monthly loop with different costumes.
64. You've stopped trying to understand - now you just want to be right.
65. Ruptures don't get repaired. They get buried.
66. "Let's just move on" becomes your only conflict strategy.
67. You know exactly what they need to hear but you withhold it anyway.
68. Counseling sounds pointless because "they won't change."
69. You've replaced honesty with peacekeeping.
70. The emotional distance after a fight gets longer every time.
When the Outside World Becomes the Escape
71. Work becomes a refuge instead of something you come home from.
72. You confide in friends about things you'd never say to your partner.
73. You have emotional intimacy with someone else and call it "just friendship."
74. Social media becomes a parallel life where you feel more seen.
75. You volunteer for every extra thing - anything to avoid being home.
76. You start comparing your relationship to other people's curated versions.
77. Happy couples irritate you instead of inspiring you.
78. You build a rich inner life your partner knows nothing about.
79. Your best self shows up everywhere except inside the relationship.
80. You stop posting about them - not out of privacy, but out of disconnection.
When Identity Gets Lost or Locked
81. You don't recognize who you've become inside this dynamic.
82. You've abandoned hobbies, friends, or parts of yourself to reduce friction.
83. You define yourself as the "responsible one" or the "emotional one" instead of a whole person.
84. The version of you your partner knows is three years out of date.
85. You feel more like roommates with a shared mortgage than partners with a shared life.
86. You've stopped growing as an individual because the relationship has no room for it.
87. You perform your role instead of living your life.
88. You've lost your voice - not because they took it, but because you stopped using it.
89. The relationship requires you to stay small.
90. You've forgotten what you wanted before "we" replaced "I."
When Hope Quietly Leaves
91. You stop imagining it getting better.
92. You stay because leaving feels harder - not because staying feels right.
93. You've replaced hope with endurance.
94. The phrase "this is just how relationships are" becomes your north star.
95. You rationalize unhappiness as maturity.
96. You read lists like this one and recognize every single line.
97. You've stopped praying for change and started bracing for more of the same.
98. You feel guilty for wanting more - as if wanting more is the problem.
99. You whisper "I love you" and it sounds like a question.
100. You realize the relationship didn't end with a fight. It ended with silence.

Everything I just told you about how men reach for their wives in ways women don't recognize? It works in the other direction too. And the other direction might be even more invisible.
Because women also make indirect bids. Constantly. Every day. In ways their husbands have never been trained to see as reaching.
And the reason this direction is harder to talk about is that the culture has already told everyone that women are the verbal ones. The emotional ones. The ones who say what they feel. The ones who use words and eye contact and direct requests. So when a woman's bid goes unmet, the assumption is that she must not have said anything. That if she'd just told him what she needed, he would have responded.
But that assumption is wrong.
Because women don't always use words either.
Women also indirect. Women also reach in code. Women also make bids that don't look like bids, that don't sound like bids, that register in the room as something else entirely while the actual reach goes invisible.
And their husbands are missing them. Every day. Without knowing.
Let me show you what female indirect bids actually look like, because once you see them, you're going to recognize about fifteen things your wife did this week that you walked right past.
She rearranged something in the house. Moved the pillows on the couch. Put out new hand towels in the bathroom. Changed the sheets. Hung something on the wall. Moved a plant. Made the bed differently.
That's a bid.
Not a decorating decision. A bid. She changed the environment and she's waiting for you to notice the change. Not because she needs your opinion on throw pillows. Because the noticing would mean you're paying attention to the space she's been tending. The space she's been making into a home for both of you. The space she pours herself into daily that you walk through without comment.
When you walk past the new hand towels without saying anything, she doesn't think, "He doesn't care about hand towels." Her body registers, "He doesn't see what I do here."
That's the wound. Not the towels. The invisibility.
She asks you a question about someone else's relationship. "Did you hear that Jake and Sarah are having problems?" or "My friend told me something about her husband today."
That's a bid.
She's not gossiping. She's opening a door to a conversation about relationships, hoping you'll walk through it. She's testing whether you'll engage with the topic of how couples work, because if you engage with it abstractly, about someone else's marriage, she might feel safe enough to bring up something about your own.
When you say, "That's too bad" and go back to your phone, you didn't just dismiss Jake and Sarah. You closed the door she was trying to open. And she won't try to open it again for a while.
She shows you something on her phone. A photo. An article. A video. A meme. Something she saw during her day that made her think of you or made her laugh or made her feel something.
That's a bid.
She's not showing you content. She's showing you her interior world. She's saying, "This is what caught my attention today, and I want to share the experience of it with you." The thing on the phone is the excuse. The sharing is the point.
When you glance at the screen for half a second and say "that's funny" without actually looking, she doesn't think you didn't like the meme. She thinks you didn't want to be inside her experience with her. And that's a completely different injury than not liking a meme.
She tells you she's tired.
That's a bid.
Not a report. A bid. "I'm tired" from a woman to her husband is almost never a weather update about her energy level. It's a reach. It's saying, "I need you to see me right now. I need you to recognize that I've been carrying something all day. I don't need you to fix it. I need you to acknowledge it."
When you say, "Then go to bed," you've responded to the report. You haven't touched the bid. And the distance between what she said and what she meant is the distance that's growing between you every time this happens.
She changes her appearance. Not dramatically. A new lipstick. A different way of wearing her hair. A piece of clothing she doesn't normally wear. Something subtle enough that you might not notice unless you were paying attention.
That's a bid.
She's asking you to see her. Physically. As a woman. Not as a mother. Not as a roommate. Not as the person who manages the calendar and the groceries and the kids' schedules. As a woman who put something on today that was for you, or at least partly for you, or at least partly to see if you'd notice.
When you don't notice, her body doesn't register, "He didn't see the lipstick." Her body registers, "He doesn't see me."
She starts a sentence and then stops. "I was going to say something but never mind." Or she trails off in the middle of a thought. Or she begins a story and then waves it away like it wasn't important.
That's a bid.
The trailing off is not her losing interest in her own sentence. It's her testing whether you'll pursue it. Whether you'll say, "No, what were you going to say?" Whether you'll lean in instead of letting the sentence die.

And she'd noticed the shutdown and concluded it was about her attractiveness. That he didn't want her anymore. She'd been carrying that conclusion for three years without saying it out loud because saying it out loud would make it real and she wasn't ready for it to be real.

He said, "I don't know. Just to be close to her."

She said, "That's what it was?"
He looked at her.

He said, "To me."
The room went very still.

He said, "I stopped reaching because I thought you didn't want me near you."

Nineteen years of misread reaches.

On her hip.

She said his hand was shaking.

His hand was shaking. Because the man who'd stopped reaching three years ago was reaching again. And the reaching was so terrifying, so loaded with the accumulated weight of every rejection his body had stored, that his hand was physically trembling against her hip.
She said, "I could feel how scared he was. In his hand. I could feel it. And I realized I'd never known he was scared. I thought he was distant. I thought he'd checked out. She didn't stiffen.
She didn't calculate whether the hand on the hip was going somewhere.
She moved toward the hand.
She rolled toward him. Slowly. And she pressed her back against his chest. And she took his shaking hand from her hip and moved it to her stomach and held it there with both of hers.
And she said, "Stay."
One word.
And his body broke.

Neither of them said anything else.
Neither of them moved.
Neither of them tried to turn it into anything.
His chest against her back. His arm around her. His hand on her stomach held by both of hers. Both of them breathing.
That's it.
That's the whole thing.
Two minutes of a man holding his wife in the dark with his hand on her stomach.
That's what they both described to me as the most intimate experience of their nineteen-year marriage.
Not a vacation. Not a wedding. Not a night of passion. Not any of the things that are supposed to be the peaks of a marriage.
Two minutes of being held.
After three years of not being held.
By a man whose hand was shaking because the reaching was that frightening and that necessary.

I said, "What happened in your body when she said 'stay'?"
He was quiet for a long time.
Then he said, "Something melted."

But it's been there for years and it melted in about ten seconds."
He said, "I didn't know my hand was shaking until she told you. But I believe it. Because I was terrified. I was terrified she was going to pull away again. And I knew if she pulled away one more time I was never going to reach again. That was going to be the last one. And she didn't pull away. She came toward me. And the direction of her body told me something that no words could have told me."
I said, "What did it tell you?"
He said, "That I'm still welcome there."
That I'm still welcome there.
That's what the two minutes were about.
Not s*x. Not desire. Not passion. Not attraction.
Welcome.
The experience of a man reaching for the safest place he knows and discovering that the safest place still wants him there.
After three years of believing it didn't.
That's what closeness bids are about.
That's what the hand on the waist is reaching for.
That's what the pull in bed is asking.
That's what the hug that lasts too long is saying.
"Am I still welcome there?"
And the answer to that question, delivered not in words but in the direction of a body in the dark, is the thing that determines whether a man stays open or closes permanently.
She rolled toward him.
That's the answer.
That's the whole answer.
Not a conversation. Not an apology. Not a twelve-step repair plan.
A body moving toward a reaching hand instead of away from it.
Two minutes of holding in the dark.
And a one-word sentence that told a shaking man that home was still open.
"Stay."
If you take one thing from everything I've written about bids and closeness and the physical dimension of marriage, let it be this.
The next time his hand finds your hip in the dark, move toward it.
Not away.
Toward.
And if you can, hold the hand.
And if you can, say the word.
And give him two minutes of knowing that the safest place on earth didn't close while he wasn't looking.
Two minutes.
That's all it takes to bring a man back from three years of silence.
Not therapy. Not a conversation. Not a weekend away.
Two minutes of being welcome.
In the dark.
In the bed you've been sharing but not sharing.
Let him back in.
He's been waiting at the door with a shaking hand for longer than you know.

Not moving. Not sliding. Not going anywhere. Just his hand. Resting on her hip. The way it used to rest there years ago when they were still in the stage of marriage where bodies find each other in the dark without thinking about it.

She said his hand was shaking.

She told me that and had to stop talking for a minute.

His hand was shaking. Because the man who'd stopped reaching three years ago was reaching again. And the reaching was so terrifying, so loaded with the accumulated weight of every rejection his body had stored, that his hand was physically trembling against her hip.

She said, "I could feel how scared he was. In his hand. I could feel it. And I realized I'd never known he was scared. I thought he was distant. I thought he'd checked out. I thought he didn't want me anymore. And his hand was shaking because he wanted to be close to me so badly that the wanting was making his body shake."

She didn't pull away.

She didn't stiffen.

She didn't calculate whether the hand on the hip was going somewhere.

She moved toward the hand.

She rolled toward him. Slowly. And she pressed her back against his chest. And she took his shaking hand from her hip and moved it to her stomach and held it there with both of hers.

And she said, "Stay."

One word.

And his body broke.

Not in the way bodies break during a fight. In the way bodies break when something that's been held too tightly for too long finally gets released. She said she felt it happen against her back. His chest. Something inside his chest let go. And the shaking in his hand stopped. And his breathing changed. And his arm tightened around her. Not pulling. Not initiating. Holding. Holding like a man who just found something he'd been convinced was lost.

She said they lay there for about two minutes.

Neither of them said anything else.

Neither of them moved.

Neither of them tried to turn it into anything.

His chest against her back. His arm around her. His hand on her stomach held by both of hers. Both of them breathing.

That's it.

That's the whole thing.

Two minutes of a man holding his wife in the dark with his hand on her stomach.

That's what they both described to me as the most intimate experience of their nineteen-year marriage.

Not a vacation. Not a wedding. Not a night of passion. Not any of the things that are supposed to be the peaks of a marriage.

Two minutes of being held.

After three years of not being held.

By a man whose hand was shaking because the reaching was that frightening and that necessary.

I asked him about it on our next Zoom call. Separately. Before the couples session.

I said, "What happened in your body when she said 'stay'?"

He was quiet for a long time.

Then he said, "Something melted."

He couldn't elaborate much more than that. He's not a man who has a lot of language for internal experience. But he said, "I've been holding something in my chest for three years. Maybe longer. And when she rolled toward me instead of away from me, and she took my hand and put it on her stomach and said that one word, the thing in my chest melted. I don't know what it was. But it's been there for years and it melted in about ten seconds."

He said, "I didn't know my hand was shaking until she told you. But I believe it. Because I was terrified. I was terrified she was going to pull away again. And I knew if she pulled away one more time I was never going to reach again. That was going to be the last one. And she didn't pull away. She came toward me. And the direction of her body told me something that no words could have told me."

I said, "What did it tell you?"

He said, "That I'm still welcome there."

That I'm still welcome there.

That's what the two minutes were about.

Not s*x. Not desire. Not passion. Not attraction.

Welcome.

The experience of a man reaching for the safest place he knows and discovering that the safest place still wants him there.

After three years of believing it didn't.

That's what closeness bids are about.

That's what the hand on the waist is reaching for.

That's what the pull in bed is asking.

That's what the hug that lasts too long is saying.

"Am I still welcome there?"

And the answer to that question, delivered not in words but in the direction of a body in the dark, is the thing that determines whether a man stays open or closes permanently.

She rolled toward him.

That's the answer.

That's the whole answer.

Not a conversation. Not an apology. Not a twelve-step repair plan.

A body moving toward a reaching hand instead of away from it.

Two minutes of holding in the dark.

And a one-word sentence that told a shaking man that home was still open.

"Stay."

If you take one thing from everything I've written about bids and closeness and the physical dimension of marriage, let it be this.

The next time his hand finds your hip in the dark, move toward it.

Not away.

Toward.

And if you can, hold the hand.

And if you can, say the word.

And give him two minutes of knowing that the safest place on earth didn't close while he wasn't looking.

Two minutes.

That's all it takes to bring a man back from three years of silence.

Not therapy. Not a conversation. Not a weekend away.

Two minutes of being welcome.

In the dark.

In the bed you've been sharing but not sharing.

Let him back in.

He's been waiting at the door with a shaking hand for longer than you know.

100 Truths a Marriage Counselor Wishes Every Couple Knew Before the First Session
The Truths About Why You're Actually Here
1. You didn't come here because of the fight last Tuesday.
2. You came here because of a thousand Tuesdays before that one.
3. The presenting problem is almost never the problem.
4. The thing you're arguing about is rarely the thing you're arguing about.
5. You've been lonely in this marriage longer than you've admitted.
6. So has the person sitting next to you.
7. One of you has been quietly planning an exit for a while.
8. The other one has been quietly hoping you'd stop.
9. You're not here to be right. You're here because being right hasn't worked.
10. If you came here to win, you've already lost.
The Truths About What You Brought With You
11. You married your mother. Or your father. Or both.
12. You married the wound you haven't finished with.
13. The things that drive you craziest about them are usually old business.
14. You're reacting to your spouse and to someone from thirty years ago at the same time.
15. Your nervous system doesn't know the difference.
16. Neither does theirs.
17. Most fights in a marriage are two frightened children in adult bodies.
18. You didn't choose them by accident.
19. You chose someone who would bring the wound up so you could finally look at it.
20. They chose you for the same reason.
The Truths About Communication
21. You don't have a communication problem. You have a safety problem.
22. Nobody opens up to someone who feels dangerous to them.
23. Being right is not the same as being heard.
24. Being heard is not the same as being agreed with.
25. Most couples don't listen. They wait.
26. Most couples don't talk. They deliver verdicts.
27. The tone you use with them is the tone they learn to brace against.
28. You've been teaching each other how to avoid you for years.
29. You are both fluent in each other's worst self by now.
30. You've forgotten how to speak to the best of each other.
The Truths About Fighting
31. Every couple fights. The healthy ones fight cleaner and repair faster.
32. It's not conflict that ends marriages. It's contempt.
33. Eye-rolling is a warning sign. So is the sigh.
34. So is the silence that goes on too long after.
35. Stonewalling is not peace. It's a slow-motion leaving.
36. When you shut them out, you teach them to stop reaching.
37. When you punish them for reaching, they eventually stop.
38. Criticism is not feedback. Criticism is character assassination.
39. Defensiveness is just fear in a suit and tie.
40. The fight after the fight is always the real one.
The Truths About Repair
41. Nothing predicts the future of a marriage more than how you repair.
42. Couples who repair badly don't last, even if the original hurts were small.
43. Couples who repair well can survive enormous hurts.
44. "I'm sorry, but" is not an apology.
45. "I'm sorry you feel that way" is not an apology.
46. "I'm sorry I was late, you always make a big deal out of nothing" is not an apology.
47. A real apology has no escape hatch in it.
48. A real apology names the thing.
49. A real apology doesn't ask to be forgiven before the other person is ready.
50. A real apology is the beginning of the repair, not the end.
The Truths About S*x and Intimacy
51. The s*x problem is almost never a s*x problem.
52. It's a resentment problem wearing s*x clothes.
53. You can't be emotionally shut out all week and physically open at night.
54. Desire follows safety. Not the other way around.
55. The lowest-desire partner sets the pace. That's biology, not punishment.
56. Chasing someone who's pulling away makes them pull further.
57. Your partner is not withholding. They're protecting themselves from something they haven't been able to name yet.
58. The bedroom is the scoreboard for the rest of the marriage.
59. If you want more in the bedroom, look at what's happening in the kitchen.
60. Most couples wait until the intimacy is nearly gone before they ask for help.
The Truths About What You Don't See
61. Your partner is lonelier than you think.
62. Your partner has been trying to tell you something for years.
63. You've been missing it because it doesn't sound like how you would've said it.
64. Your partner has a private sadness you haven't noticed.
65. Your partner is tired in a way they haven't explained.
66. Your partner has been bracing for the next version of you that hurts them.
67. Your partner remembers things you said that you don't.
68. They replay them at night when they can't sleep.
69. You do the same to them.
70. Both of you are walking around with a file of evidence against the other.
The Truths About What Each of You Needs
71. One of you needs to feel wanted. The other needs to feel safe.
72. One of you needs to feel seen. The other needs to feel trusted.
73. One of you pursues. The other withdraws.
74. This is not a flaw in either of you. It's the dance.
75. The pursuer is not needy. The pursuer is terrified of being left.
76. The withdrawer is not cold. The withdrawer is terrified of being consumed.
77. When the pursuer slows down, the withdrawer can finally come forward.
78. When the withdrawer stays, the pursuer can finally rest.
79. Most couples never learn each other's fear language.
80. They only learn each other's attack language.
The Truths About the Marriage Itself
81. Your marriage has a third presence in the room. It's not either of you.
82. The marriage has its own nervous system now.
83. You have been feeding it or starving it for years.
84. Most couples don't kill their marriage. They neglect it to death.
85. A marriage dies by inches, not by blows.
86. The day the marriage ended in your heart was probably years before either of you admitted it.
87. Or it hasn't ended yet, and you're here to find out.
88. There's no neutral in a long relationship. You're either moving toward each other or away from each other.
89. Every day you don't repair is a day the distance gets a little more familiar.
90. Familiar distance is how couples end up as roommates.
The Truths About What Comes Next
91. Therapy is not a referee. I'm not here to decide who's right.
92. I'm here to help you see what you can't see while you're inside of it.
93. Both of you will feel misunderstood by me at some point. That means it's working.
94. This will get harder before it gets easier. That's not a sign of failure.
95. Some of what you'll learn about yourself will be hard to sit with.
96. Some of what you'll learn about each other will be harder.
97. Not every marriage survives this work. The honest ones do.
98. Some couples discover they want to stay. Some discover they want to leave.
99. Either way, you'll leave here clearer than you came in.
100. The goal is not to save the marriage. The goal is to tell the truth. If the truth wants the marriage, the marriage will come back.

27. The first time one of you feels like the other's child about money.

28. The first secret credit card.

29. The first secret savings account.

30. The first time you discover a number you weren't supposed to know.

The Moments Around Children

31. The moment you find out you're pregnant and see each other's faces.

32. The moment you find out you can't be pregnant and see each other's faces.

33. The first night home with the baby.

34. The first time one of you goes back to work and the other doesn't know how to be alone with the child.

35. The first fight about whose life changed more.

36. The first time you look at them and think, "I don't recognize us anymore."

37. The first time the child becomes the third person in every conversation you used to have alone.

38. The first time you realize the child has replaced the marriage as the center.

39. The first time one of you says "we need a night away" and the other doesn't want to.

40. The first time you disagree about how to raise them and you both mean it.

The Moments Around Family of Origin

41. The first time a parent of theirs crosses a line and you watch to see what they do.

42. The first time they watch you do the same.

43. The first time you choose them over a parent, and the parent never forgives it.

44. The first time they choose their parent over you, and you never forget it.

45. The first time a sibling of theirs becomes a problem you can't solve together.

46. The first time you realize their family is in the marriage too.

47. The first time you feel ganged up on at a family dinner.

48. The first time you go home and they comfort you instead of defending their side.

49. The first time they go home and you don't.

50. The first holiday where you stop pretending and start surviving.

The Moments Around Work

51. The first promotion that takes them away from you more than you expected.

52. The first job loss that shakes who one of you thought you were.

53. The first time work becomes the place one of you feels more alive than at home.

54. The first time a coworker of theirs gets a version of them you don't anymore.

55. The first time you're more excited to tell a colleague something than your spouse.

56. The first time they come home and you realize you didn't miss them.

57. The first time the commute becomes the best part of the day.

58. The first time you realize one of you has been working late to avoid the house.

83. The first lie you tell that wasn't necessary.

84. The first time you defend someone over them to a friend.

85. The first time you say something cruel about them to someone who's going to remember it.

88. The first time you wonder if they've been keeping something from you.

The Things You Meant to Say About Who They Were
1. "I noticed everything you did, even when I didn't say it."

7. "I saw you, even when I pretended I didn't."
8. "You were more than I deserved and I knew it."
9. "You were the best part of my story."
10. "You were the person I wanted to be more like."

11. "Thank you for everything I never thanked you for."
12. "I know what it cost you."
13. "I saw the late nights."
14. "I saw the early mornings."
15. "I saw you carry things I didn't want to carry."
16. "I knew you were tired and I should've stepped in more."
17. "You kept this family alive."
18. "You were the reason we got through that year."
19. "I watched you hold it all together and I never told you I saw it."
20. "I should've been kinder about all the ways you showed up."

21. "You were beautiful to me, every single year."
22. "I loved your hands."
23. "I loved the way you laughed with your whole face."
24. "I loved the little sound you made in your sleep."
25. "I loved the weight of you next to me."
26. "I loved how you smelled after a shower."
27. "I loved the way your eyes changed when you looked at me."
28. "I never stopped being attracted to you. I just stopped telling you."
29. "Your body was the one I wanted to come home to."
30. "You were the one. Always."

31. "I loved you more than I ever let you see."
32. "I felt it, every day, even when I was quiet."
33. "I was in awe of you and I let it sound like criticism."

35. "You made me feel safe in a way nothing else ever did."
36. "I was happy. I should've told you I was happy."
37. "I wasn't bored. I was just comfortable. There's a difference."
38. "I loved our life. I loved our small, ordinary, unremarkable life."
39. "I loved you in ways I didn't have words for."
40. "I never got tired of you. I just got tired."

41. "I'm sorry for the sharpness in my voice."
42. "I'm sorry I didn't listen when it mattered most."
43. "I'm sorry I made you ask twice."
44. "I'm sorry for the nights I rolled away instead of toward."
45. "I'm sorry for the silence I used as a weapon."
46. "I'm sorry I didn't say yes more often."
47. "I'm sorry I didn't show up the way you needed."

83. "You were the person I couldn't wait to tell."
84. "You were my first call and my last thought."
85. "You were the reason any of it mattered."
86. "You made me who I am."
87. "I wouldn't have survived the hard years without you."
88. "I don't know who I am without you, and I'm finding out now."
89. "You were the best thing I ever did with my life."
90. "Everything good in me came from loving you."

97. "I would say yes to the version of you I kept asking to change."
98. "I would love you louder."

My Parents 
In our classes in The Relationship Lab, we learn a lot of things from Derek Hart  in the 30min lectures before individual sessions. One thing he said is that most Relationship issues begin in the first 6 months. 
I cringed. 
My parents issues began on Day 3 of their Honeymoon.  Somehow Mom learned that Dad had had sex with other women, and she was angry because he said he had never been married. He said, "I told you the truth, I haven't." She very heatedly said "You knew what I meant." 
She felt betrayed.
If you understand religion and their views about sex outside of marriage, particularly the cult I was raised in, the same one my Mom was raised in, that my Dad married into, you see how much shame she had now for marrying a man she thought was "pure".
Besides the fact this triggered her deep insecurities that Dad didn't choose her because he loved her, she had been chosen because she was the best on a list.
You see, my Dad made a list of all available single woman in the cult and all their attributes. He spent 2 years visiting each assembly and getting to know people. There was a woman named Helen that he really was attracted to, but she wore pants and my Mom didn't; since pants weren't allowed in the cult, that ruled out Helen. Dad always told Mom that he chose her from the list, but Mom I guess never felt chosen. She felt qualified because of a list of his prerequisites like Bible knowledge and desire to have kids, because he possibly wanted to be a Preacher. He had gone to Biola Bible College in California, but dropped out when he learned the cult didn't care about any degree.
She was so angry, she didn't speak to him the next 3 days of their Honeymoon. 
Can you imagine how punished he felt?
My heart grieves for my Dad. 
And my Mom. 
That's some deep intense pain. From my witnessing of things, I don't believe it ever got repaired. 
I don't know what changed. I don't know, or maybe just don't remember what she said that made her tell Dad she forgave him, but she really didn't. She made him "pay" the rest of his life.
My Dad was 31 and my Mom 19 when they got married, after 2 years of dating, in 1975.
She stopped her BCPs to get pregnant because she didn't want him to leave her. Dad wasn't ready for kids yet. He wanted time alone. I was born 1.5 years after they were married. I am 9 months old in this photo.
My Dad admitted to me later in life, at age 14, that he really never wanted kids. He only had them because Mom wanted them. All he wanted to do was work and study the Bible. He didn't want to be a Preacher because that was too much pressure and authority. But Mom wanted him to be one. So she put pressures on him to address "issues" he had with the church leadership, particularly with modesty and hypocrisy she saw. 
In one of these meetings, "The Men" (term for those in leadership) asked my Dad some questions about why this was such an issue with him, he told them about my Mom's concerns and his responsibility to protect his home.
Ohhhhh shit.
Wrong thing to say. 
When she learned of this, she chastised him and beat him over the head, micromanaging his every move. If they went for coffee, which was a rare thing, maybe they did 4 times in my childhood, she would demand why he looked at the waitresses butt as she walked away from the table or try to see down her blouse when she poured them a cup of coffee. This escalated to "The Men" having a "Private Conversation" with my Mom without my Dad present, which defied their laws of headship in the church, and when they questioned her about her concerns being brought to "The Men" through my Dad, she enlightened them that my Dad had a problem lusting after other woman.
Now a war had begun between them. A war that Dad never stood a chance to win. Not once.
In 1993, the modesty issues became so great, my Mom demanded my Dad "make a statement". He had told "The Men" that if things didn't change, he would have to take a stand. He chose to do that June 13th,1993 when Hans & Shelley got married. When the bride walked down the isle, with a neckline "too low", we walked out.
And yes, I as a 16 year old daughter knew what was likely to happen, but was told to not make a scene, just observe Daddy out of the corner of my eye, instructed to not make eye contact with anyone, and simply follow suit. We marched out with out heads held high, beeming that we were doing a "righteous act of God". 
My heart broke that day.
Tears slid down my face as we drove home.
I felt so empty inside. Worse than I ever had, and I didn't know why.
The following Friday Night, my Mom answered the phone to some lady telling her that she was pregnant by her husband. Mom went into shock and struggled to ask questions, and the lady hung up. We didn't have caller ID back then on rotary dialed phones. My Mom went into a full-blown rage. She already had been suspicious and accusing my Dad of having an affair. Now she had proof.
The irony? 
She opened the phonebook and called every R Gilbert, Randall Gilbert, Randy Gilbert, or Russell Gilbert and asked if they were married, how long they had been married, and if their relationship was solid because she got this call and she knew it couldn't be her husband as he would never have an affair on her!!!
I am not fucking joking with you.
The situation with Dad got worse, way worse, and she kicked him out of the bedroom to sleep on the couch. When that didn't give her enough room or feeling of safety, she made him sleep at work, on the floor in a sleeping bag. When Dad's boss caught him doing this, he put a stop to it. Dad & Mom then bought a mini-motorhome and Dad slept in that on work property, with the pretense we were eventually going to travel to the assemblies, but it was to give Dad a place to live. 
We never did travel.
We would go every weekend and take Dad groceries and gather his laundry and take it back home and wash it. 
After a period of time and no progress in the relationship, with lots more fights, Mom told Dad we were not going to do anything for him - he was on his own. This meant when Dad came to wash his clothes each weekend, we had to be gone because Mom wouldn't want to see him.
She then began threatening divorce. Pitting us kids against each other when my brother wanted to live with Dad, but us girls would get no choice because she already never left us alone with my Dad as it was, even before all of this. 
I questioned my Mom if she really loved my Dad. I asked her what evidence she had beyond the phone call that I believed was a prank, likely by girlfriends of Shelley. I made her squirm so deeply that she told me to stop asking questions and that I would understand "when I became an adult".  I risked being beaten to fight for their relationship. I said some things that made her utterly hate me and lash out in the worst rage I ever saw, until I was raped at age 17.
My parents eventually figured things out and Dad moved back in, but there is more to the story of the back and worth crazy making chaos.
No easy way to write all of this painful life I have witnessed and lived. But it is the reason why I swore I didn't want to get married for a long time because I didn't want a relationship like my parents had.
It is what drove me to read relationship books and do courses and work on me long before a man came into my life. 
Yet as I sit with the question of where do I have "Shards of Sadness" stored in my body, I am finding some really difficult memories that had to be stuffed down to just get through them. There wasn't any room for someone to tend to me and the big feelings eating me alive. 
It also is very eye opening to review your life on this kind of level. 
To feel the oppression. To sense the deep level of obligation to follow rules. To uncover all the ways I had no choice. To see how many things I had to do like an adult in a child's body. To see how much was up to me. To feel the intense pressure. To observe the responsibility I had to figure it all out. To rise to the demands to succeed and not fail. To see how I never once felt safe. To recognize that nobody had my back. To see how I was not seen, heard and held and the depth of loneliness this created. To know how hurt and scared I was. To see how much of my life, the spirit within me, has been suffocating. 
I lay on my bed and hold little Omar and sob, sob out layers of shards of sadness, releasing this pent up grief. 
It's difficult to discuss "the rest of the story" like Paul Harvey could do. Maybe because there is no good ending.

In 1993, the modesty issues became so great, my Mom demanded my Dad "make a statement". He had told "The Men" that if things didn't change, he would have to take a stand. He chose to do that June 13th,1993 when Hans & Shelley got married. When the bride walked down the isle, with a neckline "too low", we walked out.

And yes, I as a 16 year old daughter knew what was likely to happen, but was told to not make a scene, just observe Daddy out of the corner of my eye, instructed to not make eye contact with anyone, and simply follow suit. We marched out with out heads held high, beeming that we were doing a "righteous act of God".

My heart broke that day.

Tears slid down my face as we drove home.

I felt so empty inside. Worse than I ever had, and I didn't know why.

The following Friday Night, my Mom answered the phone to some lady telling her that she was pregnant by her husband. Mom went into shock and struggled to ask questions, and the lady hung up. We didn't have caller ID back then on rotary dialed phones. My Mom went into a full-blown rage. She already had been suspicious and accusing my Dad of having an affair. Now she had proof.

The irony?

She opened the phonebook and called every R Gilbert, Randall Gilbert, Randy Gilbert, or Russell Gilbert and asked if they were married, how long they had been married, and if their relationship was solid because she got this call and she knew it couldn't be her husband as he would never have an affair on her!!!

I am not fucking joking with you.

The situation with Dad got worse, way worse, and she kicked him out of the bedroom to sleep on the couch. When that didn't give her enough room or feeling of safety, she made him sleep at work, on the floor in a sleeping bag. When Dad's boss caught him doing this, he put a stop to it. Dad & Mom then bought a mini-motorhome and Dad slept in that on work property, with the pretense we were eventually going to travel to the assemblies, but it was to give Dad a place to live.

We never did travel.

We would go every weekend and take Dad groceries and gather his laundry and take it back home and wash it.

After a period of time and no progress in the relationship, with lots more fights, Mom told Dad we were not going to do anything for him - he was on his own. This meant when Dad came to wash his clothes each weekend, we had to be gone because Mom wouldn't want to see him.

She then began threatening divorce. Pitting us kids against each other when my brother wanted to live with Dad, but us girls would get no choice because she already never left us alone with my Dad as it was, even before all of this.

I questioned my Mom if she really loved my Dad. I asked her what evidence she had beyond the phone call that I believed was a prank, likely by girlfriends of Shelley. I made her squirm so deeply that she told me to stop asking questions and that I would understand "when I became an adult".  I risked being beaten to fight for their relationship. I said some things that made her utterly hate me and lash out in the worst rage I ever saw, until I was raped at age 17.

My parents eventually figured things out and Dad moved back in, but there is more to the story of the back and worth crazy making chaos.

No easy way to write all of this painful life I have witnessed and lived. But it is the reason why I swore I didn't want to get married for a long time because I didn't want a relationship like my parents had.

It is what drove me to read relationship books and do courses and work on me long before a man came into my life.

Yet as I sit with the question of where do I have "Shards of Sadness" stored in my body, I am finding some really difficult memories that had to be stuffed down to just get through them. There wasn't any room for someone to tend to me and the big feelings eating me alive.

It also is very eye opening to review your life on this kind of level.

To feel the oppression. To sense the deep level of obligation to follow rules. To uncover all the ways I had no choice. To see how many things I had to do like an adult in a child's body. To see how much was up to me. To feel the intense pressure. To observe the responsibility I had to figure it all out. To rise to the demands to succeed and not fail. To see how I never once felt safe. To recognize that nobody had my back. To see how I was not seen, heard and held and the depth of loneliness this created. To know how hurt and scared I was. To see how much of my life, the spirit within me, has been suffocating.

I lay on my bed and hold little Omar and sob, sob out layers of shards of sadness, releasing this pent up grief.

It's difficult to discuss "the rest of the story" like Paul Harvey could do. Maybe because there is no good ending.
